5-Bullet Friday

The latest from author and investor Tim Ferriss

Hi All!

Welcome to a very special holiday edition of 5-Bullet Friday!

I dislike shopping, but I do love finding the perfect gift. Alas, damn adults seem to have everything or need nothing. So… If you’re having trouble thinking up great options, below are a few goodies that deliver.

I use all of these products on a daily or weekly basis. I’ve also recommended each to my close friends and family.

I also reached out to some of my favorite companies to get special deals for subscribers. Each sponsored bullet is indicated with a star at the end of it, just like this sentence.* Literally everything I mention below lives in my home somewhere, including the sponsored gems.

Happy holidays to you and yours! 🙂

The most Japanese thing on my mind

Hibi Box of 30 Incense Matches (Amazon, Ameico, Urban Natural). Thanks to the inimitable writer Dan Levy, perhaps best known as David Rose on Schitt’s Creek, for introducing me to these via “10 Things Dan Levy Can’t Live Without | GQ.”

Air purifier I’m loving

Jaspr Air Scrubber. I’ve tried a lot of air purifiers over the years, and there are a handful of great options. This is the best combination of function and aesthetics that I’ve found. I love the design and am buying more units for my family. It’s quiet enough to sleep next to, and it’s beautiful enough to put in your living room. Thank you to Dr. Tommy Wood for introducing me to Jaspr.

Supplement I’m taking every morning

Momentous Creatine. I’ve relied on Momentous for years, and they’re my default because I trust them with sourcing, testing, and labeling. Their creatine is a daily staple. I typically aim for five (5) grams per day, both for cognitive function and the well-studied effects on strength and muscle. Their upgraded creatine is 99.99% pure, manufactured in a pharmaceutical facility, and screened for heavy metals, microplastics, and PFAS. If you take anything daily, you need to have complete confidence in purity.

Like all Momentous products, their creatine is NSF Certified for Sport®, meaning independently tested for purity, safety, and label accuracy. For an early Black Friday, save 40% on your first subscription order with code BFCM, which you need to apply at checkout.*

Book I’m gifting

Seeing Silence: The Beauty of the World’s Most Quiet Places by Pete McBride. The sublime is easy to find in this book, whether you simply flip through the gorgeous photos or do a deep dive into the prose. Pete McBride, a National Geographic photographer and filmmaker, shot the images across all seven continents, from Everest to Antarctica. The foreword is by Bill McKibben, a renowned environmentalist and journalist. The prologue is by Erik Weihenmayer, the first blind person to summit Everest.

Tiny gadget in my backpack

Sennheiser Pro Audio Condenser Microphone. This lav mic plugs straight into a USB-C iPhone and makes on-the-go recordings sound much better than any built-in laptop or phone mic. It’s remarkable what quality you can get, especially if paired with the Ferrite app that allows you to record high-fidelity audio straight on your iPhone.

Book that I’m rereading and gifting

Art Is the Highest Form of Hope. Special thanks to the amazing Susan Cain for sending this beautiful book to me, which is full of bite-size philosophy and much-needed imagination. These days, a little light goes a long way. From the description: “Advice, strong opinions, and personal revelations by the world’s greatest artists—exclusively researched for this new book.”

Sleep technology I’m using

. I’ve been sleeping on an for years, and the new Pod 6 is the first version where the hardware fully gets out of the way, with a Hub that’s 50% smaller than the Pod 5. The new thermal engine reaches your set temperature 20% faster, and the cover includes 9x more biometric sensors for tracking sleep stages, HRV, heart rate, and more. Autopilot takes those signals and automatically adjusts the bed’s settings throughout the night, creating optimal conditions for better sleep. Members report up to 34% more deep sleep and a 32% average increase in sleep quality scores. It’s also a great gift for couples. Each side runs independently, so if one sleeps warm and one sleeps cool, everyone can be happy. The Pod 6 , the lowest starting price in the product’s history. Go to to save $700 on the Pod 6 and Base in Queen, King, or Cal King. Eight Sleep currently ships within the USA, Canada, the UK, select countries in the EU, and Australia. This special offer is valid through November 30. Individual results may vary.*

One pan I use for nearly everything

has become the one pan I use for practically everything, and it is my go-to in the kitchen. Its patent-pending NoCo® technology creates a coating-free, nonstick effect and is made without PFAS (including PTFE and PFOA), lead, and cadmium.

With a titanium interior, an aluminum core, and a stainless-steel exterior, you get the high-heat searing of stainless or cast iron with the easy release of nonstick. now offers this same technology across its full Titanium Pro Cookware sets. Their Black Friday/Cyber Monday event is the perfect time to try them. . Go to to take advantage of this special offer. With a 100-day trial, you can try it completely risk-free.*

How I’m finally getting in more Zone 2 cardio

M3i Studio Indoor Bike | Keiser. I’ve tried a lot of stationary bikes, including very fancy indoor trainers, for getting in Zone 2 cardio and VO2 max training. I hate nearly all of them. This M3i is not fancy, but it does allow me to elevate the handlebars enough so that (1) I’m not bumping my thighs into my stomach like a one-hour Heimlich maneuver, and (2) it doesn’t make my low back incredibly grumpy. The controls are simple, it’s durable, I don’t use an app with it, and, so far, it’s the only indoor bike that I’ve used consistently. And more good news: it’s found in a lot of commercial gyms.

Set-it-and-forget-it robot vacuum I’m loving

Matic. This is the closest thing to a house that cleans itself. It’s quiet enough that you forget it’s running, and it’s smart enough to leave your charging cables alone. The reviewers agree: WIRED gave it a rare 10/10, and to quote The Verge, “This WALL-E-like bot fixes the stuff every other robot vacuum gets wrong.” When I asked my audience on social media about Matic, the response was euphorically positive, and I got a flood of texts from 10+ friends who are converts. Fans include Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke, my friends Kevin Rose and Naval Ravikant, and many others. Matic sold out last Black Friday, so order early. Go to MaticRobots.com/Tim for $400 off the Matic Serene Bundle or $300 off the Matic Bundle. Order before November 30th for delivery before Christmas (U.S. only).*

Tool that’s always on me

ProBody Pilates Ball. Yep, it’s a Pilates ball, but I don’t use it for Pilates. I keep it deflated in my backpack, and if I need lumbar support or butt padding anywhere on the road (in hotels, restaurants, airplanes, etc.), I give it literally 2–3 puffs of partial inflation and voilà! Deflated, this is small enough to fold up and stick in a jacket or jeans pocket.

What I’m drinking in the mornings

Brodo Bone Broth. Broth is one of the easiest ways to get quality protein and nutrition first thing in the morning. For the past two months, I’ve been having 1–2 Brodo packets per day, often simply poured into a mug and microwaved for 60 seconds. Brodo was founded by Chef Marco Canora, who was one of my primary teachers in The 4-Hour Chef. Marco is the real deal. He won a James Beard Award for Best Chef: New York City, which is like winning an Oscar in the food world, and he has plenty of other awards and accolades to boot. My favorite flavors so far are Tuscan Sun and Tom Yum, which are included in their sampler box.

Headphones I’m loving for music while working and writing

Focal Bathys wireless, noise-cancelling headphones (Headphones.com, Amazon, B&H). These are my current default headphones if working at a coffee shop or busy co-working spot.

A grab bag of fun recommendations

The Way. This is an easy one. I’ve explored a lot of meditation practices over the years. My current hands-down favorite, and the easiest way to get back in the habit, is The Way, taught by Zen Master Henry Shukman. Here are 30 days for free, no credit card required.

Premium MGO 1000+ Mānuka Honey from Manukora. I love this smooth and creamy Mānuka honey. I sometimes use it before bed to help with sleep, combined in hot water with a bit of apple cider vinegar. The exact recipe is courtesy of the late Dr. Seth Roberts (2 tablespoons of apple cider vinegar and 1 tablespoon honey, stirred into 1 cup of hot water).

Coyote the card game (46% off), which I co-created with Exploding Kittens. If you have any kids or relatives aged 8–15, you can start playing—and laughing—in minutes. Think charades + hot potato + brain fun.

Awareness: Conversations with the Masters by Anthony de Mello. Nonfiction, 184 pages. I’ve gifted this at least 50 times, so I’ll keep gifting it.

And there you go! 17 of my favorite things that make great holiday gifts. I love them all and hope you do too.

Have a wonderful weekend and wonderful holiday season, everyone!

Much love to you and yours,

Tim

items.author: Tim Ferriss
items.contentHtml:
This one is a little different. For a change, I’m the one in the hot seat. I was interviewed on stage by Zuhairah Washington, a senior vice president at Zillow. There were a lot of questions around AI, and how to be robust or anti-fragile in a fast-changing world. This was from a live event in Las Vegas with more than 3,000 real estate professionals in the audience. We get into what to automate in the age of AI and, more importantly, what to eliminate first; how to use AI as a strategist in your pocket; why booking a mini-retirement forces you to fix your systems; fear-setting; why I try to diversify my identity; the books I’ve reread the most; and much, much more. You don’t need to be in real estate to use any of it.

Please enjoy!

This episode is brought to you by:

  • Gusto simple and easy payroll, HR, and benefits platform used by 500,000+ businesses (Get 3 months of free payroll at Gusto.com/Tim!)
  • Incogni, which removes your personal data from the web, helping shield you from fraud, scams, and identity theft (BFCM deal! Save 60% on an annual plan with code TIM at Incogni.com/Tim.)

items.title: Did men evolve to fight each other? Scientists can’t agree.
items.summary: Anthropologist David Puts was a graduate student trying to decide on a dissertation topic when inspiration struck him at a mall food court. While eating a cheeseburger, he overheard two men behind him speaking in unusually deep voices. “I turned around to see what was…
items.author: Clarissa Brincat
items.contentHtml:
Anthropologist David Puts was a graduate student trying to decide on a dissertation topic when inspiration struck him at a mall food court. While eating a cheeseburger, he overheard two men behind him speaking in unusually deep voices. “I turned around to see what was happening, and there was a young, good-looking female nearby,” Puts said. 

His initial thought was that human males evolved deep voices to attract women, but he soon began to wonder whether they might also help establish dominance over other men: “A deep voice is intimidating — think about Darth Vader.” So, for his dissertation, Puts tested both possibilities. What he found surprised him.

Women tended to prefer a deeper, more masculine voice, but the effect of voice pitch on their ratings of male attractiveness wasn’t very big. Meanwhile, the effect of voice pitch on men’s judgment of another man’s dominance and fighting ability was 15 times bigger. 

The unexpected result led Puts to revisit earlier studies. He noticed that “the literature was really biased towards female mate choice” as a reason for deep voices, while findings related to male-male competition seemed to get “pushed under the rug.” This realization became the foundation for Puts’ theory that competition between males for mates, also known as “male-male contest competition,” may have played a larger role in the evolution of the human male than scientists had previously recognized. 

Puts, now a professor of anthropology and psychology at Pennsylvania State University, has continued to think about and develop this theory ever since the seed for it was planted in his brain in that mall food court in the early 2000s. Although he said he is mostly driven by a fascination with human nature, there’s more to his theory than pure academic interest. He believes that evolutionary understanding might help explain aspects of male psychology and inform positive social change.

Competition between males for mates may have played a larger role in the evolution of the human male than scientists had previously recognized. 

In November 2026, Puts and graduate student Saeed Koohgard published a review titled “The deadliest primate: Contest competition and the evolution of human males” in the Journal of Human Evolution. The review links modern-day male characteristics, including physical aggression, to male-male contest competition among our ancestors — a controversial theory. 

“This [idea] is supported primarily by evolutionary psychologists,” said Agustín Fuentes, an anthropologist at Princeton University. “Most anthropologists do not support this at all.” He said that those interested in understanding male violence should read the paper “but recognize this is a very teeny slice and a very biased view” in the midst of the wider anthropological, psychological, and sociological literature.

The ancestral mating system

For at least the past 150,000 years, the effective number of reproducing women at any given time has been roughly three times that of men, according to a 2015 study looking at Y-chromosome and mitochondrial DNA. This may reflect male invaders displacing local men, but Puts and Koohgard think it points to a polygynous mating system, where some men fathered children with several partners, while many other men had no children at all. They believe that our ancestors lived in single-male family units embedded within larger bands, as hamadryas and gelada baboons do.

This setup meant that “our male ancestors intensely fought, threatened, and killed each other to monopolize mates,” Puts said. 

In their review, Puts and Koohgard cite several findings that are consistent with their theory. For example, in a study of Eurasian Neanderthal and early modern human remains from 80,000 to 20,000 years ago, men were about six times more likely than women to show signs of head injuries. Furthermore, a study of homicide data spanning two decades and four locations (Canada, England/Wales, Chicago, and Detroit) found that unrelated men kill each other 27 times more often than unrelated women kill each other.

“A lot of male mating success may have had to do with just the plausible threat of aggression.”

David Puts

Puts and Koohgard also point to several features of the male anatomy as complementary evidence of male-male contest competition. Men are larger than women on average, with 61% more muscle mass overall and 75% more upper-body muscle mass. Size and muscularity are traits that help win fights. Men also have what biologists call “badges of status,” such as facial hair and deep voices. These traits signal dominance and help to win resources, such as mates, without engaging in costly fights.

Puts and Koohgard argue that, together, these lines of evidence suggest that male-male contest competition has played an important role in shaping men’s behaviors, including physical aggression. People might hear this theory and misread it as a justification of male violence, Puts said, but he stresses that understanding evolutionary influences is not the same as condoning violence — the idea that something being natural or evolved makes it justified is what’s known as the “naturalistic fallacy.” 

Although Puts and Koohgard’s theory centers on the idea that aggression helped our male ancestors to win mates, Puts doubts that the most violent males were ever the most successful. “There are huge costs to violence,” he said, “and if you’re living in a group and you’re a belligerent loose cannon, you’re likely to be killed or at least ostracized.” Instead, Puts thinks that “a lot of male mating success may have had to do with just the plausible threat of aggression.”

Clashing views

Fuentes is not convinced by Puts and Koohgard’s theory. The claim of a polygynous ancestral mating system is “highly disputed,” he said, and the “vast majority of geneticists who work in this area” conclude that our ancestors were most likely monogamous, with some mild polygyny. 

He accused Puts and Koohgard of selectively citing works that support their theory while leaving out research that complicates or challenges it — their paper doesn’t mention Nam Kim and Marc Kissel’s book Emergent Warfare in Our Evolutionary Past, for example. That book frames violence as complex and dependent on multiple conditions — not simply an evolved male strategy. Citing it would make it “more complicated to make the argument that [they’re] making,” Fuentes said. 

However, Raymond Hames, an emeritus professor of anthropology at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln, praised Puts and Koohgard’s review as “very comprehensive.” He said the paper’s strength is that it tests several alternative hypotheses that might explain male traits, such as sexual division of labor, and finds them a poor fit. His only objection is to the paper’s title: “The deadliest primate.” “Although we are violent, we are not the deadliest of all primates,” Hames said. Red-tailed monkeys, blue monkeys, and red-fronted lemurs are all far more likely than humans to kill their own kind, according to a 2016 study. 

“Humans didn’t evolve to punch each other — our hands are horrible at it. Our bodies actually aren’t that great for violence, but our minds are.”

Agustín Fuentes

With regard to Fuentes’ point, Hames thinks that warfare, or coalitionary violence, and one-on-one male violence aren’t interchangeable. One involves political competition over scarce resources, he said, while “the other one has to do with males striving for reproduction.”

In their review, Puts and Koohgard call out an erroneous figure on height differences by sex from Fuentes’ book Sex Is a Spectrum: The Biological Limits of the Binary. Fuentes concedes the error, which has since been fixed in the paperback edition, but said that Puts and Koohgard “ignore all the other data in my book that rejects their assertion.” He argues that men and women are not two fundamentally separate kinds of human, pointing to the fact that most bodily features — including organs such as the brain, heart, and kidneys — are not distinctly male or female.

Fuentes agrees with the point that Puts and Koohgard make about humans having evolved a capacity for incredible violence, but he believes “there is no genetic propensity for violence in males relative to females.” And while some researchers, most notably the evolutionary biologist David Carrier, argue that human hands evolved for punching, Fuentes believes that the human capacity for violence isn’t rooted in the body. “Humans didn’t evolve to punch each other — our hands are horrible at it,” he said. “Our bodies actually aren’t that great for violence, but our minds are.”

The questions worth asking

Hames agrees with Puts’ view that studying the roots of male violence can help reduce it. He said that understanding what motivates violence could help identify ways to “change the environment to reduce that motivation” and, hopefully, lower violence.

But Fuentes thinks they are asking the wrong question. In modern society, “most of the individuals who kill or rape are men, but the vast majority of men neither kill nor rape,” he said. Instead of asking “What’s the root of male violence?” he thinks researchers should ask, “Why do certain males do that and not others? In what context or situations do males act violently?”

Holly Dunsworth, a biological anthropologist at the University of Rhode Island, sees Puts and Koohgard’s paper as part of a wider trend of debating unknowable evolutionary causes. She questions the value of that work, while stopping short of saying it has none. 

Dunsworth said evolution is true but argued that the specific evolutionary causes of ancestral behaviors and traits can’t be known. “We have no systematic way of testing [Puts and Koohgard’s] idea against alternatives and for choosing the one that is closest to the truth,” she said. After years of study, Dunsworth is “very confident about what we don’t know and what we can’t know” — she has laid out her view in a book due out in June.

Instead of asking “What’s the root of male violence?” Fuentes thinks researchers should ask, “Why do certain males do that and not others? In what context or situations do males act violently?”

While anthropologists including Hames believe in uniformitarianism — a principle centered on the idea that the present is the key to the past — Dunsworth argues that knowing how evolution works does not mean we can identify the specific causes of evolutionary changes in the past. In her view, debating the details of Puts and Koohgard’s theory risks distracting from that fundamental uncertainty. She declined to offer alternative explanations, saying that would mean entering a debate “that will always be a debate.” 

“It’s always about who will win, whose argument is most preferred by most people, and sounds the most like common sense,” Dunsworth said. “That’s not what I’m interested in participating in.” 

Puts, on the other hand, is eager to debate. He thinks that male-male contest competition, underemphasized in the literature, may have been at least as important as — and perhaps more important than — female mate choice in human male evolution. However, he acknowledges that he may be wrong and sees scientific discussion as a way to improve understanding: “If I’m misunderstanding things, or there’s important evidence that I haven’t considered or my interpretation doesn’t make sense, I really want to know that.”

items.title: Apocalypse fears may be boosting Costco’s biz
items.summary: Nick Iluzada While everything else seemingly breaks down, the place you go to for free samples and toilet paper stays up. Costco is enjoying a panic-fueled sales bump following the Microsoft outage, the FAA ground stop, and “apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media,”…
items.author: Molly Liebergall
items.contentHtml:
While everything else seemingly breaks down, the place you go to for free samples and toilet paper stays up. Costco is enjoying a panic-fueled sales bump following the Microsoft outage, the FAA ground stop, and “apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media,” the financial institution Mizuho reported this week.

It’s like March 2020 anxiety all over again, except add the looming fear of AI wiping us all out:

  • As of Sunday, 21 of Costco’s 26 high-end generator models were sold out, per Mizuho.
  • Before that, Costco’s comparable US sales (excluding gasoline) rose 11% to 12% in the last week of October, compared with 6% to 7% in the previous three weeks, Mizuho estimated.
  • Toward the end of the month, members bought more rice, canned food, water, paper goods, generators, and batteries than usual, Costco’s CFO told Bloomberg.

But…all this started two weeks before the recent spate of outages, after the UK government urged the public to stockpile goods in case of an emergency and the Pentagon reportedly called for military bases to have 90 days’ worth of supplies on hand. Those warnings followed a streak of cyberattacks last month that created the nickname “Black October.”

Zoom out: Mizuho expects prepper-minded shoppers to lift sales at Home Depot, Lowe’s, and Sam’s Club, too. Yesterday, Walmart noted a jump in purchases of propane, bottled water, and camping gear.—ML

items.title: Ask Ethan: Do polonium radiohalos support a young Earth?
items.summary: One of the most beautiful things about science is that if even one single piece of robust evidence comes along that contradicts even our most deeply held ideas about reality, it means that our current way of thinking about things must be revised. The observations of Mercury’s…
items.author: Ethan Siegel
items.contentHtml:
One of the most beautiful things about science is that if even one single piece of robust evidence comes along that contradicts even our most deeply held ideas about reality, it means that our current way of thinking about things must be revised. The observations of Mercury’s orbit in the late 1800s led to the overthrow of Newtonian gravity; the observation that energy was quantized into discrete entities led to the birth of quantum physics; the observation of ultra-faint, variable stars in Andromeda led to the discovery of extragalactic objects and, soon after, to the expanding Universe. Wherever a seemingly contradictory observation occurs, there’s a chance for advancing our best scientific picture of how the Universe works.

We have to take immense care to make sure we don’t fool ourselves, but that applies in both directions. We have to make sure we don’t fool ourselves when it comes to accepting the established picture, but we must also make sure we don’t fool ourselves by believing flawed evidence that claims to undermine it. How is one to know what’s going on when different people who claim to be experts make inconsistent, contradictory assertions? That’s what Bob Brown wants to know, writing in to ask:

“I received this article — ‘Polonium Radiohalos: Strong Evidence Against Millions of Years’ — from a friend… I’m at a loss as to how anyone should explain to him how this scenario just isn’t possible. Any insights you can provide will be greatly appreciated.”

One of the hallmarks of the scientific enterprise is to be able to consider an idea, even an “out there” alternative idea, and subject it to rigorous scrutiny. If it holds up, it cannot be discarded, no matter how absurd it sounds. However, if it crumbles beneath the weight of evidence, it cannot be viable. Let’s take a good look at what’s going on with this new claim.

The conventional view of planet Earth is that it is, indeed, approximately 4.5 billion years old. The Sun and the Solar System itself is slightly older, while the Earth-Moon system was formed by a collision between two large protoplanets: a proto-Earth and a Mars-sized body named Theia. While many lines of evidence support an old Earth, including:

  • various layers of sedimentary rock with older metamorphic rock beneath them,
  • a fossil record dating back more than 3 billion years,
  • and our knowledge of solar physics, indicating the lifetime of the Sun,

the strongest evidence comes from radiometric dating: the measurements of elements and isotopes that arise from the radioactive decay of precursor elements that were present initially on our world.

By their very nature, minerals contain a wide variety of elements and isotopes: some of which are stable and others of which aren’t stable, with the unstable ones instead undergoing radioactive decay. Those decays often proceed in a chain: continuing until a final, stable product is reached. If you can know the initial concentration of the (parent) decaying element, the half-life of every element in the decay chain, and can measure the concentration of the (daughter) end product, you can calculate the age of the rock. Those are a lot of “ifs,” of course, but we’ve done that for Earth and for many other bodies in the Solar System, obtaining ages for Earth rocks in the billions of years and for several meteorites of around 4.55-4.56 billion years.

That’s the conventional view.

However, there’s a new assertion out by Jake Hebert, claiming that the conventional age of billions of years for the Earth is wrong, and that even millions of years is too long. Instead, he claims that radioisotope dating supports an age that’s just thousands of years old for the Earth: an age that’s consistent with the claims of biblical creationism. This specific claim is that one should look at rocks known as Phanerozoic granites, and at features — or inclusions — within them known as polonium radiohalos.

While Hebert notes that the conventional picture claims that these radiohaloes are typically under 541 million years old and that nuclear decay rates (like the laws of physics) are a constant over time, he instead puts forth the idea that the decay rates were accelerated a few thousand years ago, and that the radiohalos from decaying polonium survive as the evidence of that.

To understand what he’s claiming, let’s go through what he states, but let’s do it in a way that compares what he’s asserting against the conventional story told by geologists, geophysicists, and nuclear physicists to see where there’s agreement and when there’s something he’s suggesting that’s outside of the realm of what’s generally accepted.

First, Hebert talks about granites in general (and Phanerozoic granites in particular) as having formed like any igneous rock: when hot magma cools and solidifies. He notes that zirconium silicate crystals often form within these granites, and that sometimes there’s a chemical substitution of (radioactive) uranium for zircon in these crystals.

This part is generally true. Granite is a common igneous rock, and it’s generally formed when magma comes to Earth’s surface and erupts (becoming lava, but that’s not an important detail), flows over the land, and cools, becoming solid rock. During the time that the rock is in the liquid state — as magma or lava — any radioactive decays that occur will produce daughter particles that don’t remain; alpha particles (or helium nuclei) become gas and escape, while only the ultimately stable daughter particle persists. It’s for this reason that measuring things like the uranium-to-lead ratio (or the potassium-to-argon ratio, among other radioactive tracers) allows you to date how long it’s been since a rock has formed: since it solidified.

The part about this being a Phanerozoic granite just means that it comes from the geological Phanerozoic period: approximately dating from the beginning of the Cambrian period and extending to the present time. Therefore, by definition, it covers the time period of the past 539 million years or so, and Phanerozoic granites represent rocks formed during this time period. So far, this is in full agreement with what’s presently understood.

Hebert then goes on to describe how — once a solid rock containing uranium is formed — a decay chain process occurs. This is indeed true. Overall, uranium’s most common isotope starts with 146 neutrons (U-238), and:

  • after a half-life of 4.5 billion years, decays to thorium-234,
  • which very quickly (after 24 days) decays to protactinium-234,
  • which again very quickly (after 1.2 minutes) decays to uranium-234,
  • which then (after 245,000 years) decays to thorium-230,
  • which afterward (after 75,000 years) decays to radium-226,
  • which in the next step (after 1600 years) decays to radon-222,
  • which swiftly (after 3.8 days) decays to polonium-218,
  • when very rapidly (after 3.1 minutes) either decays to astatine-218 (1.5 seconds) and then to bismuth-214, or to lead-214 (27 minutes) and then to bismuth-214,
  • which after another 20 minutes, decays either to polonium-214 (0.16 milliseconds) and then to lead-210, or first to thallium-210 (1.3 minutes) and then to lead-210,
  • and then, after 22 years, undergoes a decay either to bismuth-210 (5 days), polonium-210 (138 days), and then to lead-206, or a decay to mercury-206 (8.3 minutes), thallium-206 (4.2 minutes), and then to lead-206.

At last, lead-206 is stable, and so when that product is reached, no further decays come about. Note how long the initial lifetime of uranium-238 is (4.5 billion years) compared to all of the intermediate products that come after. That’s why nearly 100% of the initial uranium-238 that begins in a sample will either still be uranium-238 or will have converted into lead-206. There will be tiny, trace amounts of the other elements/isotopes present at any given moment, where a total of eight alpha particles (helium-4 nuclei) and six beta particles (electrons) are emitted during the full decay chain process.

Hebert states that these eight alpha particles per parent uranium nucleus come in a spectrum of energies, and he’s right. He states that if you have enough uranium in one deposit, you’ll get a discolored halo from this radioactive material (a radiohalo) around it, where the higher-energy alpha particles produce longer-length tracks and the lower-energy particles produce shorter length tracks: again, correct. And then, the more uranium you start with and the more time that passes, the darker your radiohalo appears. All of this is in agreement with the consensus picture.

Now, here’s where we get into the meat of the assertion. I’ll break it up into three chunks, so we can analyze each one separately.

1.) Hebert notes that, in some locations, you don’t see a large discolored halo with eight rings, indicative of a uranium-238 parent nucleus, but rather a smaller, less-discolored halo: sometimes with just three, two, or even one ring: indicative of polonium-218, polonium-214, or polonium-210 alone.

2.) And then, since you need hundreds of millions of alpha particles to form a radiohalo, that conventionally means you must have had hundreds of millions of years pass in order to create these radiohalos. But since polonium isotopes live only for days (or less), there’s no way to produce a radiohalo without starting from uranium, and therefore the standard picture is wrong.

3.) Hebert then argues that in order to produce what he calls an “orphan” polonium radiohalo, you need to have produced a very large number of polonium atoms all at once, and then swiftly transport them a short distance away to a single, isolated location that’s nearby the original uranium halos. Therefore, the standard picture is wrong, and an alternative pathway — and Hebert proposed one that involves rapid, accelerated decays in the past, hydrothermal fluid flow, and rapid transport, allegedly occurring during the Biblical flood — is required to explain what we see.

These are the three key statements that are at the core of what Hebert is asserting. But are they true?

The first assertion is close. It’s true that, in theory, since there are eight steps to a typical radioactive decay of U-238, you’d expect eight concentric rings to appear. However, the energies of several steps in the radioactive decay chain are very close together; you can only discern up to five concentric rings under a lighted petrographic microscope. But if you have a polonium-218 halo (or a radon-222 halo), you indeed do see only three rings: one from Po-218, one from Po-214, and one from (the indistinguishable overlap of) Rn-222 and Po-210. (The immediate daughter products of U-238, which are U-234, Th-230, and Ra-226, also overlap to make one indistinguishable ring.)

For the second assertion, you do indeed need hundreds of millions of alpha particles to form a radiohalo in granite. If you start from U-238, you do indeed need hundreds of millions of years to pass for a radiohalo to form. And there’s plenty of uranium inside the Earth’s interior; it’s one of the heaviest elements abundantly produced in processes like supernovae that created the material that our pre-solar nebula formed from, and its radioactive decay generates a significant fraction of the Earth’s interior heat.

However, uranium constantly decays inside the Earth, including in magma chambers. When it does, several of its immediate downstream products — thorium, protactinium, and radium — can be solid or liquid, depending on temperature. However, the next step in the decay chain after radium is radon: a gas. When you create a gas within a liquid, even if that liquid is magma, it rises until it gets trapped against a solid-bodied chamber: a crack, vein, or crevice of solid rock, for instance. Radon diffuses as a neutral gas along or through fractures.

As was shown by Lorence and Barbara Collins many years ago, “daughter” atoms, including radon (which becomes polonium after its next decay) are continuously being produced within the Earth within magma chambers: a veritable “sea” of radon-producing (and hence, later on, polonium-producing) material.

And finally, the third key assertion is that polonium radiohalos are found nearby the uranium ones, and that an alternative scenario to the standard picture must be invoked in order to explain such a localized density of rapidly-decaying polonium atoms. But there’s a problem: polonium halos are not found in the same kind of granite where uranium halos are found. Granite that contains polonium halos occurs in rocks that have formed at temperatures above 700 ºC: rocks that have already crystallized and become solid by the time temperatures cool to 450 ºC, whereas granite that crystallizes from molten rock (which contains the uranium radiohalos) won’t have the necessary fractures within it so that the radon and polonium can collect at a particular, localized site.

Only when the temperatures drop below about 150 ºC (300 ºF) do the alpha particles begin to leave trails in the (now-solid) rock, creating these radiohalos. Depending on how much time passes between when the radon gas collects in pockets and fractures and when enough cooling has occurred for the temperature to drop sufficiently for radiohalos to form is what determines whether:

  • three-layered radiohalos (common for quick-cooling environments, if it cools in less than a week or so),
  • two-layered radiohalos (very rare, if cooling takes about 1-2 weeks),
  • or a one-layered radiohalo (common for slow-cooling environments that take months-to-years to cool)

winds up forming. Instead of invoking an alternative scenario — one favored by creationists — to explain the presence of polonium radiohalos, you simply need to apply the actual geophysical conditions present in the Earth’s interior where these features ultimately originate. And again, this is in an environment that’s different, embedded in a different type of granite, from where the uranium radiohalos, with five observed layers, are typically found.

But there’s a more fundamental problem with this type of claim that’s very different from, “I’ve found something unusual that led someone to challenge the scientific consensus on an issue.” The point of this was not to claim that someone had found evidence that supported a conclusion other than the one accepted by the scientific mainstream. The point was to go out and find a line of reasoning that could, whether scrupulously or disingenuously, be used to convince people that mainstream science had our origin story wrong, and that the conclusion reached by Young Earth Creationists was correct instead.

This is a hallmark tactic of pseudoscientists: to craft an argument that most legitimate scientists in the mainstream will be unfamiliar with, and that will require the general public to digest and process a large amount of information to understand it. Instead of a complex, nuanced story that involves synthesizing together a large suite of information to understand it properly, they tell a simple, disingenuous story that can be told quickly and simply, but that takes a mountain of evidence to debunk. From global warming deniers to those attempting to link vaccines and autism to the “alcohol is good for you, actually,” crowd to creationists and more, this technique of invoking Brandolini’s law — that the amount of energy needed to refute bullshit is an order of magnitude bigger than that needed to produce it — is as true today as it’s ever been.

In this life, it’s important to be open and curious about ideas that are out of the mainstream, but if you care about getting things right, it’s even more important to be rigorous, honest, skeptical, and thoughtful. Without those traits, and without adhering to what the evidence actually states, we cannot have a constructive conversation.

items.title: Tech execs are trying to appeal to Democrats after years of Trump allegiance
items.summary: Morning Brew Inc., Photos: Getty Images Elon Musk, who led Trump’s DOGE team and has donated more than half a billion to Republican candidates, said at Wednesday’s DealBook Summit that he wasn’t MAGA. And Musk isn’t the only tech executive to backpedal recently to save face…
items.author: Matty Merritt
items.contentHtml:
Elon Musk, who led Trump’s DOGE team and has donated more than half a billion to Republican candidates, said at Wednesday’s DealBook Summit that he wasn’t MAGA. And Musk isn’t the only tech executive to backpedal recently to save face after the midterms’ blue wave.

Musk said he felt “pretty foolish” donating $500 million to Republican candidates who lost during the midterms. The comments mark a change for Musk after his last few years of very public political spending and support. With the Democrats taking over the majority in the Senate and House, giving them new power to launch investigations, other tech execs are also talking differently:

  • Palantir CEO Alex Karp told Politico last week that he has been a Democrat his whole life, identifying as an “unhappy Democrat.”
  • He also said Palantir’s products are “essentially progressive,” although the company has received external and internal pushback over its immigration enforcement platform used by ICE.

A group of strategists told the Washington Post they are lobbying tech execs to rework their approaches to wooing communities and Congress after years of hands-off regulation from Trump and other Republicans.

The big flip. Beyond Congress, Silicon Valley’s leaders are scrambling to ingratiate themselves with Democratic governors across the country—especially since many winning candidates campaigned on pumping the brakes on the AI industry.—MM

items.title: Anthropic gets rock star welcome in public markets
items.summary: Charly Triballeau/Getty Images The AI world’s ball drop took place in Times Square yesterday, where Anthropic debuted on the Nasdaq with a 34% price pop in an IPO seen as a bellwether for the broader industry. The AI lab that former OpenAI employees founded in 2021 instantly…
items.author: Sam Klebanov
items.contentHtml:
The AI world’s ball drop took place in Times Square yesterday, where Anthropic debuted on the Nasdaq with a 34% price pop in an IPO seen as a bellwether for the broader industry.

The AI lab that former OpenAI employees founded in 2021 instantly became one of the world’s most valuable public companies:

  • ANT hit brokerages around noon, trading at $111, or 34% above the $83 price set yesterday for a pool of preferred investors. It settled at $97 by the end of the day.
  • The company’s IPO raised a record $81 billion, breaking the $75 billion record set by SpaceX in its public debut in June. Anthropic also sold $26 billion in private shares.

Though Wall Street’s willingness to snatch up Anthropic shares showed enthusiasm about the AI trade, it didn’t propel other parts of the market. The tech-heavy Nasdaq closed down 2.2%, which some analysts say was caused by investors cashing out gains from the Anthropic IPO bump and renewed anxieties about chipmakers.

More yachts are coming to San Francisco Bay: There are likely 2,800 Anthropic employees with shares now worth $10 million or more, while 600 employees are likely to have stakes valued at more than $100 million, per investment platform Hill.com. A windfall is also coming for early backers like Lightspeed Venture Partners, Iconiq, Menlo Ventures, and a VC firm co-founded by Ashton Kutcher, which owns 0.5% of Anthropic.

As for the rest of us…analysts say thatreturns from Anthropic shares will hinge on how productive the tech makes its customers, its ability to compete with rivals, and whether it can grow revenue fast enough to justify spending $900 billion on AI infrastructure. Meanwhile, Anthropic’s IPO has intensified calls from lawmakers to regulate the industry.

Anthropic has goals beyond growing your 401(k). It has legally committed to prioritizing the good of humanity by developing safe AI systems, per its Public Benefit Corporation status. Experts say this could turn off some investors, since Anthropic’s definition of public good could conflict with profits.—SK

items.title: Why everyone should be doing therapy
items.summary: I would bet my house that you’re living with something. There is some sickness, pain, or condition you’ve learned to deal with. Because there is no such thing as “perfect” health. Everyone you talk to, everyone you see on the street, everyone in the line at the coffee shop, has…
items.author: Jonny Thomson
items.contentHtml:
I would bet my house that you’re living with something. There is some sickness, pain, or condition you’ve learned to deal with. Because there is no such thing as “perfect” health. Everyone you talk to, everyone you see on the street, everyone in the line at the coffee shop, has something they have to adapt to. It might be something mild, like dry skin in the winter or being nearsighted. It might be a chronically bad back or intermittent migraines. Or, it might be something that requires more of us: diabetes tests, dialysis, the latest cancer treatment. Everyone, everywhere, is dealing with something.

Mental health is no different. I’m sometimes asked if I’m an anxious or obsessive person, and my reply is almost always the same. Yes, I can certainly feel anxious, and yes, I can display obsessive behaviors, but am I anxious or obsessive? I don’t think so. I am the way I am, and I have learned how to live with that. We all grow to deal with the world as best we can. I have strategies, tools, and ways of thinking that allow me to operate in the world, and I’m sure you do as well. The question, then, is what tools we can call upon.

The French philosopher Georges Canguilhem once argued that we shouldn’t necessarily define “health” as perfect function or as a “no boxes checked” on a health questionnaire. Instead, we should define health in terms of a “margin of tolerance” to the world’s misfortunes. To be healthy is to have hard times, experience pain, and endure mental distress, but to get back up again and to get back to living. “Health” doesn’t mean having nothing wrong with you — it’s when you have the power to live with your something.

This is a new, members-only newsletter all about how to live well. It’s about the strategies that can help us cure or endure what makes us anxious, lost, or unhappy. It’s about the tools and habits that we can call upon to enjoy the richness of life all the more. This newsletter is about how to be healthy in mind and happy in soul.

The first edition — coming this Sunday — will be free to all, and after that, it will be bundled into our membership package, where you can get all of our newsletters, articles, and videos. There, you can also register to join online events with the likes of Carlo Rovelli, Alex O’Connor, and Brené Brown. And, of course, US customers can get our quarterly print magazine for free.

Why “The Sunday Epicurean”?

Over 2,000 years ago in Athens, a man living with his own “something” started a school. Epicurus had a great bushy beard and a lifetime of digestive issues, and he founded “The Garden” — one of the four big schools of antiquity.

In The Garden, students weren’t bothered with abstract mathematics or metaphysics. They spent their days talking about human suffering and human happiness. Their curriculum focused on the natural sciences and what we now call psychology. The Friends of Epicurus, as they were called, were encouraged to have regular, introspective therapy sessions. They’d eat together, walk together, and philosophize together. Because, as Epicurus put it, in the same way that medicine is pointless if it does not cure the diseases of the body, there is no point in philosophy if it does not cure the suffering of the mind.

I strongly believe that everyone should be doing therapy. But I define “therapy” in a looser, wider sense. On the one hand, we live in an age of therapy. More and more people go to see psychotherapists and psychiatrists. We’re all much more willing to speak in the language of therapy, and many of us are better at reflecting on our inner lives. As a philosopher and an empirically minded sort, I think these are good trends. Therapy works for a lot of people. But, as any good therapist will tell you, therapy is not limited to the hour you are in the room. It’s a method. It’s a way of thinking. It’s a reorientation of your life that allows you to live better. Limiting “therapy” to once a week leaves us poorer. Medicalizing therapy — pathologizing it — makes it forever curative and reactive. Good therapy is what we keep with us.

When Epicureans talk about therapy, they mean it in a broader, lived sense. It’s something we do every day. It’s something we do with all of our friends as much as possible and not just with Dr. Carver at 3 p.m. on Tuesdays. In The Garden, Epicurus told his students to introspect often, to take control of their decisions, and to nurture their relationships. He said we should commit to who we are, what we enjoy, and where we are right now. I think he’s right. It’s why I’ve written an entire book about it, called The Art of Enough.

So, The Sunday Epicurean is a kind of philosophical therapy. It’s a weekly heart-to-heart conversation where we explore — together — what might be causing us pain and how we might alleviate it. It’s a sit-down meal with Friends in The Garden where we learn about the ins and outs of human psychology and how we can all enjoy more of life. The Sunday Epicurean is a newsletter about how to avoid pain and find pleasure.

These newsletters will give a little of me and invite a little from you. I hope you can join our Garden community. I hope you can share strategies, habits, and insights as much as I can. Because, as the Friends themselves knew, we are all in this together. We all suffer, and we all laugh. We all get lonely, and we all love. We all have to work out how to live with our “something.” So let’s work out how to live well, together.

This is an edition of The Sunday Epicurean, a weekly, members-only newsletter from Mini Philosophy.

items.title: A Van Gogh painting sold for a record $190.4m last night
items.summary: Kobei Li/Getty Images Vincent Van Gogh? More like Van Gogh get your wallet. The painter’s “Châtaigniers en fleurs” (“Blossoming Chestnut Trees”) sold for $190.4 million last night at a Sotheby’s auction in New York City after not being seen by the public in over 60 years. The…
items.author: Matty Merritt
items.contentHtml:
Vincent Van Gogh? More like Van Gogh get your wallet. The painter’s “Châtaigniers en fleurs” (“Blossoming Chestnut Trees”) sold for $190.4 million last night at a Sotheby’s auction in New York City after not being seen by the public in over 60 years. The price blew past the artist’s previous auction record of $117.2 million from four years ago.

The sale almost didn’t happen

It proceeded only after the owner selling the painting reached an eleventh-hour deal with the heirs of the previous owners. Anonymous heirs to Samuel Fischer, who bought the painting in 1909, allege the painting was sold in 1936 because of financial difficulties forced upon the family’s business by the Nazi regime:

  • Sotheby’s initially claimed there was no evidence the painting’s 1936 sale was made under duress.
  • On Tuesday, the families reached an agreement so that last night’s sale could take place. Details of the agreement were not released.

The painting was one from a collection of 12 that went on the auction block. Sotheby’s estimated that the dozen would fetch $450 million collectively, but they only sold for $412 million.

The art market is having a legendary week. Total sales at three of the biggest auction houses, Sotheby’s, Christie’s, and Phillips, are expected to hit $2.4 billion this week. That would rival 2025’s sales for the whole year. The houses already brought in $6.8 billion in the first half of 2026, per Bank of America’s recent Art Market Update report.—MM

items.title: 'Grand Theft Auto VI' is out, and it's the highest-rated game ever
items.summary: Rockstar Games Bad news: You can’t say “We got ___ before GTA VI ” anymore, because after 13 years of waiting, two delays, and several leaks, Grand Theft Auto VI , the most anticipated video game probably ever, finally came out today at midnight local time. It’s already the…
items.author: Molly Liebergall
items.contentHtml:
Bad news: You can’t say “We got ___ before GTA VI” anymore, because after 13 years of waiting, two delays, and several leaks, Grand Theft Auto VI, the most anticipated video game probably ever, finally came out today at midnight local time.

It’s already the highest-rated game in history: GTA VI scored a site-wide best 99/100 on the review aggregator Metacritic. Bloomberg called the open-world game “a masterpiece,” the New York Times said it’ll “steal your heart,” and IGN’s reviewer described it as “the single most impressive video game I have ever played.”

All those years spent crafting the franchise’s new Bonnie-and-Clyde-in-Florida installment appear to have been worth the wait for publisher Rockstar Games. Amid earth-shattering (and possibly internet traffic-shattering) demand, the company may have already made back its entire development budget, which is believed to be between $1 billion and $1.5 billion:

  • Preorders surpassed $1.5 billion, Sensor Tower estimated, putting GTA VI hundreds of millions of dollars ahead of preorders for other recent big-name video game releases.
  • Some analysts think GTA VI will sell 40 million copies in its first four months, raking in $3 billion in revenue, Bloomberg reported. For context, the highest-grossing movie in the world, Avengers: Endgame, made $2.9 billion.

Expect a ghost town today. Schools around the world anticipated empty classroom chairs, and time-off requests are ~20% higher today than usual, according to the workplace software provider UKG. Logitech gave its 7,000 employees the day off to explore GTA VI in all its alligator-quarreling, canine jet-skiing, and insurance-scam side quest glory.

Even if you don’t plan on playing…

…you’re still living in the GTA VI entertainment economy. According to Sensor Tower, over the next month:

  • Other games could see a 10% collective drop in players.
  • Streaming movies and TV shows might get 6 million fewer hours of playtime in the US.

Meanwhile…food delivery services, music platforms (the game has a 30-song original soundtrack) and livestreamers are expected to cash in.

Farewell, GTA V. In preparation for GTA VI, GTA Online players bid adieu to the franchise’s beloved fifth installment last night with a peaceful “last ride” through Los Santos.—ML

items.title: NASA’s next flagship to answer the biggest question: “Are we alone?”
items.summary: There are a few questions that humanity has always pondered, yet scarcely could satisfactorily answer until the proper scientific advances came along. Questions like: What is the Universe? Where did it come from? How did it get to be this way? And what is its ultimate fate?…
items.author: Ethan Siegel
items.contentHtml:
There are a few questions that humanity has always pondered, yet scarcely could satisfactorily answer until the proper scientific advances came along. Questions like:

  • What is the Universe?
  • Where did it come from?
  • How did it get to be this way?
  • And what is its ultimate fate?

These are questions that have been with us since time immemorial, yet remained unanswerable for nearly all of human history. Beginning in the 20th century and now into the 21st century, many of these questions are finally getting comprehensive answers thanks to incredible advances in physics and astronomy. However, perhaps the biggest question of all — the question of “Are we alone in the Universe?” — remains as perhaps the greatest existential unanswered question of all.

While the current generation of ground-based and space-based telescopes can take us far into the Universe, this is a question that’s currently the reach of any observatory that presently exists. To get there, we’ll need to acquire direct images of Earth-like exoplanets: planets with sizes and temperatures similar to Earth, but that orbit Sun-like stars, not the more common red dwarf stars like Proxima Centauri or TRAPPIST-1.

Those capabilities are precisely what NASA is aiming for with its next flagship mission: the Habitable Worlds Observatory. It’s an ambitious project, sure, but one that’s well worth it. After all, finding out we’re not alone in the Universe would quite possibly be the biggest revolution in all of science history.

At the present time, there are three main ways we’re actively searching for alien life.

  1. We’re exploring worlds in our Solar System, including Mars, Venus, Titan, Europa, and Pluto, remotely and in situ, with fly-by missions, orbiters, landers, and even rovers, searching for evidence of past life or even, potentially simple life that persists at the present time.
  2. We’re examining exoplanets, searching for evidence that there’s life on them, from the surface to the atmosphere and beyond, based on observable signatures of color, seasonal change, and atmospheric contents.
  3. And by looking for any signals that would reveal the presence of intelligent aliens: through efforts such as SETI and Breakthrough Listen.

All three approaches have their advantages and disadvantages, and so it makes sense to invest in all three. As long as we don’t find anyone else, we’ll have no choice but to wonder whether we’re alone or not. However, once we have a successful example of life that originated outside of Earth, we’ll know for certain that we have company here in the cosmos.

Given the sheer number of chances that are out there, most scientists believe that it’s the second option that’s most likely to deliver our first success. If life requires conditions similar to those found on Earth, we might well be the only world in the Solar System where life ever developed, survived, thrived, became technologically advanced, and still exists at the present time. Unless there are other intelligent, actively broadcasting civilizations nearby right now, endeavors like SETI won’t be able deliver any positive results.

However, “life of any type” is a much lower bar than actively-transmitting intelligent, technologically advanced civilizations. If even a small fraction of worlds that exist with Earth-like properties have life of any type on them, exoplanet studies can deliver a success where the other two options won’t. And we’ve come a very long way in our studies of exoplanets: we have more than 6000 known, confirmed exoplanets within the Milky Way, where we know the mass, radius, and orbital period of nearly all of those confirmed worlds.

Unfortunately, this isn’t enough to inform us about whether any of these worlds are inhabited. To make that determination, we need more than that. We’d need to be able to make the necessary measurements that could answer such questions as:

  • Does the exoplanet have an atmosphere?
  • Does it have clouds, precipitation, and weather cycles?
  • Do its continents green-and-brown with the seasons, like they do on Earth?
  • Does it have gases or gas combinations in its atmosphere that hint at biological activity, and do they show seasonal variations like Earth’s CO2 levels do?

On the cutting edge of performing these measurements, today, are the space-based JWST and ground-based 10-meter class telescopes, performing direct exoplanet imaging and transit spectroscopy.

But even those great observatories are not enough to reach the goal we’re truly after.

JWST and 10-meter ground-based telescopes cannot measure the properties of Earth-sized planets in Earth-like orbits around Sun-like stars. For direct imaging studies, we can take pictures of planets that are the size of Jupiter and that are more than about Saturn’s distance from the Sun: good for gas giant worlds, but not so great for looking for life on rocky planets. For transit spectroscopy, we can see the light that filters through the atmospheres of super-Earth-sized worlds around red dwarf stars, but Earth-sized planets around Sun-like stars are well beyond the reach of current technology.

We have, however, come far enough to know that if we can scale up our technology, acquiring that data for the exoplanets we truly desire is possible. What we need to do is build on our current technology and enhance it further if we hope to find and characterize an actually inhabited planet. Currently, we’re building the next generation of ground-based telescopes, ushering in the era of 30-meter class telescopes with the GMTO, the ELT, and potentially Exo-Life Finder as well, and looking forward to the exquisite performance of the coronagraph aboard NASA’s next astrophysics flagship mission: the Nancy Roman Telescope.

The Roman telescope will have the same capabilities as Hubble but with superior instrumentation, a field-of-view that’s 50-100 times as great as Hubble’s, and a coronagraph that allows us to image planets within the glare of their parent star’s light that are about 1000 times fainter than JWST can see. A critical test will arrive very soon, when Roman attempts to image a faint stellar companion that can sufficiently test its coronagraphic capabilities; if it succeeds, it means we’re on track to directly image Earth-like worlds around Sun-like stars with the planned Habitable Worlds Observatory.

Our technology does not remain stagnant, nor do our visions for discovery and exploration. Each decade, the National Academy of Sciences gets together to outline the highest priorities for astronomy and astrophysics, making recommendations as part of a decadal survey. Four flagship missions were proposed at the most recent (Astro2020) decadal:

  1. Lynx, a next-generation X-ray observatory, especially important given the reduced scope of the ESA’s upcoming Athena mission,
  2. Origins, a next-generation far-infrared observatory, filling a colossal gap in our wavelength coverage of the Universe,
  3. HabEx, a single-mirror telescope designed to directly image the very nearest Earth-like planets,
  4. and LUVOIR, an ambitious, giant segmented telescope that would be an astronomical all-purpose “dream” observatory.

While the recommendation was that three of these four eventually be constructed, Lynx and Origins took a back seat to what was selected as the highest-priority mission: a scaled-up version of HabEx (or a scaled-down version of LUVOIR), taking features of both HabEx and LUVOIR into account to form the Habitable Worlds Observatory. In many ways, the proposed specification hit precisely in the “sweet spot” between feasibility given current technology, discovery potential given what we do and don’t know, and cost effectiveness, incorporating lessons learned from the problems and successes experienced along the way in the construction, design, and launch of JWST.

The specifications proposed for Habitable Worlds Observatory are very encouraging. So far, the design includes:

  • a segmented optical mirror design, similar to what’s already in use by JWST,
  • an improved version of the coronagraph technology that’s presently equipped aboard the Roman Telescope,
  • up-to-date sensors that can control the various mirror segments to achieve ~picometer-level stability (orders of magnitude better than JWST or current ground-based optical telescopes),
  • planned compatibility with next-generation rockets that will be flying in the late 2030s/early 2040s,
  • planned robotic servicing of components at the L2 Lagrange point, located ~1.5 million km from Earth,
  • but, other than that, no wholly new technologies that haven’t been fully matured prior to the development/construction phase.

The most expensive components of JWST were the all-new ones; with Habitable Worlds Observatory, there is nothing that’s all-new. This is extremely encouraging, as it presents an achievable plan that isn’t particularly susceptible to the delays and overruns that plagued JWST. Without the need to develop wholly new technologies, the path to getting a Habitable Worlds Observatory to the specifications we require is one of incremental improvement, rather than of wholesale invention.

With these capabilities, the Habitable Worlds Observatory will have an excellent chance to reach what’s perhaps the holy grail of astronomy: to reveal an actually inhabited planet to humanity for the very first time. With between a 6.0 and 6.5 meter primary mirror design, comparable to JWST in size and light-gathering power, it should be able to directly image Earth-sized planets around all of the stars within about ~14 light-years of Earth. Scientists on the design team will fight for every little bit of extra diameter they can get, because that’s what counts the most in this game; if you can double the radius you can see planets out to, you increase the search volume and the expected number of objects by a factor of eight. In the vicinity of the Sun, there are:

  • 9 star systems within 10 light-years of Earth,
  • 22 star systems within 12 light-years of Earth,
  • 40 star systems within 15 light-years of Earth,
  • and 95 star systems within 20 light-years of Earth.

With its currently-planned design, somewhere between 20 and 30 Earth-like planets could be directly imaged by the Habitable Worlds Observatory. With a slightly scaled-up diameter, that number could easily be increased to around 100. If there’s even a ~few percent chance (or ~1%, in the upscaled scenario) of life taking hold on an Earth-like world, then this mission will likely bear the ultimate fruit: discovering our first inhabited planet beyond the Solar System. Perhaps, if nature is kind, we might even discover more than one.

Because we’ve already gone through the pain of developing many of the precursor technologies, including:

  • the 5-layer sunshield used with JWST,
  • the folded/segmented mirror design used with JWST,
  • and the deformable mirror used within the Roman coronagraph,

there shouldn’t be anything wholly new or novel to trip up the Habitable Worlds Observatory like there was with JWST.

However, all new developments come with risks. The idea of robotic servicing is encouraging, because we’ve done robotic servicing before, but only as far away as in low-Earth orbit. At the distance to L2, 1.5 million kilometers, even instructions sent at the speed-of-light have a 10 second round-trip delay. Upgrading the telescope and its instruments in orbit, i.e., the “servicing” component of the mission, will require both rocket technology and automated robotic technology that will need to be developed and matured.

To achieve ~picometer level mirror alignments is a technical challenge that requires advances far beyond the ~nanometer-level alignments achievable today. Although this requires only an incremental improvement over existing technology, a substantial set of resources will need to be devoted to it, and are currently being devoted as part of the “technology maturation” process inherent in the design and pre-design phases.

One big worry that hasn’t necessarily hit the right people’s radar is the suitability of the currently-designed Roman coronagraph for the Habitable Worlds Observatory. The JWST coronagraph is performing exactly as anticipated, enabling us to find and image planets that are just 1-part-in-100,000 as bright as their parent stars are. The Nancy Roman Telescope expects a factor of 1000 improvement over JWST, as their deformable coronagraph mirror is being optimized to deal with the interference patterns and stray light that emerges from a perfectly circular coronagraph shape.

However, there’s a catch: one of the reasons that the Nancy Roman Telescope’s coronagraph can perform so much better than JWST’s is because JWST has a tiled mirror with a segmented design, while the Nancy Roman telescope will have a single, circular, monolithic mirror. The shape of the JWST mirror is why it has that “snowflake-like” diffraction pattern around all of its stars and bright point-sources of light: that’s just a mathematical consequence of the geometry of its optics.

Since the architecture of the Habitable Worlds Observatory is slated to include a tiled primary mirror, this may pose a new set of compatibility difficulties.

After all, coronagraphs are circular in nature, and cannot easily “undo” the stray light that gets introduced from any sharp edges, including:

  • the hexagonal tiles,
  • the “corners” on the outer edges of the mirror,
  • and the ~millimeter-sized “gaps” between the various segments.

With a similar design to JWST, this seems like a very big problem for Habitable Worlds Observatory to reckon with, particularly since it needs coronagraphy that’s successful at the 1-part-in-10,000,000,000 (1-part-in-ten-billion) level to image Earth-like worlds around Sun-like stars: another factor of ~100 better than the Roman coronagraph will achieve.

However, there’s still the possibility that a larger-bodied rocket, capable of launching a monolithic mirror of diameters of 6.0 meters or more (and perhaps even up 8.4 meters: the largest monolithic mirrors we can reliably produce), will be available by the time the Habitable Worlds Observatory moves to its final design stage. If that occurs, this problem evaporates, and the mission becomes much less dependent on overcoming a difficult, never-before-faced problem.

A different potential solution is to launch a starshade either with the Habitable Worlds Observatory or even after-the-fact, to block the target star’s light before it ever reaches the Habitable Worlds Observatory’s primary mirror. Although this is technologically feasible, it’s both expensive and limited in its effectiveness; it has to travel some ~80,000 kilometers relative to the observatory every time it wants to switch targets. (However, there is evidence that such a starshade could be multi-purpose, and leveraged with ground-based observatories as well.) All told, the addition of a starshade can help the Habitable Worlds Observatory potentially image about one or two systems per year, meaning that it could allow for dozens or even scores of sufficiently imaged systems.

An intermediate solution that perhaps should be considered is neither building a traditional segmented mirror nor a single monolithic mirror, but a series of circular mirrors, akin to the optical setup of the presently under-construction Giant Magellan Telescope. With seven perfect circles instead of 18+ tiled hexagons, it has the light-gathering power of the area of all seven circles combined, but the resolution of the diameter across which the primary mirrors are mounted. With this design:

  • all of the stray light problems from a JWST-like design are eliminated,
  • the already-developed foldable primary mirror technology could still be utilized,
  • the picometer-level stability technology being developed across mirror segments would still apply,
  • and instead of a single secondary mirror and/or a single coronagraph, each of the seven segments could get their own.

As a bonus, there would be no wires required to cross the primary mirror optics, as the secondary mirror(s) could be held in place with wires that went in-between the gaps in the circular segments: precisely why the Giant Magellan Telescope will be the first world-class observatory without diffraction spikes on its stars.

With the right design and implementation, and the technology maturation pathway laid out by NASA’s astrophysics division, we could be looking at a Habitable Worlds Observatory:

  • that launches as early as the late 2030s/early 2040s,
  • that’s on-budget and on-time,
  • that possesses the necessary architecture to achieve its observational goals without needing a starshade,
  • that’s fully refuellable and whose instruments are fully serviceable and replaceable,
  • that could have a starshade upgrade added to it at any point in the future,
  • and that quite possibly images enough “Earth-like” planets to discover at least one (and maybe even more than one) exoplanet that’s actually inhabited.

The big question that needs to go into the design of this telescope is the trade-off between how many Earth-like candidates it can directly image versus how large and costly the telescope is going to be. While the 6-to-7 meter range seems like the sweet spot, the nightmare scenario is that we build this observatory just a little too small and cost-conservatively to find what we’re ultimately seeking: an inhabited alien planet. We’d hardly regret it if we built one that was large enough that we sampled enough of the Universe to find more than one inhabited planet!

We must remember that in the search for life beyond Earth, we are playing a lottery with unknown odds. Each Earth-like planet that we image and characterize represents a ticket: a ticket in a lottery where the odds of all of the prizes are unknown. Our chances of success depend entirely on which tickets are winners and whether we buy enough of them. The hard part is we won’t know if we have meaningful constraints on what those odds actually are until after the findings from Habitable Worlds Observatory come in, and so it’s up to us to build it in such a way that our odds of at least one success are as great as possible. If we do, we might finally have the answer to “Are we alone in the Universe?” Just maybe, we’ll know for certain that the answer is, “No, there are others.”

This article was first published in February of 2023. It was updated in November of 2026.

items.title: What’s causing all the tech outages?
items.summary: Niv Bavarsky If you couldn’t log into a Teams meeting or watch Matchbox: The Movie due to tech issues in the past week, experts say it was likely the result of companies and government agencies rushing to make system upgrades to patch vulnerabilities—not a coordinated…
items.author: Dave Lozo
items.contentHtml:
If you couldn’t log into a Teams meeting or watch Matchbox: The Movie due to tech issues in the past week, experts say it was likely the result of companies and government agencies rushing to make system upgrades to patch vulnerabilities—not a coordinated cyberattack.

It’s AI’s fault…sort of. Anthropic and OpenAI have released AI models that can detect exponentially more bugs than a human could ever find. That’s created a race between organizations trying to close the holes and hackers looking to exploit them. The speed and volume of recent patches have caused some infrastructures—like the ones at Microsoft, Apple, and the NSA—to buckle. Experts believe more disruptions will happen as institutions continue to gain the tools to patch vulnerabilities.

In the case of the infamous ground stoppage last weekend, the FAA said the problem was traced to defective routers in Arkansas and Texas, although experts who spoke to CNET doubted the explanation’s plausibility and pointed to a new AI air traffic control system that rolled out nationwide shortly before the debacle.

Paranoia is understandable. Last month was dubbed “Black October” because of the high volume of cyberattacks—many done by a new AI hacking tool called Artex. On the Friday of the ground stoppage, the FBI released a warning about Artex, but a spokesperson later said that it was just a coincidence.—DL
