items.title: The surprising science of awe — and what it reveals about consciousness
items.summary: Years ago on the way to New Zealand for my doctoral studies, I stopped in Los Angeles to visit a friend. He organized a trip to Joshua Tree, where we hiked and camped. Come nightfall, I gazed at the stars and clouds — or so I thought. My friend pointed out that the cloudcover…
items.author: Valerie van Mulukom
items.contentHtml:
Years ago on the way to New Zealand for my doctoral studies, I stopped in Los Angeles to visit a friend. He organized a trip to Joshua Tree, where we hiked and camped. Come nightfall, I gazed at the stars and clouds — or so I thought. My friend pointed out that the cloudcover was, in fact, the Milky Way. 

I didn’t realize our galaxy was ever visible to the naked eye, and I was deeply moved. The vast stillness of the desert, the free-roaming coyotes and the thick blanket of stars reminded me that we humans are only a tiny part of it all, yet also unbreakably connected to this stretching, expansive universe. More than a decade later, the awe of that experience remains important and vivid in my life.

Now, as a psychological scientist, I study awe for a living. Last summer, my colleagues and I asked 200 people in the UK to document their encounters with awe over six weeks. Because such experiences are often linked to a sense of purpose and flourishing, we wanted to know what mattered more: their frequency or intensity.

What we found surprised us. As we explain in this John Templeton Foundation-supported paper, those who experienced moments of awe that induced strong feelings of amazement and wonder reported a greater sense of meaning and wellbeing by the study’s end. It wasn’t how often people felt awe that mattered, but whether they had an experience which strongly evoked it.

What, exactly, happens to us when we experience awe, and what makes the feeling so significant, in such a lasting way?

We researchers know that it has something to do with feeling simultaneously small and connected to something larger. During awe, analytical thinking recedes; we simply experience, transcending the cerebral way in which we ordinarily engage with the world.

After years investigating this phenomenon, I’ve come to believe that awe offers a window into an overlooked aspect of human consciousness — one of science’s most elusive mysteries. If we can isolate and study the state of awe and similar self-transcendent experiences, we might deepen our understanding of our species, and of how we experience the world.

The problem with the thinking mind

When we think of consciousness, we imagine a conscious voice that says, “This is now” —  an idea that goes back at least as far as the 17th-century French philosopher René Descartes, who famously stated, “I think, therefore I am.” But what if this thinking (literally) has led us astray?

My inquiry into consciousness started in 2015, when I began researching analytical versus intuitive thinking. Having trained as a cognitive neuroscientist during my PhD at the University of Auckland in New Zealand, I’d always prioritized the rational mind, dismissing intuition as a lesser agency — one reserved for guessing games or New Age spirituality. It’s a predictable bias: Since Descartes, the Enlightenment and the Scientific Revolution, much of Western culture has privileged logic over the supposedly mercurial feelings of the body.

It wasn’t until I began working with Dr. Miguel Farias on the psychology of religion and spirituality that I questioned my assumptions about intuition. Our research challenged the idea that religious belief is necessarily rooted in intuitive rather than analytical thinking, and made me reconsider whether the preference for rational thought might be limiting how we understand the human mind. Even for an academic like me, who saw the body mostly as a way to transport my brain from place to place, experiences of awe like the one I had at Joshua Tree seemed too consequential to ignore. 

Research suggests that intuition plays an important role in how we perceive the world and make decisions, even when we’re not consciously aware of the processes guiding us. In a foundational study, neuroscientists Antoine Bechara, Antonio Damasio and their colleagues asked participants to choose cards from four decks — two advantageous and two disadvantageous. They found that subjects began showing subtle physiological signs of stress when approaching the unfavorable decks, even before they could consciously identify them as risky. The researchers interpreted these findings as evidence that the body can influence decisions before we can consciously explain them.

Psychologist Jonathan Haidt has made a similar argument about moral judgment, likening the rational mind to a press secretary: Rather than making decisions, the brain may simply explain and justify conclusions we’ve already reached intuitively. In a way it makes sense: Working memory, which supports analytical thinking, has a limited capacity. Yet there is a whole world around us that we need to take in, which the body does holistically through its various senses.

For me, these findings raised a larger question: How much of our experience of the world unfolds beyond the reach of reflective thought? And if we fail to fully study this intuitive, non-reflective dimension of our minds, how complete can our understanding of consciousness really be?

The self that thinking cannot capture

This question brought me back to an idea proposed more than a century ago by William James, widely regarded as the father of modern psychology. In his 1892 text, Psychology: Briefer Course, James distinguished between two aspects of the self, which he called the “Me” and the “I”:

“Whatever I may be thinking of, I am always at the same time more or less aware of myself, of my personal existence. At the same time it is I who am aware; so that the total self of me, being as it were duplex, partly known and partly knower, partly object and partly subject, must have two aspects discriminated in it, of which for shortness we may call one the Me and the other the I.”

In line with philosophical discussions, I developed modern definitions for the two aspects of James’s “total self.” His “Me” is what I call the reflective self-state: conscious awareness, where we think about ourselves, reflect on what we are doing or have done, interpret how we are perceived, and so on. It’s the type of thinking that can be described in language, and thus be made explicit. James’s “I” is what I have come to think of as the experiential self-state: the part of us that simply is — in the here and now, as a sensing entity. 

The experiential self-state is difficult to describe, because the moment we try to put it into words we shift toward the reflective self-state, making ourselves the object of our attention once again. But this doesn’t mean the experiential self is simply an absence of thought or intention. Rather, it’s a form of awareness in which bodily sensations, emotions and sensory information come together to guide our perceptions and responses, without deliberate thought. Deep meditation offers a useful example of the experiential self-state, as does awe.

What science might be missing about awe

This distinction between reflective and experiential awareness could help resolve a longstanding puzzle in the study of awe itself. To measure the awe we feel during concerts, psychedelic trips, collective rituals, mystical encounters and the like, researchers use the Awe Experience Scale (AWE-S), a survey tool developed by Johns Hopkins University psychologist David Yaden and his colleagues. 

I’ve used this scale extensively in my own research, and encountered a recurring puzzle. Participants sometimes describe feeling small or insignificant during awe, as I did at Joshua Tree, only for that sensation to give way to an overwhelming sense of connection. I wonder whether retrospective surveys capture this lasting connectedness more readily than the fleeting feeling of self-diminishment.

If so, it could be problematic. For example, in one study of nearly 500 ravegoers, my colleagues and I found that connectedness predicted how transformative participants considered their experiences, while self-diminishment did not. I suspect these seemingly contradictory sensations — feeling small yet big — may occur in a specific temporal sequence, such that feelings of connectedness remain, to the time of a survey, whereas self-diminishment does not.

My dual self-states theory offers a helpful framework: As the reflective self recedes, the experiential self becomes more prominent. Rather than contradicting each other, feelings of self-diminishment and connectedness may reflect two crucial dimensions of consciousness. As we become less focused on ourselves, this allows us to become more immersed in sensory experience, after the perceived boundaries between ourselves and the world begin to dissolve.

This distinction matters, because the way we measure awe determines what we can understand about it. If we capture only the sense of connectedness that people remember afterward, we may overlook the changes in self-awareness that unfold during the experience itself. Studying how these two self-states interact in real time could reveal not only what awe feels like, but also how it shapes and enriches our experience of the world and even the universe.

New windows into what it means to be human

Awe, meditation, and other self-transcendent experiences should not elude scientific inquiry simply because they are difficult to describe. I propose developing a psychological scale to measure the experiential self-state, so we can better understand these experiences.

Doing so would help us investigate experiences often described as ineffable, or beyond words, and ask more precise questions about powerful moments of awe that seem to deepen our sense of purpose and well-being: When does self-focused thought diminish, and when does a sense of connection emerge? Do bodily boundaries become less distinct? How do bodily signals shape our judgments before we can put reasons into words? And could becoming more attuned to these signals help us use them more effectively?

Perhaps the moments when we are least focused on ourselves — whether we are lost in music or immersed in nature — offer some of our best opportunities to understand what it truly means to be conscious.

This article was developed in partnership with the John Templeton Foundation.

The most transformative discoveries often begin by questioning the boundaries of what we think we know. The John Templeton Foundation’s Future of Intelligence venture supports research and dialogue that challenge what was once taken for granted: What is intelligence, and what might our conventional definitions miss in the worlds of plants, the cosmos, and AI? Learn more, apply for a grant, and sign up for the newsletter here.

items.title: How Voyager 1 became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day
items.summary: As of November 18, 2026, if you send a signal out at the speed of light in the direction of Voyager 1 — humanity’s most distant spacecraft — it will now take more than a full day for that signal to arrive . At that impressive distance, more than three times the distance to…
items.author: Ethan Siegel
items.contentHtml:
As of November 18, 2026, if you send a signal out at the speed of light in the direction of Voyager 1 — humanity’s most distant spacecraft — it will now take more than a full day for that signal to arrive. At that impressive distance, more than three times the distance to Pluto, over 16 billion miles, and over 25.9 billion kilometers away, the Sun appears 30,000 times fainter than it does from Earth. (That’s still brighter than the full Moon, but only by a factor of 14, or under three astronomical magnitudes.) It’s moving away from the Sun at a current speed of 60,770 km/hr (37,760 mph), and has reached that one light-day milestone after a cumulative journey of 49 years and 72 days.

In all the years since 1977, we’ve never launched another spacecraft that has rivaled Voyager 1. No other spacecraft has traveled as far; no other spacecraft is leaving the Solar System with as rapid a velocity; no current or even planned spacecraft is on track to ever overtake it. Voyager 1, the first spacecraft to exit the Solar System, is still the most distant, and looks to remain so for the foreseeable future. There’s a remarkable story behind this mission and how it achieved its record-breaking properties, and there’s an equally interesting story behind how we could someday catch or even surpass Voyager 1: if only we invested in doing so.

Anytime you want to send anything to any place in space, you have two options for how to get it there once you launch it above Earth’s atmosphere.

  1. The first option is to use some sort of engine — something that provides thrust, like rocket fuel — to propel your spacecraft to the needed speed in the proper direction, i.e., with the right trajectory, to get there.
  2. The second option is to take advantage of the natural gravity of other objects that you’ll encounter, such as planets that orbit the Sun or moons that orbit planets, in order to provide an “assist” to your spacecraft. This gravity assist maneuver can, depending on how it’s leveraged, provide either an increase or a decrease in speed, and can also alter your trajectory significantly in the process.

Of course, it’s possible to combine these two effects as well, in what’s known as either a powered flyby or the Oberth effect, to either gain or lose even more speed than using thrusters and gravity assists separately.

In the case of Voyager 1, it was launched on September 5, 1977, with an initial speed of around 40 km/s: the equivalent of 89,500 miles-per-hour or 144,000 km/hr. Interestingly, that launch date and launch speed were both later and slower than its twin: Voyager 2. However, they were designed for different purposes. Voyager 2 was planned to fly by Jupiter and Saturn in a way that could potentially take it to Uranus and Neptune afterward (performing a “grand tour” of the Solar System), while Voyager 1 was designed to fly by Jupiter, Saturn, and then to get a choice between heading all the way out to Pluto or to fly close to Saturn’s giant moon Titan. Because of these differences, different initial speeds and trajectories were required for each of the Voyagers.

Although Voyager 2 launched first and started out faster, it was passed by Voyager 1 on December 19th of 1977, as Voyager 1 headed on a more direct course toward Jupiter. On March 5, 1979, it arrived: Voyager 1 made a close approach of Jupiter, coming within 279,000 km of the edge of Jupiter’s atmosphere. It also flew by its moons Amalthea, Io (at a distance of just 20,570 km), Europa, and on March 6, by Ganymede and Callisto as well. Its views of Io, Ganymede, and Callisto, plus Jupiter, were the highest-resolution photos of those worlds ever taken. Its approach video to Jupiter remains one of the most iconic sequences in space history.

Another big surprise was the discovery of active volcanic activity on Io: now known to be the most volcanically active world in the Solar System. As Jupiter’s tidal forces continuously open cracks in Io’s crust and trigger massive volcanic eruptions, the entire world gets resurfaced on timescales of mere thousands of years, giving it the youngest surface in the entire Solar System. Io is the innermost of Jupiter’s four major Galilean moons, with the closest, tightest orbit around Jupiter of them all. Voyager 1 actually flew interior to Io’s orbit, passing just behind it mere hours after departing from its closest approach to Jupiter.

However, there was another purpose to flying so close to Jupiter on the specific trajectory that was chosen: to boost Voyager 1’s speed and alter its trajectory to send it on to Saturn. When choosing how to direct the spacecraft, the decision was made to go after an extremely close approach to Saturn’s Titan, rather than to go on an extended mission to Pluto. The reason was scientifically motivated: because Titan was known to have an atmosphere, and a substantial one at that. Therefore, the thinking was, more science value could be extracted by flying by Titan than by eschewing that to go after Pluto.

As a result of the close flyby to Jupiter, Voyager 1’s speed — which had dropped down to 13 km/s owing to the gravitational pull of the Sun as it sped away from it — shot back up to 23 km/s after receiving a near-maximal gravity assist.

A year and a half later, In November of 1980, Voyager 1 arrived at Saturn: double the distance from the Sun compared to Jupiter. Although its speed had slowed down to about 20 km/s owing to the continued, energy-draining climb out of the Sun’s gravitational potential well, it managed to pass incredibly close to Titan: passing within just 3915 km of its surface. Although the surface remained obscure, it was able to study Titan’s nitrogen-rich atmosphere along with the cloudy methane hazes present within it, paving the way for the later Cassini-Huygens mission. (Carolyn Porco, who became the Principal Investigator of Cassini-Huygens, was a Voyager imaging scientist prior to that.)

From November 12 through November 14, 1980, Voyager 1 also experienced close flybys of Saturn’s moons Tethys, Mimas, Enceladus, Rhea, and Hyperion, and came within 125,000 km of the edge of Saturn’s atmosphere. After experiencing a gravity assist from the Saturnian system by traveling extremely close to Titan and below Saturn’s south pole, it received both a speed boost and a trajectory change: boosting it back up to almost 22 km/s but taking it far out of the plane of the ecliptic. Because of this, it was unable to travel to other worlds within the Solar System, but the high-priority observations of Titan meant that the later-arriving Voyager 2 would be free to do exactly that. Voyager 2’s grand tour of the Solar System, which included visits to Uranus and Neptune, remain our most informative photos of both the Uranian and Neptunian systems even more than a quarter of the way through the 21st century.

Voyager 1’s boosted speed and new trajectory out of the ecliptic plane set it up for another set of amazing milestones, which it experienced as part of its still-ongoing extended mission. As it rises above the ecliptic plane at approximately a 35 degree angle, it heads, from our perspective, toward the constellation of Ophiuchus. From above the Solar System’s planets, it has the opportunity to look “down” on the planets orbiting the Sun, and to image them from a perspective that could never be acquired from within the Solar System’s plane itself.

In 1984, Voyager 1 crossed the orbit of Uranus: achieving an in-plane distance that exceeded the distance from the Sun to our Solar System’s 7th planet. In late 1988, it crossed outside the orbit of Neptune as well. That led to, in 1990, an interesting idea: Voyager 1, from its unique perch, could image each of the planets in the Solar System, one after the other, creating an iconic “family portrait” from an unprecedented perspective. Although Mercury was too dim and too close to the Sun to be imaged as part of it, and Mars was undetectable in the camera’s optics, the Voyager 1 images of Neptune, Uranus, Saturn, Jupiter, Earth, and Venus remain iconic. That view of Earth — the last picture of our home taken by Voyager 1 before its imaging camera was switched off — was immortalized as the Pale Blue Dot.

As Voyager 1 continued to recede from the Sun, its speed continued to gradually fall, yet remained higher than all other spacecraft at a comparable distance from the Sun. (Interestingly, if Voyager 2 had visited only Uranus and had skipped Neptune, it would have wound up going faster than Voyager 1.) As various milestones were reached, its speed gradually dropped even as its distance continued to increase, and to increase faster than all other spacecraft on their way out of the Solar System.

  • On February 17, 1998, Voyager 1 overtook Pioneer 10 — launched 5 years earlier than Voyager 1 back in 1972 — as the most distant spacecraft. It continues to extend its distance record over Pioneer 10’s reach as time goes on: by more than 150,000,000 km per year.
  • On December 17, 2004, at a distance of 94 AU from the Sun (where 1 AU is the Earth-Sun distance), it passed the termination shock of our Solar System, entering the heliosheath region.
  • On December 13, 2010, Voyager 1 confirmed the lack of detection of the outward flow of solar wind particles from the Sun, thought to arise when the solar wind encounters the interstellar wind that pushes against the heliosphere, turning solar wind particles sideways. The solar wind flux dropped to zero back in June of 2010, but the Low Energy Charged Particle device provided confirmation of this fact six months afterward.
  • And on August 25, 2012, at a distance of 121 AU, it crossed over the boundary of the heliopause: officially becoming humanity’s first spacecraft to enter interstellar space. (Voyager 2 did it afterward in 2018, and later, in 2023, overtook Pioneer 10 for second place in distance from the Sun.)

Over all that time, its velocity away from the Sun continued to drop: down to a current value 16.88 km/s as of November 18, 2026. It won’t decrease much more than that; at its current distance of 1 light-day, the gravitational influence of the Sun is extremely small. Overall, the Sun will “steal” about another 1000 km/hr (620 mph) of recession speed from Voyager 1, meaning that it will wind up slowing down to a recession speed of 16.6 km/s and then will remain there. This is well above the Sun’s escape velocity at the distance of Voyager 1 (which is only 3.2 km/s), and so the final stage of its voyage — to the stars — has already commenced.

Voyager 2, Pioneer 10, Pioneer 11, Ulysseys, and New Horizons are the only other spacecraft ever launched by humans that will also escape (or have escaped) from the Solar System’s pull, and the gravitational influence of the Sun. New Horizons was launched most recently, in 2006, but despite its greater initial launch velocity, it only ever received a meaningful gravity assist from Jupiter, and as of today, is only receding from the Sun at 13.6 km/s: not enough to ever catch or surpass Voyager 1. Ulysses was a Sun-observing spacecraft never intended to exit the Solar System, but a gravitational encounter with Jupiter in 2098 will put it on an escape course as well.

All five of these spacecraft are already behind Voyager 1 in terms of distance, and Voyager 1 will continue to put more distance between them far into the future as well.

It will take a little under 18,000 years for Voyager 1 to reach a further milestone of 1 light-year from Earth: something that should happen around the 199th century. After approximately 75,000 years, it will be more distant from the Sun than the next-nearest star presently is, although the positions of the stars will change substantially over tens of thousands of years, too. Although Voyager 1 doesn’t have enough power or fuel on board to be redirected to eventually encounter a star, that remains a possibility for New Horizons, albeit one that’s not favored by the current science team.

Even without the development of new space travel technologies, however, the “alignment” that enabled the historic Voyager missions to take place was rare, but not unique. A combination of:

  • a high launch velocity,
  • the proper alignment of the planets and planned gravity assists,
  • and the implementation of Oberth maneuvers, as appropriate,

could lead to several profound advances. A planetary alignment occurring in 2034 could enable a spacecraft that was properly designed, like the Origins, Dynamics, and Interiors of the Neptunian and Uranian Systems (ODINUS) mission, to reach Uranus in 2047 and Neptune in 2050, leaving orbiters at both of them. A new close-up view of the outer worlds of our Solar System remains plausible, with new windows opening up roughly every 12 years with alignments between Earth, Jupiter, Uranus, and Neptune.

If the goal was instead to leave the Solar System at maximum speed, there are several options for going much faster than Voyager 1 went at.

  • A series of unpowered gravity assist maneuvers using the outer planets could create a “velocity at infinity,” which is 16.6 km/s for Voyager 1, of up to 40 km/s.
  • A series of Oberth maneuvers, using the combination of on-board thrusters to enhance gravity assists, could lead to realistic speeds that reach up to 60 km/s.
  • And the most severe option, to steal most of a spacecraft’s velocity to bring it within just a few solar radii of the Sun and then use powered gravity assists (Oberth maneuvers), could lead to “velocity at infinity” of up to 100 km/s: about 6 times the speed of Voyager 1.

It’s vital to remember that the distances between stars is vast, so even though Voyager 1 has nearly a half-century head start on anything we’d send out to attempt to catch it, it could easily be surpassed within centuries, and that a nearby star system, such as the Alpha/Proxima Centauri system — if we were inclined to design such a mission — could be reached with current technology before Voyager 1 were even one light-year away. We can actually explore the Universe if we so choose; all it takes is a commitment to put the resources and the right people in the right places to make it happen. Voyager 1’s latest milestone is a reminder of how far we can go; we just have to collectively choose to do it.

items.title: Who’s going to profit from Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO?
items.summary: Morning Brew Inc. Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO this week really has to work, as investors question the billions of dollars the AI market has hoovered up. A record-setting market debut for the giant could revitalize the sluggish tech sector—and spill into the broader US…
items.author: Matty Merritt
items.contentHtml:
Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO this week really has to work, as investors question the billions of dollars the AI market has hoovered up. A record-setting market debut for the giant could revitalize the sluggish tech sector—and spill into the broader US economy.

The company will officially price its initial public offering today, before trading on the Nasdaq tomorrow under the ticker “ANT.” The IPO will not be very ant-like: Anthropic initially set shares at $70 to $78 apiece, and at the top end of its pricing, it would raise $90.4 billion, with a valuation at $1.4 trillion. As banks closed share orders yesterday afternoon, orders were seven times the number of available shares, according to Bloomberg.

  • Anthropic’s share price could be over $80 today, according to a Wall Street Journal report.
  • That would mean a valuation as high as $1.6 trillion.

As the first major AI lab to go public, the IPO is viewed as a high-stakes stress test for both the AI industry and the entire global economy. A disappointing opening would still net investors huge gains, but it’d also add further fuel to ongoing AI skepticism.

Who’s set to gain?

For starters, the 300 or so investors who threw money at Anthropic, according to PitchBook. Some of the biggest venture capital funds are already preparing the champagne bottles: Menlo Ventures was in for $750 million in 2023. Lightspeed Venture Partners led a $3.5 billion round in 2025, and earlier this year, Sequoia, Greenoaks, and Altimeter joined private equity and corporate buddies to raise Anthropic’s largest funding round of $65 billion.

  • In the first half of this year, AI has snagged $355.9 billion from VC funds. That’s 86% of all US venture capital funding in that time frame, according to Clearstead’s analysis of Pitchbook data.
  • Because so much of AI development is concentrated in San Francisco, the city is taking in a third of all global VC dollars right now, according to PitchBook.

Who else is getting rich? An average Anthropic employee could see their equity balloon to $72 million. The company’s biggest customers, Amazon and Google, are set to own roughly 28% of Anthropic’s stock after the IPO.—MM

items.title: Jensen’s former employer reports stellar earnings
items.summary: Cheng Xin/Getty Images Nvidia reported earnings yesterday, but much bigger than its revenue doubling in 12 months was the elephant in the room. The better-than-expected Q3 report card dropped days after Jensen Huang became Nvidia’s ex-CEO amid revelations about his romantic…
items.author: Sam Klebanov
items.contentHtml:
Nvidia reported earnings yesterday, but much bigger than its revenue doubling in 12 months was the elephant in the room. The better-than-expected Q3 report card dropped days after Jensen Huang became Nvidia’s ex-CEO amid revelations about his romantic relationships with a suspected Chinese spy, as well as two employees.

Financially, things look great. Revenue rose 20% from the previous quarter, and the company predicted it will grow 12% in Q4. Interim CEO Colette Kress said the company is boosting its 2028 growth outlook from 70% to 75%, giving investors hope that the chipmaker could persevere post-Jensanity. Nvidia shares rose in after-hours trading.

But things will be different:

  • Nvidia will stop selling certain chips to China, signifying a pivot away from Huang’s push to promote ties to the country.
  • Kress said Nvidia will be “disciplined and selective” about supporting other AI companies, a sign it might retreat from its role as a financial backstop to the industry.

Jensen spoke out. In his first public statement since the ouster, Huang said earlier in the day that he’d be “honored” to return as CEO. But board chair Harvey Jones reiterated on the earnings call that that’s not being considered.

We’ll hear from him again: Huang will testify to Congress about Nvidia’s compliance with chip export controls on Dec. 1.—SK

items.title: Kalshi bets on Martha Stewart to clean up its image
items.summary: Kalshi Prediction markets are plagued by a reputation for being susceptible to insider trading. That’s why Kalshi enlisted Martha Stewart to star in a new ad warning potential customers about the consequences of rigging markets and the platform’s new safeguards against it. The…
items.author: Dave Lozo
items.contentHtml:
Prediction markets are plagued by a reputation for being susceptible to insider trading. That’s why Kalshi enlisted Martha Stewart to star in a new ad warning potential customers about the consequences of rigging markets and the platform’s new safeguards against it.

The 90-second spot features Stewart—who was never convicted of insider trading but was found guilty of lying to investigators in a trading scandal—in a replica of the kitchen from her 1990s TV show preparing a pie but leaving out the ingredient of confidential information (it’s not the best metaphor).

Kalshi also announced it would follow the recommendation of an integrity committee to provide more tailored surveillance around markets depending on their risk profile. The company said that grouping marketswith similar insider trading risks together will “reduce false positives” and “focus review on higher-risk activity.”

Hours after the marketing blitz began, The Wall Street Journal reported that Kalshi is halting trading on markets that allow users to put money down on what words President Trump will say on a given date, after the Commodity Futures Trading Commission ordered it to do so on Friday. The CFTC said it was due to the ease with which these markets could be influenced. In August, a White House teleprompter operator settled an insider trading case with federal regulators.—DL

Big Think hosted a live event on our latest issue, Made in Our Image, which explores the philosophies behind artificial intelligence and what they reveal about us. Executive Producer Dan Hayes sat down with the writers behind the magazine for a candid conversation about the human side of this century’s most consequential technology, along with a behind-the-scenes look at what went into making our favorite issue yet.

DAN: .It's a real point of pride for us at Big Think to produce these quarterly magazines. It's amazing to have a real-life thing you can put on your nightstand or coffee table and read in the real world. The response has frankly been overwhelming since we started. We continue to find more and more people who value big ideas, who are yearning for an analog thought partner, if you will. So shout-out to the whole team who made this possible. Thank you, guys. You're the best.

I have two awesome writers with me today, Afra Wang and Namir Khaliq. Here's what we're going to get into. I'm going to throw 10 or 15 questions at you, just so you have context for where we're going.

We're going to start by learning about the AI-generated film Zombie Scavenger, and what Afra thought she was going to find exploring AI slop and AI content creation in China. At some point I want to ask Afra what the worst piece of slop she saw while reporting this story was. I want to talk a little about the relationship between censorship and art, and what AI slop might ultimately have to do with China's ghost cities. There's an interesting parallel that Afra draws in her story.

We'll also talk through the relationship between Afra's AI slop article and Namir's permanent underclass piece, which I think have some overlapping themes. I'm going to share a little about my experiences with AI as a filmmaker for the group to consider. Then, with Namir, we're going to talk about the idea of a permanent underclass. Is it real, or just a meme on X? Is AI the new industrial revolution, this time for knowledge workers? Is every generation convinced it's living through the end of history? Is it evolutionarily harder for us humans to genuinely imagine real upsides?

Is our nation's character, from Silicon Valley to Wall Street to the American West, built on the virtue of labor? What happens if intelligent machines give us everything we could ever want? What might there be left to do with our lives in an AI-delivered utopia? And the last one: Do humans have a basic need to contribute in order to find meaning in our lives?

Those are some of the topics we're going to explore. You can also put your questions in the chat, and my colleague Claire is going to pop on toward the end to share them. This is your chance to engage with some super smart and interesting people, so please feel free to load us up with questions, and we'll hit a bunch of them toward the end of the hour.

Thank you both so much for being with us today. Afra, I want to start with you. Can you give us your personal background, so people understand how you got into this space in the first place? And please be sure to touch on your brief, dreamlike internship in the film industry.

AFRA: Yeah, of course. I've been a cinephile for as long as I can remember. So when some video generation tools emerged from the Chinese AI space, I got really interested and really excited. At that moment, the whole discourse about the US-China AI race was already happening, and OpenAI had abandoned their Sora project. If you remember Sora, there was a brief moment when everyone could use ChatGPT's newest video generation tools to generate a bunch of slop. One of the most memorable was Sam Altman stealing GPUs from a random shopping mall, if you remember that.

I was really intrigued by the level of creativity AI video generation as a vertical could reach. At the same time, China seemed to have an advantage, in the sense that a lot more video generation tools were coming out of China's innovation space, and a lot more people seemed to want to jump into AI and creativity. Meanwhile, in the West, if you're a reputable director and you dare to say out loud, "I'm optimistic about AI, I want to embrace this technology," you'll probably get denounced by your peers, or feel morally delinquent, because a lot of people are protesting against AI. Unions in Hollywood are constantly organizing anti-AI activities.

So I thought, okay, is this China's big opportunity to forge its own soft power through AI-generated content? That was my sort of 4D chess in my mind. I really wanted to understand this phenomenon, so I got into the space. I talked to many filmmakers, many producers, and many young people in their early 20s who had jumped into this space. I also watched a lot of AI slop myself. I downloaded a bunch of vertical short-video apps and spent hours and hours watching them, hoping to find something touching, something moving, something fundamentally artistic. What I found was this complex, this industrial-scale slop generation machine, which I wrote about in my article.

As for my dream internship: I was a typical first-year college student who didn't know what to do over the summer. I was still a kid. I asked my mom, "If I spend two months in Beijing" (that's where I grew up, where my parents were) "what should I do?" My mom had some connections, and she got me into that internship. It was really fun. I was able to chat with a lot of Hong Kong directors. Beijing was a gold mountain back then. A lot of Hong Kong filmmakers, really the entire industry, were moving north and making Beijing a center of their artistic practice, so there was a big Hong Kong diaspora in Beijing. I was hanging out with a lot of those Hong Kong directors who had witnessed the most legendary phase of the golden age of Hong Kong cinema.

DAN: That's awesome. That sounds like a pretty cool experience. So your hopes for AI film were high, given your background. Can you share the example of Zombie Scavenger? There have been glimmers of hope in what you've seen in China in terms of creativity, and you thought maybe this was the new way forward for AI. Tell people about that film and what happened after.

AFRA: Yeah, absolutely. If you're familiar with Love, Death & Robots, the Netflix short series, Zombie Scavenger feels like one of those episodes. It's a very short piece, about three minutes, but the universe it brought me into was very real and very coherent. It's like how Love, Death & Robots gives you a complete story setting and invites you into a unique storytelling space: something happened in outer space, something happened in the future, something happened in a post-apocalyptic world. Zombie Scavenger is one of those stories. It takes place in a world where humans went extinct because of a zombie outbreak, and the whole story is a romance between a robot and a mannequin.

It's really whimsical and romantic, and it has a lot of interesting motifs from '60s Hollywood movies, from the cowboy genre, and from the zombie genre. It really paid tribute to a lot of familiar motifs we all know. Then I learned that this short wasn't produced by one of those top-notch teams at Netflix. It was produced by a nobody, a 28-year-old nobody from Yunnan province. Not even Beijing or Shanghai, those cosmopolitan cities, but a very distant province. The filmmaker himself is a wedding photographer. He doesn't speak English; he didn't even make the film in English. But in the end, you get this Hollywood-quality output. That became huge news in the Chinese AI filmmaking industry.

DAN: And real quick, Afra, you said it was produced in 10 days for $442. And it led to American filmmakers calling this kid and saying, "You should come and produce stuff with us." So this was a real moment in AI filmmaking.

AFRA: Yeah, absolutely. The film became internationally renowned in a sense. Chinese AI filmmakers were very invigorated by it, and American filmmakers were thinking, okay, China is probably going to have an asymmetrical advantage. A lot more hidden talent is going to flourish because this tool lets people make something like this for a few hundred dollars. I was excited, a lot of Hollywood filmmakers were excited, and there was an effort to scout for talent from Hollywood. I personally know this filmmaker was contacted by a lot of Hollywood producers at the time, and many more young Chinese people were dreaming of being contacted by Hollywood filmmakers. So that was a very optimistic moment, and it got me started on this scavenger hunt through Chinese AI innovation in moviemaking.

DAN: And so then you were like, all right, cool, let's go find all the other cool examples. But basically, you watched 15-plus AI films and tons more shorts, and you felt like you were in an uncanny valley that was terrible. What's some of the worst stuff you saw? And what makes this AI content actually slop? There are blurry lines, so why do you consider it slop?

AFRA: Mostly, the reason you don't feel good after watching them is very similar to why you don't feel good after spending two hours scrolling TikTok. You've viscerally been hacked by the algorithm. Your dopamine is being depleted by the algorithm. While you're watching, you're hooked by very tacky, shocking, dramatic plots. Someone accidentally gets pregnant with a baby by both her husband and her husband's brother. There are certain elements of those dramas that are just subversively controversial and make you want to keep going. And the reason you want to keep going is not good. It's not your artistic curiosity or your intellectual curiosity. It's just that your dopamine has been hacked.

You're like a monkey that's been fed one bite of banana and wants to chase the next bite. I really felt like an animal being harnessed by the algorithm to keep watching, and I honestly don't appreciate that feeling. All those AI slops don't have deliberate or thoughtful plotlines. The plotlines just maximize how much drama can happen within three or four minutes. Then you need to hit the next one, and three episodes later, you need to pay to keep watching.

DAN: I feel like it's not necessarily slop, but even modern YouTube influencer content has a certain characteristic, and definitely a certain pace. As a filmmaker, I can see it's going so fast. There's no space, no breath, because they're just trying to give people that story hit, that bite, to keep propelling them through a narrative. When I watch even modern YouTubers, it's hypercut, and the shots are so quick that I feel assaulted, or just tired watching it. It's kind of crazy.

That's super interesting. And you're saying they're creating this stuff at incredible scale, basically trying to find a hit that makes this economic engine for producing slop viable. Talk a little about the scale of this. Afterward, I want to chat about the ghost cities, and then we'll head over to Namir for a bit.

AFRA: Totally. After you watch enough AI slop, you start to notice that a lot of the female and male faces are converging into a very similar shape. They have very similar layouts of noses and eyes and ears. All of a sudden you think, there must be a vast industry behind this, probably because of economic incentives. So I started to dig in, and, not entirely to my surprise, it's highly tied to China's regional competition.

China has 30-plus provinces, and each province, whether economically advanced or not, wants a share of the most advanced technological development that the central government is signaling to the entire state. Since 2024, Xi Jinping himself has publicly announced many times that AI is going to diffuse into many industries in China. AI is what they call the highest-quality "productive force." This is a very Marxist term. It means electricity was once that, energy was once that, and now it's AI. So Beijing sent a very clear signal to all the local governments and entrepreneurs that AI will be the thing that fuels the engine of China's innovation.

This is basically how China works: Beijing sends out a signal and lets the local governments interpret it and figure out what it means. After the AI Plus initiative was announced, many local governments started to think, okay, how can we participate in this new innovation, this industrial upgrade? How can we not be left behind? How can we have a piece of this strategic technology when we don't have enough talent?

I'm not talking about Beijing, Shanghai, or Shenzhen. Those advanced coastal cities were already participating in the AI revolution. I'm talking about many distant provinces and regions. One example would be Nanjing. It's a city with a large population, but nobody really sees Nanjing as a tech hub or AI hub. There's Hefei. There are many second-tier and third-tier cities saying, okay, we want to jump on this AI bandwagon and create a strategic AI initiative in our region. But what can we do that has the lowest barrier to entry? That's AI video generation. You can just get some compute, get a bunch of young people, plant some seeds in their minds, and have them be creative.

That's an easy, participatory action a local government can take. So many governments started talent incubation programs, where they held public AI video generation competitions to attract people to submit their work and start their own studios. The local government would then give them subsidies or rewards to make the whole space more prosperous and popular. The whole industrial AI slop complex was pretty much a result of this regional competition among different local governments in China.

DAN: So that's one of the reasons there's been such scale and volume in producing this AI slop. By the way, this is all totally new to me. I had no context for the Chinese cultural and policy side of this, so this was a really good educational article. Last question for you, and then, Namir, we'll head your way. You compare this to the ghost cities in China, these huge cities that were built at massive scale but are now empty and full of weeds. Help us understand that analogy.

AFRA: I think it goes back to the downside of regional competition. China's regional competition has its own merits. The reason China is winning the EV race, the reason China was able to produce so many solar panels, the reason China was able to generate so much electricity and harness so much solar and hydropower, is that different regions compete against each other. They want a strategic advantage in certain important industries.

At the same time, you have a very severe issue called overcapacity. Overcapacity is essentially something like a ghost city, where local officials were convinced that building infrastructure was fundamentally important. It's their way of getting promoted, of showing they're diligent civil servants, of being part of China's economic miracle. So everyone started building infrastructure, building cities, inviting real estate developers, and lending a bunch of money for those projects. In the end, China has a tremendous number of unoccupied, vacant high-rise buildings and residential complexes that nobody was able to afford or buy. And right now in China, the real estate bubble has burst too, so the ghost city scenario is even more severe. You drive to the suburbs and see a brand-new city appear in front of you, but it doesn't have many people.

The exact same thing happened with China's high-speed railways. Today, 80% to 85% of Chinese high-speed rail lines are losing money, because many were built to connect distant cities to other distant cities, and there isn't enough traffic to cover the cost.

And the exact same thing happened in AI slop generation. After all this talent and compute and local subsidies poured into the space, you get a tremendous amount of content that nobody is watching. If you understand the YouTube or TikTok algorithms, you know they follow a power law. The top tier of creators, the 1%, occupy maybe 90% of people's attention. The same thing happened on those short-form AI video platforms. The result is a tremendous amount of stuff being produced that nobody watches, and people trying to squeeze out that 1% of good content and replicate it. So you see this homogenizing tendency, where all the characters look very similar, because a similar face was probably in one of the hits from two months ago, and they're trying to replicate that exact face in the next plotline. All these weird, uncanny things happen, and it just isn't a pleasant experience. In the end, I felt like I was venturing into many, many ghost cities. It's just not very good. I think I wrote this out of some slop PTSD. I got really overwhelmed. I wanted a mental cleanse.

DAN: You've got to go watch some classic old films. Watch 8½ by Fellini or something, get yourself out of there. I thought it was really interesting. First of all, I think we should solve the US housing crisis by airlifting China's ghost cities into the US. I don't know if that would work, but maybe if we get big enough ships. But no, this article is awesome. The industrial slop complex, and the design is really cool. So if you members have your magazines, check out Afra's awesome article. Thank you so much, Afra, for educating us on this. It was really, really cool.

AFRA: Thank you so much, Dan.

NAMIR: Can I jump in with a final question? One: Who is watching this sort of stuff in China? Is it young people? Old people? Everyone? No one? And two: Do you have a theory as to why China hasn't been able to develop the same sort of international cultural reputation as even South Korea or Japan, let alone the US? Do they just not have the same internal culture developed as these other places, or what's the cause?

AFRA: I'll answer the first question first: Who's watching AI slop? Everyone, from 70-year-old grandpas to 15-year-old high schoolers. If there's a US-China AI race, I think the US and China are also racing to brain-rot each other's populations. And if there's a brain-rot race, China is probably winning right now.

A couple of weeks ago, there was a huge debate online about compute usage in China versus the US. Some argued that half of Chinese compute goes to AI slop generation, while a lot of US compute goes to R&D, software

The consciousness theory that connects you to everything
We’ve learned that even single-celled organisms can make intelligent decisions. What else can you expect from consciousness? Neuropsychiatrist Iain McGilchrist explains.
Iain McGilchrist
