How your brain’s hemispheres actually work
Iain McGilchrist
9mins
The Well
The consciousness theory that connects you to everything
Iain McGilchrist

Psychiatrist Iain McGilchrist has spent 35 years studying how the brain shapes consciousness. In this full interview, he explains why the two hemispheres attend to the world in radically different ways, and how one narrow, grasping mode has come to dominate Western civilization. He then explores the nature of reality: a creative cosmos that flows at the edge of chaos, where consciousness is primary and matter is one of its phases. He closes with what makes a human life flourish.

IAIN MCGILCHRIST: One thing one can say about the cosmos, pretty much without fear of contradiction, is that it is creative. It begins, we are told, with this very simple compact mass and then has expanded into the vast universe that we are still exploring and in which there is so much complexity unfolding. This seems to be key to the nature of everything that exists.

When it comes to the brain and the ability to understand the creative nature of the cosmos, the right hemisphere alone sees it.

I really argue very strongly that unless we take seriously the demonstrable differences — anatomical, physiological, neuropsychological — between these two hemispheres, unless we take that seriously, we're missing something that is at the core of our being.

My name's Iain McGilchrist, and I've spent the best part of 35 years studying how consciousness is structured by the brain.

Part 1: Our brain hemispheres and their split worlds.

Chapter 1: What do we get wrong about the left and right hemispheres?

Everybody thinks they know what the real differences between the right and left hemisphere are. Because in the 1980s, 90s, there was a lot of loose talk about what the differences were. And you know, the left hemisphere was a little bit boring, but down to earth, reliable and really intelligent. Whereas the right hemisphere was a bit airy-fairy and sort of creative, but unreliable. Everything in that is wrong.

So, first thing that I would say about the differences between the hemispheres is that there is absolutely no question that they're there and that they're important. This is a vital thing to say because once people realized that the pop psychology on this topic emanating at the end of the 20th century was wrong, they simply gave up the topic altogether as a bad job and decided that since we knew that both hemispheres were involved in everything, there were no differences. But that's quite illogical. Just because they're both involved in something doesn't mean to say that they do things the same way. They importantly don't. It wasn't the what of what they did, it was the how. And by the how, I don't mean by what mechanism, I mean the manner in which they approached what they were doing.

I think I've always been very interested in ideas. That's my probably greatest motivation. So I wanted to read theology and philosophy at Oxford, and I went to all the philosophy seminars on the mind-body problem, which had obsessed me since studying English, because it seemed to me that what happened in the seminar room when people approached the work of literature was that it became suddenly terrifically abstract and disembodied.

And in that time, almost by accident, I went one afternoon, I almost didn't, but I'm glad, very, very glad I did. I went to a lecture at the Institute of Psychiatry in London where I was training. And it was by a man I didn't know called John Cutting, who was a consultant at the Maudsley Hospital. And he'd just published a book called "The Right Cerebral Hemisphere and Psychiatric Disorders." And I was just intrigued because I'd not heard much about the right cerebral hemisphere. Nobody really knew what it did. And here was a man who'd written a long and learned book about all the things that the right hemisphere of the brain does do. And when I heard him talking that afternoon, my life was transformed. The direction of my life was changed.

Because I heard him talking about what the right hemisphere is able to do. And he — he said three things that immediately struck me. One is that the right hemisphere understands implicit meaning, whereas the left hemisphere takes everything at face value and entirely explicitly. So it doesn't understand poetry, doesn't understand metaphor, doesn't have a sense of humor, sarcasm, irony, all those things that make the art of literature alive. That was one.

The second was that the right hemisphere had closer and more profuse connections, intimate connections with the body than the left hemisphere.

And the third was that the right hemisphere understood the unique case, whereas the left hemisphere always saw something as an example of a kind, of a general type. It made the unique general, it took everything out of context, and that context was partly the body, and it made the implicit explicit, and its power suddenly vanished. It's like explaining a joke. Once you've explained it, it's not funny anymore. Once you've ripped a poem apart, it's not a poem anymore. And so the right hemisphere is the one that actually enables us to understand what's going on in the world.

Chapter 2: Why are the left and right hemispheres different?

First of all, there is the question, why are they divided? Because after all, the brain is just a mass of interconnected nerve cells or neurons. The number of neurons and the number of connections gives you an idea of how powerful they are. They have a band of fibers at the base of the brain called the corpus callosum. Only 2% of neurons actually cross that commissure, and a lot of the traffic is inhibitory. It's going from one hemisphere to the other and saying, you keep out of this, I'm dealing with it. What's that about?

They have differences in physiology, so they react differently to endocrine hormones, they use different neurotransmitters, or at least different preponderances of those neurotransmitters. They respond differently to drugs. And they are massively different in the ways in which they construe reality. And that is the bit that really interests me.

So why are there all those differences? Because ultimately they need to see the world differently. Every creature has to solve the ultimate conundrum of survival, how to eat without being eaten. And that is much harder than it sounds because to eat, you have to be able to look out for things that will grab your attention. Yes. Yes, that, yes. So you have to be locked onto a small target, and you have to be able to see it with great precision as a detail that you know where to get it very quickly. So all that attention is locked on to a tiny detail that is not part of a big picture that makes any sense. It's just a seed, a worm. As creatures have become more complicated, they can be things like, for a bird, picking up a twig to build a nest or whatever it might be. And in humans, it becomes fashioning a tool. So all that is the left hemisphere's job.

But if that's the only kind of attention a creature pays, it will not last longer than a few minutes, because it has to be looking out at the same time for a predator. It has to be looking out for its mate, for its kin. These are key elements of the survival of any creature.

And so the solution is that there must be two neuronal masses, each of them complex enough to sustain consciousness and attend to the world, but in two utterly different ways. One with this detailed, focused attention to a tiny particle, and the other completely differently, a broad, open, sustained, vigilant attention for anything, without any preconception as to what it might be.

Now what this means, since how we attend to the world changes what we find there — if you're attending to something and looking just for one thing, you'll only see that one thing — that means that if these two hemispheres are attending quite differently, they will find different worlds. What are those two worlds like?

Chapter 3: What two worlds do the hemispheres see?

I sometimes think, suppose I'd never seen a motorbike before. Somebody produced a motorbike and perhaps I'd never seen a machine of its kind at all. And I think, sort of, well, how do I understand this? With my left hemisphere, I said, right, I'm going to take it into the garage and I'm going to lie it on its side and I'm going to unscrew all those bolts and separate all the parts and count. We've got 15 of those and three of those and one of those and one of those. That's what a motorbike is. That is, as it were, a parody of the left hemisphere's attempt to understand it. But the right hemisphere's attempt would be, I'm going to get on this thing and ride it. And it's only in the riding of it that you understand what it is.

In the case of the left hemisphere, there's a world of bits. None of them mean anything on their own except they're useful. You want them. And they're decontextualized, they're abstract, they're non-unique, they're just another seed, another worm, whatever it is. And they're just stuff. And the whole drive is to amass more stuff. That's its only value is to get, get, get. Grab, grab, grab.

Meanwhile, the right hemisphere is seeing another world, which is not made up of things that are certain and fixed, as they are in the left hemisphere, but may be something other than what you expect. These are things that change with context. The context changes everything. They're things that may well be implicit, and if we don't see them, we're missing most of what is important. The things that give life meaning and are massively important to us are things like love, friendship, sex, religion, art, poetry, music, ritual, narrative. All these things depend on being implicit. You can make them explicit, but when you've made them explicit, they become something else. And often you just fail to grasp what it was that you were trying to express. So the right hemisphere picture is massively more imaginatively rich and intelligently understood than that of the left hemisphere, which is just, oh yeah, more stuff, I'll have that.

This is really, really crucial. Emotional and social intelligence, cognitive intelligence, creativity, all those are better done by the right hemisphere. But there is one category, apprehension, grasping things, say, I've got it. That one thing is so much better in the left hemisphere that it explains why the left hemisphere has developed just to do that one thing, getting stuff without which we can't survive. But all the understanding, the intelligence is in the right hemisphere.

But, you know, for me, just going about my ordinary life, why would I need to know that? I mean, why do I, as long as my brain's working, I don't care where it's going on. But there is an important payoff, and it's this, that we can tell when people have arrived at a conclusion using the typical mode of understanding of the left hemisphere. And we can tell when they've used the typical mode of understanding of the right hemisphere. And we can now say that the conclusion according to the left hemisphere mode is much less likely to be true to reality than the way of understanding that comes with the right hemisphere.

Part 2: Where our left brain has led us.

Chapter 4: What kind of society have we created?

People say, you seem to argue we've lost the ability to use the right hemisphere. And I say, no, no, no, no. It's just there. We're just not using it. You can use it right now. And in that sense, it is like a radio set. You know, I can imagine if you bought one, and when you first get it, you tune into two channels. This is great. And then after a while, you start listening only to one. If you decided you missed the other channel, you don't have to buy a new set. It's still there. So we can always tune back into these things.

Einstein said, "The rational mind is a faithful servant. The intuitive mind is a precious gift. We live in a world that honors the servant but has forgotten the gift." So the left hemisphere has something definitely to offer. It's just that when it thinks it understands the whole picture, it very definitely doesn't, and it leads us astray.

And what I think I have been able to see is that three times a civilization seems to have moved from a position in which it was benefiting from the best that can be offered by both the left and the right hemisphere. Around the 6th century BC in Athens, around the year dot in Rome, at the end of the Republic and the beginning of the Empire, and then again in Western Europe, perhaps in the 15th century, roughly speaking. The beginnings of the Renaissance. So these were three periods in which, in each case, there was an enormous, sudden step forward in the arts, in drama, in music, in poetry, in architecture, but also in science, in maths, in mapping the heavens, in mapping the Earth. And that impetus toward something wonderful lasted for usually two or three hundred years, but gradually decayed in every case into a society that was dominated by a very crude vision, and that crude vision is that of the left hemisphere.

But then the question arises, why? And I think the answer is this. It's something to do with the size of a society. It's very hard for us now to realize how small ancient Athens was. It was a small community. So people knew one another. And then through trade, it expanded, it had colonies and so forth. Now, that's just one strand, but it's an important strand. Because what it means is that something that was tailor-made for a small group of people gets formularized, if I can put it in that way, and is, as we now put it, rolled out as a single blanket answer to government. So enormous bureaucracies that follow rules set at the center and are dealing with situations at the periphery that are completely different from those for which this set of rules was devised.

And I talk about ways in which we dealt more and more in concepts, not in embodied realities, in abstractions. Indeed, one of the interesting things is the advent of money, which are tokens that stand for real things. But these are virtual, interchangeable, very left-hemisphere tokens for things.

But another is this. When a society begins to develop a formal philosophy, not in the way that in the East this happened, but the sayings of a few sages, but actually people debating. So is this right or is that right? And what do you think and so on? Now, when you get that, what tends to happen is you move into left-hemisphere mode because the left hemisphere tends to say, well, they can't both be right. One of these has got to be right. Now, ancient wisdom, both West and East, says that very often both of these things need to be validated because both of them can be true. They depend on the context. But what you get is that one must triumph over the other. And this process leads to becoming rigid of the way of thinking and abstraction in the way of thinking. And soon you're in a world where everything is decided by chopping logic. That's what happened.

And I think that in our own case, it was massively accelerated by three things, really. First was the so-called scientific revolution at the end of the 17th century, in which people began to think, actually, science can answer all our questions. And, of course, what was wonderful is that science was beginning to give very good answers to all sorts of things that we hadn't known before. And, you know, it's not surprising that if you were alive at that time and involved in the process, you'd jump quickly to the conclusion that science can answer all our questions. Subsequent history has revealed that that actually is never going to be the case.

Then there was an extension of that, which was the Enlightenment. So the 18th century philosophers who believed once again that the answers to all questions were coherent with one another, could be argued for in such a way that you could present them on a piece of paper to another person and they understood it completely.

Then there came the Industrial Revolution, and the Industrial Revolution was a perfect example of the externalization of the left hemisphere's mode. We need more and more power, and we need more and more stuff, and we now have machines that can make it faster. More than our greatest dreams can be realized by amassing stuff and exploiting people to work for gain, for me. It's so very left-hemispheric. The Industrial Revolution exemplified this drive towards the mechanistic, the analytical, the amassing of stuff.

And then in the 20th century, we had these movements in ideas that got us further and further away from reality. The denial that there was any reality, that there was any truth, that there was any beauty, that there was any real goodness. And that corrosive cynicism destroyed art, destroyed the cohesion of a good society, and we're reaping the benefits of it now.

And what I think excites me is that I believe I can see in the reactions, principally of young people, that they feel they've been sold a pup, that they've been taught something that cannot be right. They've been shortchanged by this ridiculously crude philosophy that it's all just stuff without any meaning. And they're beginning to see the places where meaning can be found.

And sometimes you have to look back in order to look forward. So it's not bad to realize what is it we've lost. And sometimes you only see what you've lost by reading the literature, looking at the art and understanding something of the history of where you've come from. After all, the Renaissance, which was the biggest step forward in the history of the West, was a rebirth. That's what the word, of course, means. And it happened because people look back to the ancient world. They didn't try and reinvent Greece and Rome. That's impossible. Don't worry. But what they did see was what was missing, and they found it and moved forward. That's the hope for our future, I believe.

Chapter 5: How can we perceive reality using both hemispheres?

How do we tell, especially if our brains are capable of telling us two quite different things about the world we're experiencing, how can we tell which is the better guide to reality? And how can we formulate what that reality is like?

And I think that's so important because during my lifetime, I have seen the three great values which have always inspired me, and as I get older, seem to me of absolutely critical importance, namely goodness, beauty, and truth. In my lifetime, I've seen them all travested. I've seen goodness reduced to having the right received opinions, ticking boxes. I've seen beauty scorned by artists themselves. During my lifetime most artists didn't want their work to be called beautiful, they wanted it to be called powerful. And I thought, no, that is no way to respond to how the experience of living teaches one about these great things, goodness, beauty and truth.

And so I wanted to work from the brain, explaining what the left and right hemispheres can do and contribute, then going to what's known as epistemology, i.e. the paths to truth, which I took to be reason and science, intuition and imagination. And I do think we do need to use all of them.

And the first thing that I want to stress is that science itself does not simply draw on reason, it draws very strongly on intuition. Practically all its great discoveries were made intuitively. So don't feel worried about intuition. Intuition is a very good guide. Of course it can be mistaken. And so philosophers have devised what I call intuitive illusions.

So, for example, I can show you an optical illusion, which is very hard to believe. It involves a checkerboard in which two squares that look obviously quite different colors are actually the same color and can be demonstrated to be so. So sometimes your eyes, by devising a very clever specialist illusion, can be made to deceive you. But I never knew anybody who, after seeing it, said, oh, well, that does it. From now on, I'm never going to use my eyes. I'm just going to lead my life with my eyes closed. Of course not. It would be idiotic. And the same is true of intuition. If you really want to be a dunce, then do away with your intuition. But that intuition needs to be tempered with reason and with what science tells us. These things need to work hand in hand. But above all, they all need to work under the superintendence of imagination.

And perhaps I should just say something about the nature of imagination. Imagination is not fantasy, it is in some ways the exact opposite, because fantasy is what leads you away from reality, whereas imagination is what gives you the only chance you have of entering into the depth of reality. So, for example, a fantasy will make you see an aristocrat playing in a play dressed up as a shepherd, as a shepherd. But it's not a shepherd. It's whoever it is, the lord of whatever. So that is fantasy, is make-believe, when you play a little game. But imagination is nothing like that. Imagination is what enabled Wordsworth to steal his way into something as banal as the great outcrop of rock, and to see it suddenly as if for the first time, to see it as almost alive, to see it as powerful.

Now, I think that seeing the world as alive is by no means a deceit. I have, since my teens, not been able to believe that the world out there, for example, the fields, the trees, the streams, the meadows, the hills in which I grew up, were just stuff that had no anything about it. It was just passively responding to chemicals. No, the world, especially the natural world, seems to me to speak. It was a two-way communication. It was speaking to me, I was speaking to it. And out of that encounter came what is.

Now that's an important point, that everything that we can know comes from an encounter. Something in me meets something that is not wholly something in me. So my consciousness contacts something that I didn't just create or dream up. And out of that coming together comes the world, the only world that I can know.

Part 3: The Nature of Reality

Chapter 6: What is the nature of reality?

One thing one can say about the cosmos, pretty much without fear of contradiction, is that it is creative. So it begins, we are told, with this very simple compact mass, and then has expanded into the vast universe that we are still exploring, and in which there is so much complexity unfolding. This seems to be key to the nature of everything that exists.

This idea that everything flows is an important part of this because there is a huge difference between a sequence of steps and a flow. The left hemisphere only understands things broken down into discrete steps, but the right hemisphere sees that they can't be broken down in this way and that something is lost when you do it. Now, literally, when people have damage to the right hemisphere, they see movement as jerky. So they begin to see things going doot, doot, doot, doot, doot, as though stop-go animation. So that is a key difference.

But why is that so important? Because when there are just steps, you can calculate what's happening next. But in flow, you can't. And there's a saying, a lovely thing, by one of the presidents of the Royal Society early in the 20th century, that in the next life there are two things I really want to understand. One is the quantum nature of reality, and the other is flow. About the quantum nature of reality, I feel confident. In other words, about flow, it's so complex, it is unfathomable.

And what really struck me was that if you take liquid flowing down an absolutely straight-sided channel, and you put into it at right angles a couple of rods that are rectangular in cross-section, you just bring them down into the flow, what do you get? The most incredibly beautiful thing that unfolds. It's almost impossible to describe. It looks like something that an Art Nouveau genius would have worked out. And it does have structure, but it is also very hard to see where this thing comes from. And it's called a Kármán vortex street. And sometimes these things occur in the ocean and can be seen from space.

In any case, the point is that you take something very predictable, even flow down a rigid channel with nothing else, two rods, and suddenly you've got something that is asymmetrical, complicated, beautiful, contains all ki

items.title: 8 size and distance comparisons: from subatomic to cosmic
items.summary: Here in this Universe, there are multiple different ways to look at all that exists in terms of size. You can look at the physical size, or volumes, that the objects occupy, and you can do that in a variety of ways. For humans, we can measure our dimensions — things like our…
items.author: Ethan Siegel
items.contentHtml:
Here in this Universe, there are multiple different ways to look at all that exists in terms of size. You can look at the physical size, or volumes, that the objects occupy, and you can do that in a variety of ways. For humans, we can measure our dimensions — things like our height, width, and depth — or the amount of volume we displace when placed in a bath of water. Whichever method we choose, we get a proxy for our size. For planets, we can look at the edges of their solid surfaces or atmospheres; for stars, we can look at the boundary of their photospheres; for atoms, we probe them through techniques like force microscopy or scattering experiments.

But in addition to these physical sizes, we can also examine such objects relative to other objects of the same type as found in nature. We can look at the distance from one human to another, for example, under a variety of common conditions. We can examine the distances between atoms, or stars, or planets, or galaxies, or anything else that we choose. And if we like, one interesting comparison that we can make, on any scale we choose, is the ratio between the physical size of the object itself to the distance from it to the next similar object.

If we were to do this, which scale would be the most extreme, and how does that relate to human scales that we’re familiar with? Let’s examine eight different scales, from the quantum to the cosmic, to find out.

1.) Subatomic scales

On scales smaller than an atom, we run into things like atomic nuclei, electrons, individual protons or neutrons within the nucleus, and quarks and gluons. Of these particles, it’s not necessarily fair to talk about “size” for most of them: quarks, gluons, and electrons are consistent with being what we call point particles, or particles consistent with having an actual size of 0. From scattering experiments, we’ve determined that if they do have a size, that size is no larger than about 10-19 meters, or a tenth of an attometer. Protons, neutrons, and atomic nuclei, however, do have an actual size: about that of a femtometer, or 10-15 meters.

Within this context, you might consider looking at the distance from one subatomic particle — like a proton or the nucleus — to an electron as a measure of distance on subatomic scales. (If you went to look between two protons in the same nucleus, you’d find that they were practically adjacent: a distance-to-size ratio of around 1-to-1.) Since electrons are typically around a tenth of a nanometer, or 10-10 meters, away from the nucleus, that results in a ratio of around 100,000-to-1. If the atomic nucleus were the size of a basketball located at Pepperdine University in Malibu, the electron would be roughly 24 kilometers (15 miles) away on the Santa Monica Pier.

2.) Atomic scales

Atoms are the building block of nearly everything we find on Earth, with enormous numbers of these very, very small entities combining together to compose the entire world and so much more. Atoms make up the atmosphere, the seas, the rocks and soil, every living creature on our planet, and the entire world itself, as well as pretty much every other known world in the Universe and much more. Atoms are generally the same physical size everywhere in the Universe — with the smallest atom, helium, having a diameter of 0.06 nanometers and the largest well-measured one, cesium, having a diameter of between 0.520 and 0.596 nanometers — with a typical atom’s size being around 10-10 meters.

But atoms can come in a huge variety of configurations, with some configurations placing atoms almost perfectly adjacent to one another and others creating great separations between them. Some examples include:

  • in a water molecule, hydrogen and oxygen atoms are separated by 0.1 nanometers,
  • in a diamond, two carbon atoms are separated by 0.15 nanometers,
  • in the Earth’s crust, silicon and oxygen atoms are separated by 0.16 nanometers,
  • and in a helium balloon, gaseous, monatomic helium atoms are typically separated by 3.4 nanometers.

In solids and liquids, or wherever atoms are bound together into molecules, the next atom over is approximately only one or two atomic diameters away, while in a gas composed of atoms, the next atomic particle (at Earth’s standard pressure and temperature) is only a few dozen atom diameters away. If an atom again were a basketball on a basketball court, the next atom over for solids and liquids would be at the distance of a very tight defender, while for gases, the next atom over would be standing over by the 3-point line.

3.) Molecular scales

This is an interesting one, because the separation distance between molecules depends tremendously on which type of molecules we’re talking about and the environment that they’re found in. Sure, when we think of molecules we typically think of something like water, which is a small molecule just 0.28 nanometers across: barely larger than an atom. But human DNA is also a molecule, albeit one that’s about three billion base pairs in length, spanning over a micron in length when coiled up (over 1000 nanometers) or extending for more than two meters if stretched out end-to-end. The protein Titin, found in striated muscle, is similarly large when coiled.

But what about the distances between molecules? Again, the distance depends on the environment, and it varies tremendously.

  • In red blood cells, the distance between hemoglobin molecules is about 7 nanometers, compared with the size of hemoglobin at about 5 nanometers.
  • In the ocean, water molecules are separated by about 0.31 nanometers, compared to a size of 0.28 nanometers.
  • Nitrogen molecules in Earth’s atmosphere at sea level are separated by 3.4 nanometers, while a nitrogen molecule is just 0.3 nanometers in size.
  • In Mars’s carbon dioxide-rich but thin atmosphere, however, the average separation distance is more like 17 nanometers, compared to a molecular size of 0.3 nanometers.

Although gases can be very sparse indeed, for most applications, if a molecule was the size of a basketball, the next molecule over would still be on the same basketball court, and in many cases, just around one basketball-diameter away.

4.) Human scales

At last, something we’re familiar with: the scales at which we live. A human being ranges in size from about 45 centimeters (18 inches) at birth to 2 meters (6’7″) for a very tall human. (There are greater extremes, but most of us fall somewhere in the middle.) For a full-grown adult human, most of us are somewhere between 150 cm and 190 cm: a narrower range that encompasses nearly 90% of the population over 18 years old. However, how well-separated we are varies tremendously depending on where we live.

  • If all 8.3 billion humans were evenly distributed across the Earth, we’d be spaced approximately 270 meters apart. (Including uninhabitable places like oceans or ice sheets.)
  • In the densest Tokyo wards (like Toshima), the average distance between the two closest people is just 3.25 meters apart.
  • In a Tokyo subway car during rush hour, the average spacing between humans is just 40 cm.
  • But in a rural area like northern Siberia, Russia, the average distance between any two people can rise to several kilometers.
  • And outside of the capital city of Nuuk, there are 17 towns and 56 small settlements along Greenland’s coastline; the average spacing between two nearest-neighbors outside of this rises to between 3 and 7 kilometers: the largest human-spacing on Earth.

Even in the sparsest, least population-dense places on Earth, humans are more closely packed together than subatomic particles are within an atom: with a maximum ratio of just a few thousand-to-1 in terms of distance-to-size. If a human were a basketball, those of us in cities would make a court that looked like the fans had just rushed it, but those of us in the most rural areas would still have other humans in the arena, but not necessarily on the court.

5.) Planetary scales

But as we turn to planetary scales, things suddenly get very, very large in terms of both sizes and distances, with distances far exceeding the size scales. A planet like the Earth is large: about 12,700 km in diameter. Rocky planets can be significantly smaller, of course: Mercury is the smallest major planet in our Solar System with a diameter of 4880 km, but planets could, in theory, be just a few hundred kilometers in diameter and still meet all of the necessary criteria for being classified as a planet. On the largest end, Jupiter is 143,000 km in diameter, and several super-Jupiter exoplanets up to double Jupiter’s size are known.

Nonetheless, as impressive as those numbers are, they’re absolutely paltry compared to the distances between planets.

  • Relative to Earth, our nearest-neighbor planet at closest approach is Venus: 38 million km away, or about a factor of 3000 greater than Earth’s diameter.
  • For an outer planet like Uranus, its diameter of 51,000 km is peanuts compared to its separation from Saturn or Neptune: 1.43-1.45 billion km away, or a factor of 28,000.
  • Even in a close-packed planetary system like the TRAPPIST-1 system, the average spacing between planets is 1.26 million km, or more than a factor of 100 larger than the average TRAPPIST-1 planet diameter, at 12,100 km.

If a typical planet were a basketball, the most closely-spaced planetary systems would put the next-nearest planet somewhere still in the arena. If Earth were a basketball, the nearest planets would still be in the same town, while the outer distant planets would be quite a way down the highway. Still, the distance ratios are less extreme than inside an atom, but that all changes when we go to the next scale up.

6.) Stellar scales

Even compared to the sizes of and distances between planets, the scales of stars are far more impressive. Our own Sun is a whopping 1.4 million km in diameter. Even the smallest red dwarf stars are significantly bigger than Jupiter, with Proxima Centauri coming in at 200,000 km across. On the other end of the spectrum, a blue giant like the brightest star in the Beta Centauri system is over 13 million km across. An evolved red giant like Arcturus is closer to 35 million km in diameter, while a massive, evolved red supergiant like Betelgeuse is closer to a whopping 900 million km across. Some stars even cross the billion kilometers mark in terms of physical size!

But the distances between stars are in a whole other league. From the Sun to Proxima Centauri, our closest star, it’s 4.24 light-years, or 40 trillion km: a distance-to-size ratio of 28 million-to-1 for the Sun. Stars in globular clusters can be closer together: separated by as little as 0.15 light-years in the cluster core, but that still yields a distance-to-size ratio of a million-to-1 for most stars. And in the sparser places — like the ultra-diffuse galaxies of the Universe — average stellar separations can rise to 20 light-years, while the average star is even smaller than the Sun: exceeding a 100,000,000-to-1 distance-to-size ratio.

The distances between stars, even relative to the massive size of a star itself, provide the most extreme distance-to-size ratios of any object on any scale in the Universe. If our Sun were a basketball, the next-nearest star would be located on the opposite side of the Earth from our gym!

7.) Galactic scales

Stars aren’t completely isolated, however. They’re bound together in extremely large-magnitude collections of their own: galaxies. The distances between galaxies absolutely outscales the distances between stars in impressive fashion. Therefore, you might wonder about the scale of a galaxy compared to the distances between galaxies; perhaps it’s even more impressive.

Our own Milky Way contains approximately 400 billion stars, largely confined to a disk 100,000 light-years across. Smaller galaxies, like a variety of dwarf galaxies, are often only a few thousand light-years in diameter. Meanwhile, the largest known single galaxy of all, IC 1101, has a diffuse halo of starlight that extends for over 4 million light-years (and maybe up to 6 million light-years) across. Galaxies can be tiny or enormous, with Milky Way-like galaxies sitting squarely between them.

The nearest Milky Way-like galaxy to our own is Andromeda, which is the only other galaxy in the Local Group with as much mass as our Milky Way possesses. It’s quite distant, too: 2.5 million light-years away. However, that means we have a distance-to-size ratio of just 25-to-1! If the Milky Way were a basketball located at the basket itself, Andromeda would be roughly at the free-throw line. Galaxies are often grouped together, and even isolated galaxies — or field galaxies — are usually between 10-15 million light-years from another major galaxy. Because galaxies themselves are so big, the distance-to-size ratios for these objects aren’t nearly as impressive as we find on even planetary scales.

8.) Super-galactic (galaxy group/cluster) scales

You might think, then, to look to the largest scales of all: the scales at which galaxies collect together into groups and clusters. We’re a part of the Local Group: a collection of galaxies that includes Andromeda, our Milky Way, and a few hundred smaller galaxies all bound together. We’re not all that big of a group, as many galaxy clusters contain thousands of large galaxies all bound together, but we still extend for between 3-5 million light-years in total span. The largest galaxy clusters, like the Coma Cluster, can span more than 20 million light-years from end-to-end.

Sure, space is vast and mostly empty, but the separations between galaxy groups and clusters is even less severe than it is for galaxies when compared to their sizes. We have other galaxy groups relatively close to our own: the M81 group, for example, is less than 12 million light-years away, for a 4-to-1 distance-to-size ratio at most. For bigger structures, like galaxy clusters, the separation distances are greater, but the sizes are also greater. The Virgo cluster and the Fornax cluster are two of the nearest galaxy clusters to Earth, separated by around 100 million light-years in space from each other. But with a diameter of 15 million light-years, the Virgo cluster has only about a 7-to-1 distance-to-size ratio.

If galaxy groups and clusters were basketballs, their neighboring groups and clusters would be able to make up a “starting 5” as well as an opposing team, and fit them all on the same half of the basketball court. It’s a fairly crowded place when you consider such large structures, after all.

This means, in terms of a distance-to-size ratio, it’s the stellar scales that are the most impressive. Compared to even the size of the largest stars, the cosmic distances separating them are absolutely tremendous, typically reaching ratios of several million-to-1. As big as a star is, the distance separating the stars gives us the most extreme ratios.

In second place is the separation between subatomic particles within an atom: electrons within an atom or the separation between the atomic nuclei and an electron. That ratio of 100,000-to-1 outclasses all scales except the stellar, putting it in a strong second place on this list.

In third place are planetary scales, which are less extreme than subatomic particles, but which have more extreme separations than humans do on planet Earth, which (perhaps surprisingly) comes in fourth on this list. Galactic scales typically follow next in fifth, with atomic separations (at least, in gases) coming in sixth.

It’s fairly remarkable that the two most extreme examples of a distance-to-size ratio occur on such different scales than one another: one of them on interstellar scales and one on tiny, subatomic scales. The reason for it is the same in both cases: the objects are simply physically much, much smaller than the distances separating them from the next-nearest such object. From the quantum to the cosmic, the Universe is full of delights and surprises.

This article 8 size and distance comparisons: from subatomic to cosmic is featured on Big Think.

items.title: US reacts to Nvidia scandal by curbing chip exports
items.summary: Xinhua/Getty Images Uncle Sam is limiting China’s access to AI chips after last week’s revelation that Nvidia’s now-resigned CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Yesterday, the Commerce Department took steps to close a loophole Chinese…
items.author: Sam Klebanov
items.contentHtml:
Uncle Sam is limiting China’s access to AI chips after last week’s revelation that Nvidia’s now-resigned CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

Yesterday, the Commerce Department took steps to close a loophole Chinese companies exploited to skirt US export controls on advanced AI chips by using data centers in nearby countries. Under the department’s new rule:

  • Chipmakers like Nvidia will be barred from supplying advanced chips to overseas data centers servicing companies in places like China and Russia.
  • There’ll be a new licensing process for exporting chips to several countries that often serve as a stopover for China-bound chips.

Huang chip diplomacy is kneecapped. The change endangers a Huang-fostered ecosystem of Asian data centers offering Chinese companies like Alibaba and ByteDance remote access to Nvidia’s AI chips. Shares of Nvidia, as well as its rivals Intel and AMD, dropped yesterday.

Two hands, one pen

The Commerce Department said its new rule was written by the Treasury Department, an unprecedented disclaimer experts say exposes a long-running rift in the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently accused Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick of slow-walking chip export controls. Both secretaries will accompany President Trump on this week’s Asia trip, where he’ll meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping on Thursday.

Meanwhile…Trump said he would “not mind” seeing Huang return as CEO, but Nvidia’s board is reportedly not considering his reinstatement.—SK

items.title: Amazon MGM has a new 007: Robert Pattinson
items.summary: Illustration: Morning Brew Inc., Photo: Amazon MGM Studios Finally, a story about a spy that has nothing to do with Jensen Huang. Amazon MGM announced yesterday that Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond, a casting decision that ends seven years of speculation and finally has…
items.author: Dave Lozo
items.contentHtml:
Finally, a story about a spy that has nothing to do with Jensen Huang. Amazon MGM announced yesterday that Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond, a casting decision that ends seven years of speculation and finally has the studio positioned to see a return on its heavy investment into the franchise.

  • In 2022, Amazon acquired MGM for $8.5 billion—that included a 50-50 split of the Bond rights with the Broccoli family, who had final say in creative decisions.
  • So Amazon tossed another reported $1 billion at the longtime stewards of the martini-swilling character in March 2025 to wrest away their veto power.

And now, the studiothat brought us Red One and Mercy has tapped Pattinson, the first new Bond since Daniel Craig announced in 2019 that 2021’s No Time To Die would be his final appearance after 15 years as the character. The 40-year-old Pattinson, who may consider himself the first Gen Z Bond, eclipsed rivals for the role that reportedly included Jack Lowden (Slow Horses), Josh O’Connor (Challengers), and Callum Turner (Dua Lipa’s Husband).

It’s a deviation from previous Bond casting choices under the Broccoli family, who preferred lesser-known actors that wouldn’t overshadow the character. But as Puck News theorized, a known entity like Pattinson, who has already anchored franchises as Batman and a sparkly vampire, may feel more necessary considering how much Amazon has invested.

What else is likely to change?

Since Bond made its big screen debut in 1962 with Dr. No, the official franchise has earned an inflation-adjusted $7 billion at the domestic box office. Now, imagine how much more it would have made if there was a spinoff series centered around Le Chiffre, or a Pussy Galore origin story available to stream in your home? There’s been speculation that those types of Bond-related projects could be in the offing with Amazon in possession of the IP.

In theaters when? Production timelines suggest that Pattison could make his Bond debut in 2028—and, if true, that seven-year gap between movies will be the longest in the franchise’s history.—DL

items.title: International students are ditching US colleges
items.summary: Paul Kuroda/Getty Images A growing number of young adults overseas cannot relate to the West Side Story lyric, “I like to be in America.” Amid the Trump administration’s changing visa policies and an overall jump in higher education costs, international enrollment is falling at…
items.author: Molly Liebergall
items.contentHtml:
A growing number of young adults overseas cannot relate to the West Side Story lyric, “I like to be in America.” Amid the Trump administration’s changing visa policies and an overall jump in higher education costs, international enrollment is falling at US universities, according to data released yesterday.

New international student enrollment dropped 15% for fall 2026 compared to the fall 2025 semester, according to a survey of 800+ colleges by the nonprofit Institute of International Education:

  • Graduate students accounted for the bulk of the dropoff.
  • Among schools where international enrollment declined, 88% cited the visa application process as a contributing factor, while 70% noted travel restrictions, and 45% referenced degree costs.

Though some government officials argue this benefits US students, leaders in higher education say otherwise: International students tend to pay full tuition, which makes their matriculation a key revenue source for colleges and universities—one that can help subsidize financial aid and other services for domestic students.

Feeling the burn: Citing drops in international enrollment (along with a drop overall for both undergrad and graduate students), Penn State University is facing a $124 million budget gap for its next fiscal year, and the Illinois Institute of Technology said it plans to borrow $200 million from its endowment.

Zoom out: With international students contributing almost $40 billion to the US economy last school year, this fall’s enrollment dropoff is expected to cost Uncle Sam $2.4 billion, according to NAFSA, an international education association.—ML

items.author: Lenny Rachitsky
items.contentHtml:
Claude Code + Obsidian: My family’s AI brain | Scott Farrar

Listen now on YouTube • • Apple Podcasts

Brought to you by:

  • WorkOS—Make your app enterprise-ready, with SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and more

  • Jira Product Discovery—Prioritize with insights, build with confidence

Scott Farrar is a math educator and parent who built a shared household brain using Claude Code and Obsidian. In this episode, he shows how the system tracks appliances and warranties, compares insurance quotes, organizes family projects, and keeps household tasks moving through a shared to-do list and wall display. He also explains why persistent files work better for him than long AI chats, and how the same philosophy shapes his approach to using AI without taking the thinking away from students.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. The problem with chat is not intelligence, but memory drift. Scott moved to Claude Code because it stores context in Markdown files he can inspect, correct, and reuse across sessions. His memory is no longer trapped inside an opaque conversation.

  2. Let the AI tell you what context it needs. When Scott asked Claude how to document his home, it suggested photographing every appliance. Those photos became a searchable inventory of model numbers, serial numbers, and warranty details.

  3. Unstructured input is fine when the system handles the organization. Scott gives Claude raw information and lets it maintain the underlying files. A custom linter prevents verbose agents from bloating documents such as his household to-do list.

  4. Better context helps people ask better questions. Claude compares insurance quotes with detailed information about Scott’s home, identifies potential coverage gaps, and prepares specific follow-ups. He no longer has to rely entirely on the agent selling him the policy.

  5. One master list can eliminate a house full of mental clutter. Scott and his wife captured every household task they could think of, then Claude organized them by priority, cost, and supporting information. The system now surfaces overdue work before it becomes another fire.

  6. Multiplayer household systems require practical compromises. Claude recommended GitHub to avoid file conflicts, but that added more complexity than Scott’s wife wanted. They settled on GitHub for shared scripts and Dropbox for everyday files, matching the tools to how they actually work.

  7. A household system becomes more useful when it leaves the laptop. Scott’s wall display shows upcoming trips, open tasks, recent wins, and small daily suggestions. It turns a private collection of files into something the whole family can see and use.

  8. Scott rebuilt his father’s file cabinet as an AI system. His dad saved every receipt and warranty and could explain repairs from decades ago. Claude now gives Scott that same dependable household memory, only searchable through conversation.

  9. AI should help children think, not think for them. Scott prefers tutors that ask students to explain their reasoning and work through productive struggle. He also believes some children may share unfinished ideas more comfortably with AI than with another person.

  10. Infinite patience is not always good teaching. Scott wants AI to act as a “warm demander” that encourages students without doing the work for them. When his own agent goes off track, he starts fresh or investigates its reasoning before incorrect information reaches his memory files.

How I fight token fraud as a solo founder

Listen now on YouTube • • Apple Podcasts

Brought to you by:

  • WorkOS—Make your app enterprise-ready, with SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and more

  • Auros—The human network behind AI

In this solo episode, Claire explains how token fraud cost ChatPRD tens of thousands of dollars and consumed much of her engineering time. She walks through six forms of abuse, including farmed free trials, resold promo codes, card testing, product relays, and a custom MCP running as a 24/7 compute worker. She also shares the business and technical defenses she built, how Jev classifies suspicious activity in real time, and why she ultimately eliminated free trials.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. Token fraud is a business risk most AI founders underestimate until the bill arrives. Unlike traditional SaaS abuse, every fraudulent model call costs real money. It cost Claire tens of thousands of dollars despite ChatPRD being SOC 2 compliant, regularly penetration-tested, and run by an experienced technical founder.

  2. Free trials may no longer work for AI products. Fraudsters automated account creation and used ChatPRD’s most expensive models for unrelated work. Claire ultimately removed free trials, sacrificing a valuable source of product-led growth and enterprise leads after credit-card gates and paid trials also failed.

  3. Promo codes have become a serious attack vector. Codes intended for partners were stolen, resold, and used to power other AI businesses. After discovering that roughly half of her promo codes had reached resellers, Claire stopped issuing them entirely.

  4. MCP access creates a new category of abuse. One fraudster turned ChatPRD’s custom MCP support into a compute worker that ran around the clock. Claire responded by restricting approved hosts and blocking free tunnels and infrastructure that did not appear connected to legitimate companies.

  5. Cheap decision models can classify fraud in real time. When a session crosses ChatPRD’s abuse threshold, a zero-data-retention Jev loop categorizes the activity. Confirmed fraud results in either a ban or a silent downgrade to a less expensive model.

  6. AI support agents need firm boundaries around fraud. After mass bans, ChatPRD received both clumsy appeals and polished messages written by AI. Claire equipped her support agent with fraud tools and explicit rules preventing it from restoring accounts or distributing promo codes.

  7. Blunt defenses are sometimes the most effective. Blocking traffic from certain countries using Vercel Firewall significantly reduced abuse and forced Claire to reconsider ChatPRD’s international strategy. Her new default is simple: trust must be earned rather than assumed.

  8. Token fraud is affecting companies of every size. Claire found the same people abusing ChatPRD through rotating proxies across several major AI products. She has started discussing the problem publicly and filed FBI cybercrime reports with help from Codex.

  9. If a company sells AI, it is ultimately selling compute. Founders should track dollars instead of requests, monitor model spending continuously, close every free entry point, and verify the client rather than only the account. Claire also learned that fraud disappears quickly when expensive models are no longer available to steal.

↳ Detect Automated Abuse on AI Routes with Vercel BotID: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/detect-automated-abuse-ai-routes-botid
↳ Use an AI Assistant to Create Payment Fraud Rules: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/use-an-ai-assistant-to-create-payment-fraud-rules

I was a Claude hater. Fable 5.2 changed my mind.

Listen now on YouTube • • Apple Podcasts

In this solo episode, Claire tests Claude Fable 5.2 to see whether Anthropic has finally built a model she enjoys using. She turns a tweet into an animated marketing video, creates assembly instructions from photos of unboxed furniture, reworks a complex ChatPRD pipeline, and builds a fully functional 3D typewriter. She also explains where Fable fits alongside Opus 5.5, why its creative work impressed her, and why she still would not trust it to design a website on its own.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. Fable 5.2 turned Claire from a Claude skeptic back into a fan. She found the original Fable difficult to understand and unpleasant to use, with Opus 5 offering little improvement. Fable 5.2 feels fast, capable, creative, and dramatically easier to work with.

  2. Fable 5.2 complements Opus 5.5 rather than replacing it. Opus remains the better default for most coding and knowledge work. Fable is the model Claire would choose for greater complexity, broader scope, or tasks that demand more creativity.

  3. Its speed changes how the model feels to use. Many benchmark tasks finished in under a minute, and even a complex animation took only 16 minutes. Fable also communicates sparingly during autonomous work, surfacing only the moments that require input.

  4. Fable 5.2 made AI video feel animated instead of assembled. From one tweet and the CXO.dev brand guidelines, it created a narrated story featuring custom invader-bot sprites that walk, jump, and cheer. No other model Claire tested produced anything comparable, so the task is becoming a permanent benchmark.

  5. Its spatial reasoning solved a real-world problem every other model failed to. Claire gave Fable low-resolution photos of an unassembled piece of furniture with no instructions. It identified the parts, created a diagram, and produced the correct assembly sequence, which her household successfully followed.

  6. Fable 5.2 is unexpectedly funny. It designed a bug-fighting game around real engineering tradeoffs, then made a trailer in which finance sees the token bill and downgrades the team to a cheaper model. The humor felt intentional enough to make Claire genuinely laugh.

  7. It also holds up on serious engineering work. Fable created a sensible migration plan for ChatPRD’s messy product-intelligence pipeline and aligned closely with Claire’s own roadmap. It worked autonomously and paused at appropriate moments, though the migration is still underway.

  8. Fable needs strong direction for visual design. It follows an existing brand system well, but its unguided web and storybook designs were unattractive. Claire expects to pair it with Opus 5.5 for frontend work and use a separate image model when original visuals are needed.

  9. The 3D typewriter was Claire’s “AGI moment.” Fable built a working keyboard in one shot, then added white-out, music, weather, timers, writing prompts, and multiple immersive settings. It turned an idea Claire never imagined building into a tool she wants to use every day.

  10. Fable 5.2 is available now, with an even faster mode coming. It is launching across the Claude API, cloud platforms, Claude apps, and Claude Code. Claire plans to compare it with the other new models in a full How I AI benchmark.
