items.title: Doing More vs. Doing What Matters: The Productivity Shift You Need
items.summary: This article was originally published on Substack . The Hollow Chase The day I accomplished more in 6 hours than I had in previous weeks of 40+ was the day I realized everything I knew about productivity was wrong. During my PhD, I found myself working one full-time job plus…
items.author: Lia Luzong
items.contentHtml:
This article was originally published on Substack.

The Hollow Chase

The day I accomplished more in 6 hours than I had in previous weeks of 40+ was the day I realized everything I knew about productivity was wrong.

During my PhD, I found myself working one full-time job plus five part-time gigs (bartending, TA for two classes, assistant for the HDR office, and, only in Australia, delivering the school’s tea service for longer classes) while studying full-time in order to raise $22,000 for one semester’s tuition. And I had two semesters left to go.

My schedule, unsurprisingly was compressed to breaking point. I would wake up early, work late after one or more of my jobs had finished, and weekend breaks were a myth.

The surprising part? In the mere 15-20 hours I had left for my PhD work each week, I was accomplishing twice as much as when I had 40+ hours available in the years prior.

Scarcity had created clarity.

With so little time available, I became ruthlessly focused on what would move the needle. Everything else was stripped away. There was no time for second-guessing or procrastination—only the essential remained.

Saturdays became my heavy work day. Wake up at 7am, meet my friend at the gym at 730, sit down for coffee, breakfast, and work at 9am and knock out 3-4 sessions of focused 120 minute working time, changing location (I am a notorious café hopper) to keep it fresh, and usually ending my day around 5pm with an insane amount of articles read, notes written, and next steps laid out.

In contrast, when I first started the PhD with all the time in the world to focus, I tracked my progress by counting deep work sessions—tallying each 25-minute focused block. At first, this input-focused approach helped build the focus muscle, slowly building to 90 minutes of pure, focused flow time.

But eventually, I had to ask: What was all this productivity actually producing? Sure I was putting time on the calendar, but was I moving the needle? Was I actually getting closer to producing a written thesis?

The answers were all a resounding no. And it took adding 60 hours of real job(s) to my calendar to finally do something about it.

This is the hollow chase that traps so many of us: we optimize our systems, track our metrics, implement the latest productivity hack to pursue recognition—all while avoiding the harder question of whether we're moving efficiently in the entirely wrong direction.

Now that I work in consulting, I find this focus even harder to maintain. Work, social life, identity, building my own business, and sales all blur together. The clear boundaries have disappeared, and with them, the clarity of purpose that had made those limited PhD hours so productive.

And it’s not something that can just be fixed by “WORK HARDER!” As a former athlete, and since my earliest days of soccer, I knew how to push through pain and work. I knew how to grind. I can white knuckle and throw long hours at a problem.

But hours worked can’t solve everything. It’s a good starting point, but it’s probably not enough on it’s own to get you to the finish line you need.

This struggle illuminates something essential about real productivity: it's not about doing more. It's about doing what matters.

Real vs. Shallow Productivity

Busyness as a badge of honor is bullshit.

"Being busy is a form of laziness—lazy thinking and indiscriminate action." — Tim Ferriss

There's lots of work we can do simply to make people leave us alone. Work that looks impressive but doesn't move the needle. Work that creates the appearance of productivity without the substance.

This was me early on the PhD attending workshops that had very little direct value to writing my thesis. This is everytime you open your inbox pretending to check emails in order to make it look like you’re doing something while at the office. In fact, part of why virtual work is effective is because it removed the need for this fake productivity virtue-signalling.

That's not fulfilling. That's not energizing. That's shallow, unecessary shenanigans.

Real productivity, by contrast, tries to tick as many of these boxes as possible:

  • It's aligned with our meaning and purpose

  • It helps us grow and improve

  • It allows us to reach deep levels of concentration (flow)

Sometimes you only get one. The holy trinity is when you can reach all three—what I call "Value-Aligned Productivity." These are the supercharged hours where you accomplish in 60 minutes what used to take four hours, working at the intersection of flow, purpose, and mastery.

Value-Aligned Productivity means aligning your work with your core values at a time when you do your best work, creating a virtuous cycle where your actions reinforce what matters most to you, rather than depleting your energy on tasks that feel meaningless. Having just two hours of this type of work in your week can transform your experience from good to great. Having one hour of this every day can absolutely change your life—creating momentum that carries into all aspects of your work and personal development.

This is where our values enter the equation. When I approach sitting down to write as something I have to do versus this is a practice of my value of growth, in getting better at writing and documenting my own journey in order to better serve others, my relationship with the work transforms entirely. It becomes something I look forward to as opposed to dread.

The approach, the energy, and ultimately the output are fundamentally different when the work connects to what we truly value.

Think about the last time you were so locked in on a task that time seemed to disappear. Maybe it was writing a report on a topic you found fascinating, perfecting a slide deck just so, or solving a complex problem about trying to sell to a specific client. That flow state wasn't just about pRoDuCtIvItY—it was about alignment.

The Awareness Connection

Awareness—that muscle we build through meditation, journaling, and mindful practice—is crucial to distinguishing real from shallow productivity. It gives us the "catch" for interrupting patterns that don’t serve us. We either:

  1. Notice and choose our intention before approaching a task ("Even though this is a chore I dislike, I'm going to make it as enjoyable as possible" or "I'll approach this meeting by dialing up my warmth and playfulness.")

  2. Notice what we're bringing to the table during the task and choose a reframe ("I hate this, it's pointless" becomes "This is about integrity—I said I would do this, so I must.")

One of the simplest practices is setting an intention before beginning work. "I'm going to do this as fast as possible." "I'm going to approach this with humor." "I'm going to pretend this is fun." You find what you look for, so use intention to create a nudge back toward who you wish to be and how you wish to move through the world.

Without this awareness, you'll find yourself grinding through tasks that drain your energy while wondering why you're exhausted at the end of each day.

The Flow State Checklist

Flow states serve as powerful signposts that you're engaged in Value-Aligned Productivity. Research from psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (I dare you to try and pronounce his name) shows that people in flow states are up to five times more productive than when working under normal conditions, with neuroimaging studies revealing distinctive brain activity patterns during these peak performance states.

Here's what to look out for:

Typical Work:

  • You check the clock constantly
  • Your phone becomes incredibly interesting
  • You find excuses to take breaks
  • Ideas come slowly if at all
  • You feel drained afterward
  • You dread returning to it

Flow State Work:

  • Time seems to disappear
  • You forget to check your phone
  • You have to remind yourself to eat or take breaks
  • Ideas come more easily than usual
  • You feel energized after, even if physically tired
  • You look forward to returning to it

The challenge in modern workplaces is that they're often designed to inhibit flow. Open offices, constant notifications via email, slack, teams and whatever other messaging platform is out there now, back-to-back-to-back meetings, and the expectation of immediate responses… all of this is in a deep, full-fledged conspiracy against deep work. The enemy is inside the gates. The call is coming from inside the house.

The countermeasure?

Boundaries.

The Liberation of Limits

The hardest thing about boundaries is keeping them.

It's easy to say, "I want more time for things I care about—the gym, writing, going for a walk." But that requires sacrifice. It requires trading and choosing your opportunity cost.

Because you can do and accomplish just about anything you want.

But you cannot do everything you want.

To choose to go for a walk without your phone is to choose not to respond to emails or plan your work week. And you have to be okay with paying that cost.

This is what Oliver Burkeman in his best-selling book Four Thousand Weeks: Time Management for Mortals reminds us. Because we have a limited time on this earth with an infinite list of things to do, it means we have to choose, and we have to be ok with the price of those choices. That it’s not about more work, it’s about choosing the right work more often.

For me, it was so easy, for so long, to choose my job. Long hours and a lot of mental energy were dedicated to showing up and performing well as an exceptional learning designer and strategic consultant. For me, being good at my job guaranteed respect and safety. But eventually, that ran out.

Consistently choosing more work over the right work, especially the work that involved taking care of myself, is not sustainable. And it's not actually my job's responsibility to prioritize for me.

That's my job.

If I can, with a straight face and a genuine heart, tell work that I'm doing good work and that shutting my phone off at 6pm is going to help me sustainably produce great outcomes for them, then I have an obligation to protect that time.

Work is often the first place I have clients start to set boundaries, which can sound scary. Work takes up (usually) 8 hours of your day, 5 days a week. Work adds up to a third of your life, a third of the 4000 weeks you have on this planet. But at work, unlike in personal relationships, you have a job description and a contract that makes some expectations explicit about what needs to happen for "good work."

Because if you don't protect yourself and what you need to do your best work, no one will.

As long as your requests and boundaries are couched in clarity—"Here's my role, here's what I need to do my best work, and here's what I'm doing about it"—the conversation becomes much more productive. At best, they never cared in the first place. At worst, they push back strongly, and then you have every signal you need to know you're in the wrong environment.

"Daring to set boundaries is about having the courage to love ourselves even when we risk disappointing others." — Brené Brown

Where I am still a work in progress is setting boundaries with myself to protect my important-but-not-urgent time. Writing my morning pages, time for workouts—I don't treat these as sacred as I should. I get caught in immediate feelings ("I'm tired," "I want to meet friends," "I just have 30 mins of work left"). These occasional slips might be okay sometimes, but for me, they happen far more often than they should.

There's also an anxiety cost—the price you pay for not having done them in your day yet, reaching 5pm knowing you still need to workout, write a new post, and meditate. When you knock these things out early, it gives you freedom later.

This is why ritual and consistency—doing specific activities at specific times that you don't miss—are so important. They create room that you and others can plan around.

As scary bald man Jocko Willink says, "Discipline equals freedom."

Common Objections and Realistic Solutions

When discussing these approaches to productivity, I frequently hear three main objections specific to work (but hint, hint, it applies to life in general):

  • "My job doesn't allow for this kind of flexibility." Even in highly structured environments, you often have more agency than you realize. Start with small boundaries—like taking a proper lunch break or blocking 30 minutes for deep work—before attempting larger changes. Research shows that even micro-breaks of 5-10 minutes can improve focus and sustainability. The key is to begin with changes so small they don't require permission, then gradually expand your autonomy.

  • "I can't afford to work less in my competitive industry." This approach isn't about working less—it's about working differently. You have to be doing the work that only you can be doing. Your work, your team, your organization does not benefit from the time you spend on low-level tasks. We may not be able to cut out admin tasks entirely, but what and how are you working on the things that directly benefit the business? Outside of work, the same question remains. If you think you don’t have enough time, check your screen time on your phone and then re-evaluate that answer. The question isn't whether you can afford to change your approach; it's whether you can afford not to.

  • "What about urgent demands and unexpected crises?" Value-Aligned Productivity doesn't mean ignoring genuine urgencies. It means having the awareness to distinguish between true emergencies and manufactured ones. Build what author and researcher Cal Newport calls "slack" into your system—buffer time that absorbs the unexpected without derailing your most important work. When emergencies do arise, having clear values actually makes triage decisions easier because you know exactly what matters most.

The Productive Pendulum

While boundaries protect your time and energy, they're only part of the equation. The question remains: how intensely should you work within those boundaries?

This is where finding your rhythm becomes essential.

There's a tension between the David Goggins endorsed "grind" mentality and a more ‘let’s just wing it’ approach to productivity. I've found that neither extreme works perfectly.

Grind is good to have on call. You want that capacity in your engine for the days you really need it, so if this is missing, it is certifiably the place to start.

My problem, and the problem of so many high-performers I see, is learning how to shut the engine off.

Currently, I’m suffering from a little of both extremes. Between having started a new full-time job 5 months ago, just added a sales target to the role which is totally new, and launching the substack, there is a lot on my plate, and I feel like I’m doing ok on some of it, excelling at none of it.

To address this, my current approach looks like entering seasons of "push" to step up to my line of capacity, possibly a little bit over it. I’m trying to increase my capacity to work because I know I’m selling myself short in that domain. So this looks like adding an hour before work on the Substack, sometimes 2 hours after work, and usually 5-6 hours across the weekend. Between the job and this extra work, it can end up at a 60 hour work week. One week of 60 hours is doable, 6 months of that could be a superhighway to burnout.

So after these intentional push periods, I flip the focus: Where and how can I concentrate only on the highest leverage activities?

The goal becomes sustainable effort on move-the-needle tasks rather than sheer volume of hours.

It's similar to how I approach training Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. If I am always rolling at max intensity with competition-level rolls five times weekly, injury becomes inevitable. I’m 100% going to hurt myself (or be hurt by all the scary people engaging in death cuddles). And those months I would have take off injured, could have still counted if I had just dialed it back. Strategic intensity is key.

There's a rhythm and a balance to this work. Some weeks you push to your edge. Other weeks you recover. The goal isn't constant intensity, but rather a sustainable pattern and tempo that builds your capacity over time.

This approach aligns with what sports scientists call 'strategic overreaching'—temporary, planned training intensification followed by adequate recovery. Like a muscle under progressive overload, you stress your capacity, allow time to recover, and go-again, maybe just a little bit longer or harder this time. The same principles apply to cognitive work.

What's crucial here is setting a time limit for these "push" experiments. We don't want to grind indefinitely. So I might say: three weeks of doing two hours of focused work after my regular workday.

This is an experiment with a clear endpoint and evaluation: How's my energy at the end? When was I drained? What did I learn about my best times to work and how to do it sustainably?

Recognizing these patterns is half the battle. Correcting it is the other half.

Systems as Servants

After years of experimenting with productivity approaches from authors like Oliver Burkemann, Cal Newport, James Clear, Charles Duhigg, Ali Abdaal, David Allen, and others (you name it, I’ve probably read it), I've distilled a set of principles that actually serve meaning rather than just efficiency.

These are systems designed to be servants to your purpose, not masters of your time:

Single-task. Multitasking is the enemy of depth. Choose one thing and give it your full attention. This isn't just intuitive advice—it's backed by science. Heavy multitaskers pay a ‘focus tax’ for constantly switching between tasks compared to those who focused on one thing at a time. Put simply, people who believe they are 'good multitaskers' are lying to you, to me, and to themselves.

Aim for deep work and flow. Structure your environment and time to minimize distractions and maximize your chance of entering a flow state. Turn off notifications, look at a blank screen, lock the door to your office.

Know your prime time. Figure out when you work best. We can't always perfectly control our schedules, but we often have more influence than we give ourselves credit for. I'm not doing creative work in the afternoons—it has to be mornings, so I block that time out. I can meet and chat with people all day in the afternoons. This is a negotiation, not a dictatorship, but start moving your schedule toward the times and types of work that suit you best.

Have a place to track incoming tasks. Write it down. This gets things out of your head, and by seeing everything in one place, priorities often become clear.

Use the Pomodoro Technique. Start with shorter focused sessions (the standard time is 25 minutes) and increase the length as you strengthen your focus muscle.

Work around people. This isn't for everyone, but I thrive when working around others who are also working. Focusmate is a great online tool for this, where you jump on a virtual call and both work on your own thing. During my PhD, we did something called "shut up and write" that was incredibly effective. You can also ask a friend to jump on a Zoom call or meet at a café (my girlfriend and I call this "parallel play.")

Balance inputs with outputs. At the start, it's about revs and reps—how many can you do in a day/week and how do you increase those over time? Eventually, you need to shift to "What are you producing that moves the needle?" For example in sales, this means asking, "How is your activity helping to generate revenue?" This is your ultimate check against useless spinning or productivity for its own sake.

Small and consistent beats perfect and nonexistent. Some people can jump in and go all-out right away. That might work for you—I've had moments like that, usually with impending deadlines. But it's rarely sustainable. What works better is the ramp-up. With Pomodoros, my goal was always 4 hours (or 8 sessions of 25 minutes)—3 hours was not great, 5+ was exceptional. I increased session length by 5 minutes every week until eventually I was doing 90-minute blocks, consistently hitting 4-5 of those daily (6-7.5 hours of deep work). But that took about 4 months to build up to, and then I maintained that pattern for nearly 4 years.

Homework

Start by identifying one activity in your current schedule that energizes rather than depletes you. Schedule an additional 30 minutes for this activity next week, protecting this time as if it were your most important meeting. Small shifts in how you allocate your attention often trigger the biggest transformations in productivity and fulfillment.

Reimagining Productivity: The Path Forward

I still think about that period during my PhD—when financial pressure forced me to compress 40 hours of work into 15, and somehow doubled my output in the process.

The scarcity that once forced clarity can be recreated by choice. The boundaries that once felt like limitations can become the very structure that liberates your best work. What initially felt like a crisis became my greatest teacher.

These systems aren't just productivity tricks—they're unique, personal expressions of a deeper philosophy that prioritizes your alignment over sheer volume. When we step back from both the hustle culture and the work-less movement, a more nuanced approach emerges.

In the productivity conversation, most voices fall into one of two camps: the hustle-harder crowd promising that sleeping four hours a night is the secret to success, or the work-life balance advocates suggesting that the key is doing less.

Value-Aligned Productivity offers a third path—one that focuses not on how much you do, but on the alignment between what you do and who you are, and holding you to account for doing work on what you decide matters.

When I was tracking 25-minute Pomodoro sessions at the start of the PhD, I thought productivity was about showing up and putting in time. When I was juggling six jobs, I learned it was about focus and elimination. Now I understand it's about something deeper—the intersection of values, flow, and impact.

Working on this Substack has been a great example so far. It is deeply tied to my vision, mission, and values of who I wish to become in the world. It allows me to work on and improve the craft of writing. And I am able to enter deep states of flow when I set aside concentrated blocks of time - the 90-120 minutes spent writing on a Saturday morning, coffee in hand, is consistently some of my favorite and most productive time of the weekend.

For those of us who've experienced excellence in other domains—whether on the field, in academics, or early career wins—this approach offers a way to recapture that sense of purpose and mastery without sacrificing sustainability. The game has changed, but the fundamentals of meaningful achievement remain.

The path starts with awareness—noticing when you're caught in the hollow chase and choosing a different way. It continues with the courage to set boundaries, even when that means disappointing others or going against cultural norms. And it's sustained through systems that work with your natural rhythms and strengths rather than against them.

The question isn't whether you can squeeze more into each day. It's whether what you're doing matters deeply enough to warrant your limited time and precious energy.

The most productive day of your life won't be measured by tasks completed or hours logged, but by how aligned your efforts were with what truly matters to you.

What would it look like if your productivity served your purpose rather than replaced it?

What's one boundary you could set tomorrow to create space for what truly matters?

About the Author

Danny Kenny is a PhD behavioral scientist & former athlete helping high-performers bridge the gap between success and fulfillment. I transform excellence mindsets into purposeful life direction using frameworks that combine ancient wisdom with cutting-edge science.
You can find him on LinkedIn.

items.summary: Today I’m walking you through a problem that has cost me tens of thousands of dollars over the past year and eaten almost all of my engineering energy: token fraud. I’m the solo founder of ChatPRD, a bootstrapped AI platform for product managers, and fraudsters have been…
items.author: Claire Vo
items.contentHtml:
Today I’m walking you through a problem that has cost me tens of thousands of dollars over the past year and eaten almost all of my engineering energy: token fraud. I’m the solo founder of ChatPRD, a bootstrapped AI platform for product managers, and fraudsters have been farming our free trials, reselling promo codes, wrapping the product in relays, and installing a custom MCP that ran as a 24/7 compute worker. I’ll walk through the six abuse patterns I’ve seen, the business and technical controls I put in place, the Jev loop that classifies fraud in real time, and why I finally killed free trials for good. items.title: Huang and allies eye his Nvidia C-suite comeback
items.summary: Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images Over 150,000 people, including Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, signed petitions over the weekend signaling their steadfast support for ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang by jensisting that it is jenstrumental to the US economy…
items.author: Holly Van Leuven
items.contentHtml:
Over 150,000 people, including Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, signed petitions over the weekend signaling their steadfast support for ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang by jensisting that it is jenstrumental to the US economy to jensure that he is returned to his old job.

Translation please? Fanboy energy aside, a superabundance of people want Huang to return as CEO of Nvidia just days after he resigned following reports of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, as well as two Nvidia employees:

  • On Saturday, Musk said on X that he and Huang had several high-value deals in the works and, “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.”
  • The CEOs of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management, investment firms with large holdings in Nvidia, signed a letter requesting that Huang be given “a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him” and a chance to return.
  • The “Stand with Jensen” petition circulating online says it has over 160,000 signatories, including more than 8,000 current Nvidia employees (out of about 42,000 worldwide).
  • Huang himself has not commented, but the Financial Times reported yesterday that he supports his allies’ efforts to get him restored.

But obstacles remain

While it’s unprecedented for a disgraced ousted CEO to get this much immediate support for a return, it’s unclear if that’s enough for even someone with Huang’s rockstar-like following to get a top job back at a $4 trillion company amid federal investigations.

And the board did accept his resignation for…reasons. One anonymous supporter of Huang’s return to power told the Financial Times, “Having an affair with a subordinate is a fireable offense.”

At least one important figure very publicly doesn’t want him to return: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. He told Fox News yesterday that Nvidia needs “a dramatic shake-up,” saying it was “obvious” it was selling chips to Singapore shell companies, and that investigations would reveal whether this was “a low-level fail” or “up in the C-suite.”—HVL

items.title: SpaceX catches a falling Starship
items.summary: Ricardo Arduengo/Getty Images Some things are easy to catch, like a cold or an unflattering glimpse of yourself in a Target checkout camera. Some things are not, like a 171-foot-tall spacecraft plummeting back toward Earth. Nevertheless, SpaceX managed to do just that on…
items.author: Brendan Cosgrove
items.contentHtml:
Some things are easy to catch, like a cold or an unflattering glimpse of yourself in a Target checkout camera. Some things are not, like a 171-foot-tall spacecraft plummeting back toward Earth. Nevertheless, SpaceX managed to do just that on Saturday—an “epic day” that brings the company closer to a fully reusable rocket, SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said on X.

A new stage

Starship launched on Friday afternoon from the southern tip of Texas, successfully entering Earth’s orbit to deploy 26 Starlink satellites. SpaceX failed to catch the rocket’s first-stage Super Heavy booster, which aborted the attempt because of a “slight underperformance of engines,” Musk said on X. SpaceX has caught Super Heavy on three previous occasions, and Musk said the failure “does not change” the timeline for fully reusable rockets.

Shipshape: The upper part of Starship made it back, though. As it approached Earth on Saturday, three of its engines kicked back on, helping it hover next to the launch tower, where two robotic “chopsticks” clamped down as smoothly as someone who just told the waiter they didn’t need a fork.

When you wish upon a Starship: Being able to quickly reuse rockets would save millions of dollars per mission and allow Starship to undertake more launches. The company said it also plans to use Starship to transport people and cargo to the moon. The spacecraft is supposed to participate in its first NASA mission, Artemis III, next year.—BC

items.contentHtml:
In the latest version of set-jetting to Croatia to see where they yelled “shame” at Cersei in Game of Thrones, travelers are increasingly planning their next vacations around locales from their favorite books.

According to Skyscanner’s 2026 trend report:

  • More than half of travelers (57%) had either booked a trip inspired by literature or would consider doing so.
  • Hotel searches using the site’s “library” filter surged 70% globally from the previous year, reflecting a general love for vacation reading that’s led some resorts to start their own book clubs.

Get ready with me to go to Greece: The travel company EF Ultimate Break has launched a slate of trips that take a page from BookTok, including a Percy Jackson-inspired voyage to Egypt, Greece, and Italy for $3,229. There’s also a $3,549 voyage around Switzerland for the millions of A Court of Thorns and Roses (ACOTAR) fans who want to see the places that inspired their favorite fairy smut.

Tiny but mighty? The literary tourism trend has emerged despite a 40% drop-off in Americans reading for pleasure from 2003 to 2023.—ML

items.title: This vintage printing press is a hit with tech legends
items.summary: Arion Press The hottest company in Silicon Valley moves very slowly in an effort to break nothing. Arion Press has been making books by hand for more than 50 years, armed with the second-largest collection of antique metal type and a whimsical machine from the 1960s. The…
items.author: Matty Merritt
items.contentHtml:
The hottest company in Silicon Valley moves very slowly in an effort to break nothing. Arion Press has been making books by hand for more than 50 years, armed with the second-largest collection of antique metal type and a whimsical machine from the 1960s.

The company publishes just three titles per year, usually ornate reprints of classics. The bespoke books, often with new illustrations and carefully crafted covers, are sent to subscribers, who pay either $3,500 or $10,000 per year depending on the tier. Its titles sell individually for thousands, with some of its most iconic prints going for tens of thousands secondhand:

  • Arion’s latest edition of Alice in Wonderland cost $2,100 on its site, but it’s already sold out with only 230 copies printed.
  • One book from the press’s 1979 run of Moby-Dick is currently selling for $25,000 at Book Alley in Pasadena, CA.

Old-school fans. Last year, the company sold out of its annual subscriptions for the first time. Its backers include megawealthy tech vets like Salesforce co-founder Parker Harris; Caitlin Kalinowski, a robotics expert who has worked at OpenAI, Meta, and Anthropic; and several private equity bigwigs.—MM

items.title: For 4 hours, all US flights ground to a halt
items.summary: Thiago Trevisan/Adobe Stock From just before 4pm ET until 8:15pm, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop, which halted all planes departing in the United States due to “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” It was only the second…
items.author: Holly Van Leuven
items.contentHtml:
From just before 4pm ET until 8:15pm, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop, which halted all planes departing in the United States due to “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” It was only the second time since 9/11 that a national ground stop went into effect.

What went down

At a White House press conference just after the ground stop was lifted, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the incident stemmed from new technology upgrades “overwhelming” the aging air traffic control communication system and did not appear to be the result of a cyberattack or anything “nefarious.” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said of those upgrades, “I didn’t anticipate that we would have an outage like this.”

Duffy also urged Congress to allocate $50 billion to fix the aging system and warned that more disruptions like this would happen unless the systems’ technical underpinnings were completely overhauled.

By 9:30pm ET, more than 6,600 flights had been canceled for Friday, and another 1,500 for Saturday:

  • Travel data firm Cirium estimated that 1.5 million travelers were stranded by the cancellations.
  • Sports teams ranging from college football to the NHL and NBA traveling for games were hard hit, and NFL teams had to wonder if their flights for weekend games would get jostled in the aftermath of the ground stop.
  • All air cargo and parcel shipment operations were also halted during the ground stop, impacting delivery times of consumer packages as well as supply chain logistics.

Lifting the ground stop helps get passengers moving again, but delays and cancellations are expected to carry into the weekend as planes, pilots, and crews are out of position.

Looking ahead: Duffy said that it was “going to be slow” to get air travel back to its baseline, but that he didn’t expect disruptions during Thanksgiving travel in a couple of weeks.—HVL

items.title: World recovers from the day Microsoft stood still
items.summary: Nick Iluzada Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft services slowly began returning to normal yesterday, after the tech company’s massive outage disrupted business-as-usual around the world on Thursday, causing somewhat of a syllabus day for some workers, and leaving others to…
items.author: Molly Liebergall
items.contentHtml:
Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft services slowly began returning to normal yesterday, after the tech company’s massive outage disrupted business-as-usual around the world on Thursday, causing somewhat of a syllabus day for some workers, and leaving others to resort to…fax machines.

The outage hit Microsoft Outlook, Teams, Copilot, cloud, and security software users in more than 70 countries and territories, according to the outage tracker Downdetector.

  • Government offices, public transit networks, retailers, banks, and countless companies were affected.
  • All in all, the outage could cost at least $7 billion in lost productivity from tens of millions of Microsoft users, according to a Michigan think tank.

“We are deeply sorry,” Microsoft said yesterday on X. The company noted “encouraging recovery progress,” but said that “intermittent issues” might continue.

It’s not clear why this happened

“This was a technical issue” unrelated to AI, with “no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity,” Microsoft said. The company referenced an “elevated load” and said it’ll share more information as it reviews the incident.

Zoom out: This is another reminder of why the modern economy’s reliance on hyperscalers can be risky, as one company’s technical difficulties can mess with an entire planet’s daily operations. Similar concerns arose when Cloudflare and Amazon Web Services crashed huge swaths of the internet last year.—ML

items.title: November 13, 2026
items.summary: November 13, 2026 Reader 🌙 NEW! Sleep Timer — You can now set a sleep timer for text-to-speech in the Reader app and the Readwise Books app. Tap the moon in the Speed sheet and choose an amount of time, or have it stop at the end of the chapter in books. Playback will pause on…
items.contentHtml:
November 13, 2026

Reader

  • 🌙 NEW! Sleep Timer — You can now set a sleep timer for text-to-speech in the Reader app and the Readwise Books app. Tap the moon in the Speed sheet and choose an amount of time, or have it stop at the end of the chapter in books. Playback will pause on its own when time is up. Thanks to Samuel for building it.
  • 🔖 Fixed Ghostreader Shortlisting — When using the Triage library configuration, asking Ghostreader to add documents to your Shortlist could move them into a location your layout doesn't show, so they seemed to disappear. Tristan made Ghostreader add the shortlist tag instead, so those documents now show up in your Shortlist view.
  • 🏷️ Fixed Ghostreader Tags — In Reader on web, if you asked Ghostreader to tag a document and moved your mouse to another row before it finished, the chat said "Added tag" but the tags never saved. Cam made Ghostreader apply the tags to the document it was working on, so they stick even if you keep browsing.
  • 📄 Fixed PDFs Saved by Link — When Reader couldn't download a PDF you saved by its link, for example because the site was down, Reader on web said "This PDF is downloading to your device" indefinitely. Tristan made Reader mark those saves as failed, so you now see an import error instead of a page that never loads.
  • 📖 Fixed Stuck EPUB Pages — Some EPUBs wouldn't turn past a blank page near the start, so you couldn't get any further into the book. Cam fixed how empty sections load, so paging carries on through them in the Reader app and the Readwise Books app.
  • 🔗 Fixed Tag Links on iOS — Tapping a tag or filter link copied from Reader on web, like one pasted into a note, opened an empty "No documents found" list in the Reader app on iOS. Cam taught the app to read web filter links, so they now open the matching filtered view.
  • 📱 Fixed iPhone Duo Toolbar — On the iPhone Duo's side rail, tapping the triage button in an article's toolbar opened the Actions sheet instead of the Inbox, Later, and Archive menu. Cam gave each toolbar button its own full-size tap area, so every button opens what it shows.
  • 🔲 Fixed E-ink Sheet Animations — With E-ink mode on, the "…" menu, the Appearance sheet, and other bottom sheets still slid into view, which smears on an E-ink screen. Andrew made every sheet appear and close without the slide when E-ink mode or reduced animations are on.
  • 🗑️ Fixed Erase Reader Content — “Erase Reader content” signed you out as if it had worked, but if you'd ever uploaded an ebook to Readwise Books, the erase quietly failed and your Reader documents and feeds stayed put. Tristan fixed the erase for those accounts, so it now clears your Reader content as expected.
  • 📡 Fixed Adding Feeds by Page Link — Pasting a page's address into Add Feeds could subscribe you to an empty third-party copy of the feed instead of the site's own feed, when both pointed at the same page. Cam made Reader pick the feed the most readers follow, so you get the official one.
  • 🗣️ Fixed Gujarati Text-to-Speech — Gujarati documents played their text-to-speech audio at about double speed, even at 1x. Tristan added the timing Gujarati needs, so it reads at a natural pace.
  • 🛜 Parsing Updates — Krzys improved how Reader handles documents from chronicle.com, inkandswitch.com, anthropic.com, thecut.com, arxiv.org, theankler.com, and substack.com.

Highlights

  • 🛫 Fixed Launch Hangs — The app could sit on its logo at launch, for minutes on Android when the network quietly dropped part of the connection, and indefinitely on iPhone in airplane mode. Ibai added timeouts and an offline check, so the app opens to your highlights, or to the offline screen, either way.
  • 📲 Improved iPhone Duo Layout — On the iPhone Duo, content ran under the status column along the side of the screen. Cam kept the app clear of the column, while the cards on Home still use the full width when the Duo is folded.
  • 🎨 Fixed Missing Covers — When a book or article cover failed to load, like an old Twitter avatar or an expired publisher image, you got an empty frame. Ibai made the app show the same painted cover it uses for books without one.
  • 🔢 Fixed Clearing Page Numbers — Deleting the page number on a highlight you typed in and tapping Save kept the old number. Ibai made an empty field clear it, so the highlight saves without a page number.
  • 🔣 Fixed EPUB Endnote Links — Highlights from some EPUBs showed their endnote links as raw text like * in the app and in shared highlight images. Tristan taught the app to recognize more endnote styles, so those links now show as a small footnote marker.
  • 🎯 Fixed Mastery Card Scrolling — In the list view of Daily Review, saving or canceling a Mastery card sent you back to the top of the review. Ibai keeps your place now, so you pick up right where you left off.
  • 💬 Fixed Ghostreader on Recommended Books — Tapping “Ask Ghostreader” on a highlight from the recommended book at the end of Daily Review ended in an error. Ibai fixed the lookup, so Ghostreader opens on those highlights like any other.
  • 📧 Improved Export Emails — Export emails from Highlights and Reader only had a download link, and that link stopped working if you deleted your account after exporting. Thanks to Tristan, exports of 5 MB or less now come attached to the email, and the link keeps working for its full seven days either way.

Books

  • 🧩 NEW! Match to My Edition — If the same book showed up twice in your library, like an EPUB you uploaded next to the copy Goodreads imported, there was no way to combine them. Now you can open the book's ··· menu and choose the Match option, then pick the copy to keep. Books merges the two, with your reading sessions, posts, and review on the one you keep. Tristan built the matching, and Artem made new uploads join the book their ISBN already matches, so fewer duplicates appear in the first place.
  • 🚪 NEW! Delete Only Your Books Account — Deleting your account from Readwise Books used to delete your whole Readwise account, Reader library and Highlights included. The Manage Account page in Books now also offers Delete Books Account, which removes your Books profile and reading history, but keeps your Reader and Highlights data. Thanks to Johannes.
  • 🔄 Improved Goodreads Sync — Changes you made on Goodreads only reached Readwise Books when you tapped Refresh, and Refresh re-imported your whole shelf every time. If you've turned on any Goodreads cross-posting option, Books now checks your Goodreads shelves in the background, about once a day or every six hours while you're actively changing them. Refresh now brings over only what changed, usually in seconds, and moves books between shelves to match Goodreads. Mati built both.
  • 🔑 Improved Sign-In — Long-time Readwise users who sign in with Apple or Amazon couldn't find those buttons in Readwise Books, because sign-in asked for an email first and Hide My Email users didn't know which address to type. Tristan put Apple and Amazon right under the email field. He also stopped the "Sign in with Apple didn't work" alert from appearing when you cancel, in Books and the Reader app.
  • 🛡️ Improved DRM Warnings — Uploading a DRM-protected EPUB to Readwise Books said "Uploaded", but the book never showed up. Cam made Books check the file first, on the readwise.io/books/upload page and in the app, so you see right away that DRM-protected books can't be opened.
  • ➕ Improved Add to Currently Reading — Add to Currently Reading on the Home screen wouldn't let you pick a book that was already on your Want to Read shelf. Cam made those books selectable, so you can move them straight to Currently Reading, and books already there show an orange check.
  • 🎧 Improved Audiobook XP — Listening to an audiobook earned the same XP at 2x as at 1x, because it counted the minutes on the clock. Johannes now credits XP for the audio you actually heard, so faster listening earns more.
  • 📸 Fixed Photo Highlights in Weekly Stats — Highlights you took with the camera during a manual reading session didn't count toward the weekly stats on Home. Tristan added them, so your weekly highlight count includes the pages you photograph.
  • 📅 Fixed Goodreads Details — Goodreads reviews with a spoiler came into Readwise Books as just the spoiler, and dates from Goodreads could show a day early if you live west of UTC. A reading session with no page progress could also clear the progress bar Books had posted to Goodreads. Mati fixed all three, so your reviews, dates, and Goodreads progress come through intact.
  • 🧷 Fixed Connecting Goodreads — On iOS, tapping Connect Goodreads in Readwise Books could show "Connecting to Goodreads" for a moment and drop you back without ever showing the sign-in sheet. On Android, an import started after the app had been in the background could fail within seconds. Mati fixed both, so the sign-in sheet appears and imports reload and carry on.
  • 🛍️ Fixed Purchases After Samples — If you finished a sample and then bought the book, it could open on its last pages, so it looked like you only had the sample. Cam fixed where the purchase picks up, so it opens where the sample's text ended.
  • 🚫 Fixed Books Deleted in Reader — Deleting an uploaded EPUB in Reader left it on your Books shelf, and tapping Read showed a loader that never finished. Tristan made Books tell you the book was deleted in Reader, so you know what happened instead of waiting.
  • ⏳ Fixed Reopening Downloaded Books — Reopening a downloaded book could show a spinner that never went away. Artem made the reader wait for the page to finish loading before it returns you to your spot, so books reopen where you left off.
  • 🔎 Fixed Return to Reading After Search — After jumping far ahead with “Find in document” and tapping Done, the Return button didn't show up until your next page turn. Tristan made it appear right away, so you can jump back to where you were.
  • 👤 Fixed Reviewer Profiles — Tapping a reviewer's avatar on a book's Reviews tab closed the book page, which meant that going back skipped past it. Samuel made the book page stay open underneath, so back returns you to the book.
  • ⏱️ Improved Last Session Recap — The Last Session recap could still pop up when you picked up a book on a second device an hour after reading it on the first. Artem now opens it automatically only when your last session on any device ended at least six hours ago.
  • 📐 Fixed iPad Rotation — After you rotated an iPad, the reader could stay laid out for the old orientation, leaving the page cut off or squeezed to one side. Cam fixed the screen size the app reads after it updates itself, so books fill the screen in either orientation.

Please enjoy this transcript of part 2 of my recent subscriber Q&A.
