Q&A with Tim — How to Get Unstuck, Resilience in Hard Times, Tools for Brain Health, Finding Inner Peace, Optimism as a Learnable Skill, and More

Additional podcast platforms

Listen to this episode on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, Overcast, Podcast Addict, Pocket Casts, Castbox, YouTube Music, Amazon Music, Audible, or on your favorite podcast platform.

Transcripts may contain a few typos. With many episodes lasting 2+ hours, it can be difficult to catch minor errors.

Tim Ferriss: Next one is from Mary, “I know Alzheimer’s prevention is a big focus for you. Can you give a concise listing of the preventative measures you are taking, including drugs, all therapies, i.e. TMS, hot, cold, et cetera, food and movement?” Mary, you’re in good luck. In fact, I already have a draft of a blog post that is also going to be turned into a podcast where I’m going to go through all of this in excruciating Tim Ferriss detail, but I will give you a few things that come to mind and there will be much more in terms of detail and non-obvious choices.

But I’m going to preface it by saying that we are in the Dark Ages still with Alzheimer’s and many neurodegenerative diseases. Having shepherded a few relatives through treatments for Alzheimer’s, I will say that it is primitive AF and many of these drugs are a Faustian bargain. In my opinion, I have access to a lot of great researchers and there’s very little consensus on the best way to try to address these things. I would say the only consensus I can point to is that prevention is the name of the game. And these processes, at least as we currently understand them, that culminate in what we would diagnose as say Alzheimer’s start pretty early, 30s, 40s, right. So I won’t get into all the mechanisms of action that I think are most interesting because that’s beside the point, you asked what I’m doing. Some of what I’m doing, sauna a few times a week, 20 minutes, somewhere between 170 and 180 degrees.

Hotter is not better. You can look at some of Rhonda Patrick’s, Dr. Rhonda Patrick’s coverage of the research. You don’t want to overcook your head. That is going to push you in the wrong direction, not the right direction. Interval training, Dr. Tommy Wood and I talked about this at length. It remains, I think, one of the most interesting interventions that I’ve come across, certainly at least as supported for maintaining hippocampal volume in the brain. And we can talk about the importance of the hippocampus another time. But doing this Norwegian 4×4 training, which is hard, I’m going to warn you, it’s also helpful for VO₂ max. And we can talk about how that’s correlated to all sorts of good things, but you’re basically doing four minutes of all out intense exercise. By last minute, you feel like you’re going to die and you’re being chased by wolves, getting to a very high heart rate.

I use a heart rate monitor, Morpheus, for tracking all of this. And then you take three minutes off and then you do four again and you do four rounds of that. Okay. Doing this, I think it was three times a week for six months, produced durable changes out five years, if I’m remembering correctly. That is nuts. That is pretty wild. Is that the perfect protocol? Is that what you need? We don’t know, but the evidence so far, at least that’s been documented, supports that. There are other things you can do. Zone 2 training, certainly for mitochondrial health. Urolithin A is a supplement I’ve decided to take also for predominantly mitochondrial health. We don’t have time to dig into that, but I do find the research there pretty compelling. You can buy that on Amazon or online. It’s produced by a company called Timeline. Mitopure is their patented Urolithin A.

And there are other things that are light lifts. And again, I’m not saying any of these things cure Alzheimer’s. I think by the time someone’s far gone, it’s pretty much far gone. However, five milligrams of lithium orotate, I do take five milligrams of lithium orotate. That is also OTC, you can get it easily. And listen to my podcast with Tommy Wood, tripling down on dental health, air purifiers, water, creating systems such that your environment and your routines are as supportive as possible. I have become a huge fan of, so in the case of dental health, for instance, using gum or mouthwash that includes xylitol. And don’t have time to get into it right now in great depth, but a blog post and podcast is coming that’s going to be dedicated to this with the enormous grain of salt that I am not in the business of treating disease.

However, I am genetically predisposed to Alzheimer’s with APOE3/4 and other risk factors, so I am throwing the kitchen sink at it or everything in the kitchen sink, I suppose the expression goes. So thanks for the question, Mary. Hopefully that is somewhat helpful, but my blog post and podcast will have a lot more.

This is from, I think a different Susan. “I’ve spent nearly 30 years practicing acupuncture and previously worked as a psychotherapist. I observed that people can desperately want to heal while unconsciously holding under the very patterns that keep them suffering. Have you ever recognized exactly what was keeping you stuck yet found yourself unable to let it go and what finally allowed you to?” Oh yeah, all the time. And just look at anyone’s New Year’s resolutions, mine included. And look, I do the past year review and I’ve got my behavioral engineering and so on, but there’s still things that I can see.

And I remember hearing Sam Harris talk about sorting other people’s problems out. It’s like you can sort out other people’s problems in two seconds. Giving advice is easy, but actually moving into the catalyzing stage where you translate good intention to behavior is something else. So psychedelics I’m not going to spend a lot of time on. They do allow you oftentimes to step outside of yourself as the protagonist in your own movie and watch that movie on a screen as someone in the audience. So it can be very helpful for developing an awareness and opening a window of opportunity for rewriting some of the beliefs and patterns that govern your life. But outside of that, IFS, Internal Family Systems created by Dick Schwartz, I think is very useful and no drugs required, although it is often implemented in some form in the preparation and integration for say MDMA-assisted psychotherapy. CBT, very helpful, might not be sexy, but in large part originating out of Stoic philosophy. If you have not looked into the genesis story, it’s actually a good read.

But CBT, cognitive behavioral therapy, very interesting. DBT, also very interesting. People can look that up if they’d like. And Atomic Habits, I mentioned it once before. There’s a reason it sold 25 million, 30 million copies. Good God, non-recurring phenomenon. Good for you, James. And the last two things I would say is that the pain has to be painful enough. Sometimes people just aren’t in enough pain to change. I mean, I’ve seen this with addicts over and over and over again. I’ve sadly had family members who have died from addiction. I’ve had best friends who’ve died from addiction. I’ve had friends who have friends who are currently addicted. Sometimes they have to really hit rock bottom. I hate to say it, but sometimes the pain isn’t painful enough. And then last but not least, I’ll mention fear setting. People can find fear setting, which I’ve talked about quite a bit before. My TED Talk, which has God knows how many views now, I don’t know, many millions, focuses on this exclusively.

I think tim.blog/ted will take you to that and you can find it online for free. Don’t have to buy anything. There are many aspects of this fear setting, which is intended to methodically remove different emergency brakes in your life, which are nebulous fears or inhibitions of one type or another. But there’s one aspect of fear setting. It’s the piece that is most neglected and most applies to this question, which is describing in writing the cost of inaction. All right. And so what that looks like, you can take a piece of paper. It’s very straightforward. Grab a piece of paper. I like doing this analog, create three columns. You got one year, three years, 10 years, and then put at the top whatever it is that you would like to change. And then you have cost of inaction. So now you have three columns with three timelines.

And in each of those columns, you’re just going to write down if nothing changes, if you continue doing what you’re doing or not doing what you’re not doing, what are the costs physically, financially, relationally, whatever it might be, one year from now, three years from now, could be five years, pick your poison, 10 years from now. And chances are, if you get to that stage with something, the picture that it paints that is, let’s just call it nearly inevitable, is not going to be pretty. And that is how you take something that isn’t currently painful enough and you magnify it with a reality-accelerator to make it compelling enough so that you make a change, recognizing that the change involves less pain, likely temporary, less risk, also probably reversible than the status quo. Because we think of risk or downside risks or problems as the byproduct of something we do that is new, but we don’t often take the time to consider the atrocious cost of the status quo and inaction.

Remember the format question I planted? Here’s the question from Jason A. “Hey, Tim, I’ve been a big fan since The 4-Hour Workweek. I have all the books and was in a test group for Coyote.” Thank you for that. Appreciate it. That was a fun little experiment with the card game. “Really appreciate you and everything you do. Question, I really love the more relaxed and less polished format of The Random Show and the Q&As. Wondering if those are less effort.” Fuck yeah, they’re less effort for me. Okay. “Wondering if those are less effort for you compared to the researched intentional guest episodes.” Yes, I put a ton of time into those. “And it seems like there are just too many interview format podcasts in the world at the moment.”

Okay. I know I’m interjecting with my own director’s commentary here. “Any chance you would pivot towards a more consistently extemporaneous format in the future?” Yes, I’ve wanted to do this and I have had a number of different thoughts on how I might experiment with it. I’ve done some co-hosting experiments in the past, you might have noticed, where I’ve had say Kevin Kelly on, good friend of mine, and they invite the guest and we both interview them. Did this with Danny Hillis, amazing, amazing, such a fun interview. And for me, those are extemporaneous, more extemporaneous. I think that may not be as obvious to the listener or to the viewer, but that is the case. And I am eager to hear what you would like to see me do. So please add in the comments what formats you would watch or listen to, what you think could be fun for me to experiment with.

I am very, very interested in this. So of course, as I am doing this in real time, we have a feed of comments. I’d love for you guys to drop in a bunch of comments. But if you want to gestate and come back with a suggestion, you can also shoot me an @reply. Just tag me on X @tferriss, T-F-E-R-R-I-S-S, and use #format in that tweet somewhere. All right. So that’s the ask. I would love your input. I would love your thoughts, recommendations for experimental formats. This is something I really would like to do because it’s fun for me to do. It’s lightweight, but I get to exercise my brain more in some respects than a fixed-format interview. I think interview formats are largely dead. I think almost every interview-based format in the world of podcasting, AKA, if we’re looking at the latest vintage television shows on YouTube, are basically islands in the middle of the ocean with a rising water level.

And it’s not a question of if they will be consumed. It is just a matter of when with respect to AI and other things. I’ve talked about the canary in the coal mine, which is prescriptive nonfiction in the form of books. I published my sales numbers and so I’m looking at trend lines post introduction of ChatGPT 3.5 in, I believe it was November of 2023. And there are many reasons therefore that I would love to experiment with this and let me know. I would really love to take a stab at it. So keep dragging them in. I will have access to this chat after we stop the live stream and certainly I will be watching the specific tweets that go up with @tferriss and format. So please do let me know.

There are lots of questions in translating thought or introspection or brainstorming to action. 

MIDROLL #1

This is from Vedant, “How do you stop being an intellectual collector and start being a builder?” And honestly, I would look at some of the older videos by Casey Neistat, who was a very famous, still is a very famous creator who’s had the longevity of decades at this point. He is very good at verbalizing and giving a rationale for consistently shipping something, whether it’s once a day, once a week, once a month, it can be anything, which relates back to developing a bias towards action with the smallest next-possible action. It doesn’t need to be big, but you’re reconstructing an identity and then the identity will lead you to habitual behaviors and that will lead to more output.

John T, “As it pertains to AI, 12 months from now, what will we wish we were doing today that we aren’t?” Probably more defining and elimination as described in The 4-Hour Workweek, but you don’t need to read The 4-Hour Workweek. You could buy books like The 80/20 Principle by Richard Koch. There are many different options. I have already recommended The Effective Executive by Peter Drucker. These are evergreen topics that are going to increase in importance.

Question from Mitchell, “As the current events seem to continue to turn darker and darker, how are you staying positive in supporting your own mental health at this time? How are you remaining hopeful? What strategies have you implemented?” Well, I have not had any social media apps outside of YouTube, which I use daily for learning. I’ve not had any social media apps on my phone for probably five years now. I think that is a very simple step that you can experiment with doing a social media cleanse/fast for one or two months. Trust me, it’s like doing 20 years of therapy. So you can swim upstream against this raging waterfall of bullshit and rage, or you can step out of that and just sit in an inner tube and float down the stream without social media. So in other words, it removes the need to do a lot of things when you remove that input. I would say, related to this, deciding on in your calendar where you’re going to have upside time and downside time. And what I mean by that is you spend an hour or two, it could be on ChatGPT, it could be on YouTube, could be elsewhere, looking for optimistic cases, asking questions about possibility and opportunities in the age of AI, in, fill in the blank, in sector X, whatever it might be. This is upside time. So you are deliberately putting on your optimist hat. Somewhat echoes the thinking hats of Edward de Bono and lateral thinking, but you’re putting on your optimism hat for upside time. This is in your calendar, right? This is dedicated study hall.

And then downside time is similar. You are proactively setting aside time to look at risks, kind of like strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats. You’re going to be focusing on weaknesses, threats, risks, et cetera, with the focus on finding descriptions of what can be done. It’s not just a description of the problem. So I would use, for instance, an LLM as the front end to your YouTube search. And the reason for this is that to the extent possible, you really want to avoid, in my opinion, a passive feed of rage, nihilism and pessimism. And that’s what you get if you go to youtube.com and immediately get pulled into your curated fear, uncertainty and doubt clips and shorts collection. This is how the platforms continue to make you the product. Their customers are advertisers. They’re selling your attention. That is the sole purpose of these platforms from a business model perspective.

Do not be fooled. The goal is not to entertain. The goal is not to help. The goal is to keep you on for as long as possible. And we have a heavy human proclivity to spend a lot more time on the things that upset us than things that make us optimistic. So the approach that counterbalances that inclination is having upside time and downside time and calendaring it. I would say two other things for me personally. Look at your past. You made it to where you are right now. There have been recessions, there have been wars, there have been lots of problems, and you somehow figured it out. Sure you had stumbles along the way, you probably had some disasters and you recovered from those things. So I am reading, for instance, and this might seem like it’s in my downside time, but I would actually put it in my upside time, I’m reading a book right now called Hard Times by Studs Terkel. 

So Studs Terkel is amazing, won the Pulitzer Prize. This is an old book, Hard Times: An Oral History of the Great Depression. And it is dozens and dozens and dozens of vignettes that have been organized thematically with people who went through the Depression explaining in their own words what happened to them. And you have destitution, but joy. You have people who did better than ever during the worst of times. And they weren’t necessarily bankers, a lot of those went the other way. Jingle writers, for instance. There’s a very, very concrete example of someone who wrote jingles and just had this outpouring of creative productivity during the Depression. And there are dozens and dozens and dozens of examples, people of every gender, every race imaginable. And it’s deeply humanizing of something that most of us are really only familiar with in a very passing way. It was a hard period in US history and we’ve seen black and white photos of women sitting on doorsteps with underfed children and we know a thing or two about it.

Maybe we know about the stock crash and brokers jumping out of windows, et cetera. Okay, fine. But that’s a very cursory glance at what was an incredibly important historic event. And this book just personalizes the whole thing. That’s upside time for me because it highlights again and again and again and again human resilience and how good people are at surviving, recovering and then thriving after the fact. So those are a few. And look, not to sound like a shill for my own books, trust me, I make next to nothing from my books and you don’t have to buy it, I’m sure you can find it on Pirate Bay or something, but the meta section of The 4-Hour Chef, which focuses on accelerated learning, is the most important section in that book. And it’s about 80 pages. The name of the game on some level is having confidence that you can adapt in the future.

And it’s a chicken and the egg situation because as Mike Maples Jr., a very accomplished entrepreneur and investor, told me at one point, “One of the few things that you’re responsible for with your kids is teaching them to be optimistic because if you teach them to be optimistic, they see options. They feel like they have agency.” So does the optimism come first and then the action or is it action and then the optimism? I think it actually points both ways. The arrow is bidirectional. So reading a book like this, Hard Times, makes me more optimistic that I can figure things out. Spending time on meta learning makes me more confident that I can figure things out. Even if I’m test driving the toolkit on something that seems as trivial and unnecessary as rock climbing, as is the case currently, or it could be working on portrait drawing using Procreate and following along with YouTube videos, applying the toolkit. It doesn’t matter where you apply it, it’s the same toolkit.

So if you’re refining your use of that toolkit on anything, you are getting better at cultivating the metacognition and ability to learn that will give you adaptability in a rapidly changing world, et cetera, et cetera. And then the social media cleanse is in the elimination bucket. It is turning off the torrent of inputs of the trivial many. And look, I have no social media on my phone. Do my friends still send me the dumbest and most entertaining memes on Instagram? Do I get sucked into it? Yes, but I can only go so far because I don’t have the app on my phone. So I can waste a few minutes on some dumb, so many dumb things that I receive every day from my ridiculous friends. And I enjoy it. I’m not going to lie. Look, the internet is built for entertainment, among other things, sure, but I limit the damage to the downside risk of my own human inclinations by taking those apps off my phone.

So I’ll stop there for now, but those are a few of the things that come to mind.

Question on wabi-sabi is from Eman. I’m probably mispronouncing that. Will handmade work and human connection become more valuable? In other words, human imperfection. Yes, I do think it will. I’m not sure quite how to capitalize on that or what to do with that assumption, but I do think that’s definitely going to be the case.
I’m going to go for a bit more, and then I’m headed to the gym. Oh, that’s another thing. Yeah, state, remember that? Go to the gym or just work out at home.

Exercise, folks. Like mind-body separation, that whole Cartesian duality, bunch of nonsense. If you want to feed your brain, you want to feed your mood, you want to be optimistic, fix your state, exercise. So I’m headed straight to the gym after this.

Ox the moron, that’s a good one. Best way to spend five to 10K today to get current on AI. I don’t think you need to spend five to 10K. I would use the tools, create projects. Use the tools to help you use the tools. I guess there are two thoughts on this. So there is a company called Oboe that I am involved with, but it is custom designed for learning. Certainly the frontier models are going to be going after this, but AI for learning, “I want to learn—” You just fill it in. Oboe.com, O-B-O-E.com.

And I would type in, “Effectively give me 10 different projects. I am new to AI tools and LLMs. I want to get more familiar with these tools. Give me 10 project based learning opportunities. In other words, 10 projects where I’m creating something, that I could consider for learning how to better use these tools and their various capacities. Each one I should be able to finish in one hour, three hours or less,” whatever your number happens to be. And I would also drop that into Claude, drop it into ChatGPT, let them all compete for best answers, and then you can go from there. I would build things. I would make things. I would try to automate some workflow. Generally, that doesn’t give me a hard on because I think the definition and elimination are more important, but making things. Maybe there’s something beautiful you want to make. I mean, give it the spin that’s actually going to energize you. That is how I would get current on AI, is by doing stuff.

I don’t think you need to spend five to 10K. But whatever the upgraded models are, frankly, even the slower models from six months ago are plenty. Yeah, actually I can’t speak out of school, but I’ve seen some amazing hackers, just to prove a point, use older models to do staggeringly powerful things to say, “Hey, we don’t need the latest and greatest to actually move the needle. They’re already here. They have been for a while.”

This question on psychedelic experiences, if I’m still interested, if I’m still present. I do still find them useful. I have decreased my frequency dramatically as I’ve had other tools to bring to bear on state and mental health and so on, like neuromodulation. In other words, the accelerated TMS and the ONE-D, O-N-E hyphen D, protocol that I described earlier. But they still have incredible applications. I mean, I do believe that these compounds are still one of the most straightforward, not risk-free, but straightforward ways to elicit some of the greatest adventures that humans can have on this planet.

I still believe that. And insights and touching the timeless in ways that perhaps the mystics referred to and experienced via other means. So I do find them deeply fascinating. What’s new on that front, which is the second part of that question, I would say shorter duration. There are shorter duration compounds that may have equal efficacy to, say, MDMA in treating conditions like PTSD without the typically combined dyad psychotherapy. In other words, separating the drug effect from the therapeutic wrapper in some respects. Methylone is one at the forefront right now. I’ve had experience with this. I mean, I’ve known methylone for at least 10, 15 years, but it is effectively the shorter acting, gentler cousin of MDMA. And Transcend Therapeutics, which was co-founded by Kevin Ryan, who I interviewed on the podcast not too long ago. He also co-founded Business Insider and MongoDB and Gilt Groupe and many, many companies.

But I think that stands a chance of reaching millions of people because it is easier to slot into the preexisting healthcare system on many levels. There are many, many developments in this field. I’ll just give you one more that I think is arguably most interesting to me and I’m funding research that Chuck Nichols is doing on this, but looking at the potent anti-inflammatory effects of various psychedelics at doses that are unbelievably small. So let’s just say—I’ll give you an example. So in the case of mushrooms, let’s talk about dried psilocybe mushrooms. I mean, we could get strain specific, but I’ll keep it simple. If we’re looking at the mushrooms of Terrence McKenna’s day, a heroic dose would be five grams. All right. If you’re taking a microdose of these same mushrooms, it might be 50 to 100 milligrams. What would happen if you took one 1000th of that? Well, psilocybin is actually not the best candidate, but some of these other psychedelics, many of which you would not recognize, or most people wouldn’t, at sub-perceptual but sub, sub, sub-perceptual doses, I mean almost seemingly homeopathic doses, have incredibly potent, multi-mechanism, anti-inflammatory effects.

And I think pet hypothesis is that many of the benefits we see from psychedelics, antidepressant effects and so on, in many, many people, many subjects even in some of these clinical trials, are derived from anti-inflammatory effects on chronic neuro-inflammation. And double clicking on that, that chronic neuro-inflammation is often downstream of an acute infection that you had at one point. It can be caused by many other things, so it’s not to use that as the sole lens through which you explain these things. But those are a few areas that I find currently very interesting.

Matthew, “I tried Hugh Jackman’s trick for becoming extraordinarily jacked, which was to row 2,000 meters in seven minutes.” I want to hear how that went. So Matthew J, please let me know. That’s quite a tease.

Matthew J, that is impossible. Yeah, the 2,000 meters in seven minutes.

Hugh Jackman is an elite level athlete. Yeah, you might kill yourself trying to replicate some of what he does. 

MIDROLL 2

There’s a question here from, I apologize if I’m mispronouncing this, but Daniel Taga, MD, not sure how you pronounce it.

But your question here is, okay, Doc here, building Quantified Self 2.0 with metabolomics. I do think metabolomics are incredibly interesting. Starting from a real definition of health. Tim, what would QS 2.0, that’s Quantified Self, I assume, 2.0 have to show you to be worth it? All right. Bookmark, because that’s going to tie in here.

Question from Jon C, that’s J-O-N. Tim, your name came up when Gary Wolf and Kevin Kelly spoke in the Ferry Building last week, that’s in San Francisco, to launch Gary’s new book, The Quantified Self. I know you were at the very first Quantified Self meetup 18 years ago at Kevin’s house. It’s true. I have a blog post with photos from that. I was still white knuckling a little bit of a faux hawk with my remaining hair at the time. What role has self-quantifying played in your life since then, please? So these tie together. And I will answer Daniel’s question and this question. So what would Quantified Self 2.0 need to show me? It would need to show me, I would say, a filtered high signal version of the lens that I’ve used for myself with Quantified Self. And that is a distilling from data to interpretation to action, and last mile being behavioral change. So where I think we are drowning at the moment is the volume of information, right?

It is very, very easy to gather an overwhelming amount of data with wearables. Back in the day, it was pretty painful to painstakingly gather this stuff with your own spreadsheets and so on. Now it’s trivial. It is easy to amass an ocean of ones and zeros related to yourself with your Oura Ring, which I use, or your WHOOP Band or whatever it might be, plus add any number of other inputs, right? So much like a lot of books and presentations, we’re not failing from too little information, we’re failing from too much information, I think. So there’s the interpretation layer, and I do think your inputs matter. So the metabolomics and proteomics, I think all of that I think is incredibly interesting. But ultimately what it comes down to—for instance, in the realm of Alzheimer’s disease, there are people who have these very fancy collections of very esoteric biomarkers, and that’s great, and you can watch how they trend, but how does it change the clinical intervention? And the answer is, as it stands right now, it doesn’t.

Okay, fine. Maybe this is a case of harvest now, decrypt later. So maybe we gather all this stuff on my relatives and it’s too late for them, but five years in the future we have this data so we can do a retroactive analysis with fancy tools, AI, quantum computing, whatever, I don’t think we need quantum computing for that, but to derive some type of directional signal for people now who have better interventions. Okay, fine, but I think that’s kind of a leap as it stands right now. So I’m looking for how something informs action, and that’s not always terribly clear. And then how do you facilitate action? This is the big one, because for healthy normals who are wearing any number of different tools or having various tests done, they get back all this stuff, maybe they’re given an interpretation, maybe it has to get pushed to their primary care physician, and in some cases it’s going to spot something that is really nefarious or a trend line that deserves intervention.

So I’ll give a simple example. Not to say that hemoglobin A1C is the end all be all, I recognize this, but it’s a simple marker. Well, in some ways not so simple, but it’s an easy one that a lot of, at least Americans will recognize. So hemoglobin A1C is described by many doctors as your three month or so running average of glucose, and it’s used to infer your insulin sensitivity and so on. Because your fasting insulin can swing all over the place, and certainly your insulin can swing all over the place. Ultimately, I do think an OGTT, like most people, if they can afford it, which they can, should get an oral glucose tolerance test where you’re kind of taking blood and measuring things every 30 minutes for two hours. Talk to your doctor. But if you have hemoglobin A1C and you’re looking at your trend line, all right, it’s creeping up. Hemoglobin A1C appears to be going up over three quarters. And if you telescope that out, uh-oh, I’m going to end up being a type two diabetic. We should do something sooner rather than later. What’s the advice?

Now, you could have a pharmacological intervention. Who knows what that is, right? Put someone on low-dose tirzepatide, maybe somebody thinks that metformin is a good idea, frequently it isn’t, whatever that might be. But for a lot of folks, the answer’s going to be clean up your diet and do more exercise of some type. How do you get those fucking people to do that, especially when the pain isn’t painful enough? They’re like, “I’ve got plenty of time. It’s not that bad. I’m still in range.” Even though the trend line would say, “Sooner or later, you’re going to be out of range. And if you wait and wait and wait, you’re going to have a much larger problem that is lodged deeply into your physiology that’s going to be problematic.” The behavioral change piece I think is huge, right? And that is currently what’s missing. I’m hoping to do a bunch with that with a company that I probably shouldn’t name, so I won’t get into it, but I am hoping to do a lot on that side since that’s effectively what I do professionally, is focus on behavioral change.

That’s a very, very long answer, but hopefully that’s somewhat helpful. Sorry for, again, the accidental TED Talk. Beware of those ketones, gets you all fired up.

What was Tim like before he took psychedelics? What was the biggest shift? I’m sighing not because it’s a bad question. I’m sighing because I have to keep saying it’s important. I talk more people out of psychedelics than I talk into psychedelics. If your buddy invites you to your first psychedelic experience, which is some rent-a-shaman giving ayahuasca in Topanga Canyon, I would run the other direction. I mean, these are, as my old friend, who sadly passed away, iconic researcher in the field, Roland Griffiths would say, “You’re using nuclear power. It is very, very powerful. You have to be very careful.” And I would treat these compounds as if you’re considering having spinal surgery or neurosurgery. You would do a lot of homework and you would measure twice and cut once.

With that disclaimer said—I mean, before psychedelics, there were gigantic psychological and emotional icebergs causing incredible problems in my life that I was wholly unaware of. I was also completely unaware of how 17 different problems all related to one or two core problems. So there’s a value in diagnosing or seeing the unseen. And I’m not talking about mechanical elves in this case. That’s a separate Q&A. I’m talking about simply seeing your life and behavior as an objective third party would see it if they had 20/20 vision, right? That’s incredibly difficult to do in sort of ordinary consensus reality. It’s very, very hard to do. And in that experience, it is very common that you’re able to take off the glasses you didn’t realize you were wearing and inspect the lens and see how it’s affecting everything else. So that’s part one.

Part two, aside from the diagnostic capability, is the, I don’t want to say curative, but the therapeutic potential of contending with issues like PTSD, contending with issues like depression. It is not a panacea on any level. It’s contraindicated for lots of people who might have a family history of schizophrenia or borderline personality disorder. The most interesting tool for those types of conditions that I’ve found is metabolic psychiatry, the ketogenic diet effectively, but it doesn’t really need to be 100% ketogenic. Look at what Sami Inkinen is doing. Look at what Chris Palmer’s doing. Dom D’Agostino has also commented on this at great length. I know this is a real pregnant pause.

I was able to put down a lot of very, very heavy, exhausting boulders that I didn’t even realize I was carrying. That’s the way I would put it. Life is lighter. Also, let’s say you’re afraid of water and a lot of people are. I didn’t even learn to swim until I was in my 30s, really. I was deathly afraid of drowning. Couldn’t swim even two laps in an Olympic-size swimming pool, not even one lap, half a lap, I guess, if we’re considering back and forth a lap. And if you look at how that’s best overcome, that fear, this is going somewhere, I promise, you might find a great method like Total Immersion swimming, created by a guy named Terry Laughlin, who became a friend. I did his last interview before he passed away. And where they start is not trying to do laps, it’s not swimming in deep water, it’s simply submerging your head as if you were trying to teach an infant how to do survival swimming. Also something very interesting that I’m not going to get into.

So simply dunking your head, dunking your head, dunking your head. And then you might start with studying gliding positions. How do you use the least energy to go the furthest distance? You go to the shallow end and you would practice getting into, say, fuselage right, fuselage left position. No attention to breathing. You’re kicking off the wall, going as far as you can, and then you’re standing up and then you’re rinsing and repeating. And before long, literally within a handful of months, I swam more than a mile open water in the ocean. I don’t think that’s actually an outlier if you practice this technique and this type of repeated exposure. Psychedelics are a very, very unusual form of repeated exposure. And there is such a thing as doing too much psychedelics. I know people who have lost the plot, you can really slip and get lost and you should take that seriously. Spend more time in consensus reality than you do in psychedelic land, or you can end up in a semi-permanent state of Alice in Wonderland. It’s not a good idea.

But what I mean is if, over time, and that could only be once or twice, maybe three times, but what you see, for instance, in some terminal cancer patients is fear extinction of death. That is pretty interesting. They lose their fear of death. Why? Because they already experienced what they subjectively felt to be ego death.

That’s a scary way to put it. That’s how it’s phrased often. Ego dissolution. What does it mean to experience consciousness without any sense of self, without any name, without any perception of time? It’s pretty strange is what it is, but it also ends up being, for a lot of people, very peaceful, even if it’s type two peace, like type two fun. Hard in the moment, then afterwards you’re like, wow, I feel really at peace.

I have fear of deterioration and things like Alzheimer’s disease, but death, not really so afraid of it. And that’s been true for a long time now. I credit that almost exclusively to psychedelics and it’s hard to put a value on that. It’s such a bizarre thing to even posit. But writ large, it does seem to remove a base layer of anxiety that comes with the awareness that you are going to die. That’s a big one. All right. So I didn’t expect to give such a fucking long answer, but I guess that’s the theme of the evening.

just to reiterate what I said about building, this is Daniel H., number three commenter, meaning like number three ranked with a crown. Claude Code is mind-bendingly good. It can take you from zero to hero or at least reasonably competent. Yeah, it is really remarkable what you can build with these things.

So here’s a question once again with the caveat that I’m not a medical professional, so talk to your doctor. This is actually a variant of this question I get a lot. Val had a question on natural statins for those healthy young fellows with genetically high cholesterol/heart disease, what do you think?

This returns to a very old topic, which I unpacked at length in The 4-Hour Body. So there is that, but I’ll give you the TLDR and that is all natural versus synthetic. All natural does not automatically mean safe. And I do take certain supplements. I do take certain herbs. The challenge with that is there’s very little regulation and very little standardizing. So for instance, if you look at examine.com or other places that have taken 10 off-the-counter or off-the-shelf melatonin supplements and had them analyzed, let’s just say they’re all supposed to be three milligrams. By the way, you can’t even buy melatonin in some countries for pretty good reasons, but forget that part. You have 10 of them analyzed, they all say three milligrams of melatonin. Some have precisely fuck all of melatonin, zero, they contain no melatonin, and some contain up to 20 milligrams of melatonin. That is a problem. If you are making the assumption for the moment that a supplement does something, having that variability on dosing is a bad thing. It is a bad thing.

Also, there are many things that are all natural, hemlock, arsenic, that are incredibly dangerous. So if you take ephedrine hydrochloride and then you are like, “Well, I’m going to use Ma Huang instead,” this Chinese—you can still get yourself into a lot of trouble. There are cases where it’s interesting to consider what the mix of various alkaloids and so on does versus in isolation. So you might look at, in the case of psychedelics, iboga versus ibogaine hydrochloride. It’s a worthwhile question. I would just say it needs to be studied with rigorous scientific controls for us to feel confident that we are not fooling ourselves.

And you can do that, right? So in the case of say ayahuasca, how does ayahuasca differ or how might it differ in its effects versus vaporized N,N-DMT? Since ayahuasca contains N,N-DMT and the way it is commonly explained is ayahuasca contains this N,N-DMT that’s found in the leaf of this plant called the chacruna, and it is not bioavailable when you take it orally, therefore you consume and the ancients figured out as they did, you macerate, smash and combine it with this vine, which contains monoamine oxidase inhibitors and voila, suddenly you absorb it. And at the end of the show, the molecule that did the most action is N,N-DMT.

Well, in a case like that, it turns out that the beta-carbolines in the vine itself, harmine and harmaline and so on, have some really interesting effects of their own. But to come to your specific question on cholesterol, I don’t know if you’re talking about red rice extract or other things, but when it comes to mortality, in my family, for instance, which horsemen, which of the four horsemen of death is going to get you? Is it neurodegenerative? Is it cardiovascular? Is it something else? And I think Peter Attia does a good job of describing these in his book Outlive, but in my family, all the males die of heart attacks. That’s basically it. Everyone dies of heart problems.

So if I were to use something that were an herbal supplement, number one, I would need to have it tested and I would need to get multiple batches over a period of several months. So I’d buy one, I’d have it tested. Maybe I wait, maybe I take it, maybe I wait. Another month later, I buy a bottle. Hopefully it’s a different lot number. I have that tested. Do the results come back the same? This is an important question.

Now, I also said though, these organic broad spectrum products, if they haven’t been sufficiently studied, some of them have been, can have unintended off-target effects. So if I’m trying to avoid death, and I’m no spring chicken, I’m 49, I would prefer to take what has the longest history of supportive data with the lowest downside risk. And if you do more sophisticated lipid analysis and so on, look at your genetics. In my case, you can figure out I’m a cholesterol hyper absorber. That’s not true for everyone, but if a doctor of mine says, “We want to put you on these four medications,” I could look at those medications. You really have to be your own advocate in medicine. And I could say, “Well, which of these medications have been on the market the longest and been studied most rigorously? Which is the most innocuous of the whole lot?” And in this particular case, it ended up being something called ezetimibe, which has been extensively studied, brand name Zetia.

And the question I posed was, “Well, okay, if the goal moving forward is to be under the curve, it’s sort of like total surface area under the curve of having these values at certain target levels or below certain levels, there’s no immediate rush. I’m not getting triple bypass, quadruple bypass surgery. Is it okay with you if I start with this most innocuous, best studied drug to see if I am a hyper responder?” Answer, “Yes.” Tried it. Guess what? I’m a hyper responder. I don’t need to take the other three. So this is how I approach it, but I do like the specificity, repeatability, consistency of certain drugs over their all natural alternatives just because there are so many unknowns in the supplement world or all-natural world.

By the way, that’s also why I think, broadly speaking, since a lot of people are interested in psychedelics, that something like LSD or a methylone or an MDMA is more interesting from a mainstream healthcare perspective, if we’re talking about mental health, because 50 micrograms is 50 micrograms is 50 micrograms if you have your synthesis dialed. Whereas with ayahuasca, if it’s sort of the shamanic eyeball dose, there are too many variables. Either there’s cook time, there’s concentration, there’s leaves, there’s admixtures. It’s like a cup of ayahuasca is not a cup of ayahuasca is not a cup of ayahuasca, even if you’re doing your best. Now, there are some interesting approaches. Hamilton Morris and I spoke a lot about pharmahuasca and basically trying to replicate the combination using drugs. I’ve never messed around with that personally, but I have seen more people get very destabilized from ayahuasca and underestimating LSD, but that’s a separate problem because it’s not the cool kid on the block right now. It’s old so people underestimate just how potent it is.

But in the case of ayahuasca, it’s because people have one or two cups that are really light in terms of consistency and then they’re like, “I’m an ayahuasca pro,” and they go to South America and they have something that has a consistency of honey and they get destroyed. It’s that inconsistency that I don’t like. So long answer to a short question as per usual this evening.

Tim is a supplement company’s worst nightmare. Yeah, most of the time. It’s also a reason why it was so expensive to build my first company because I actually did all the due diligence and standardizing. It’s much more expensive to try to put in those standard operating procedures than to not. So most people choose the not.

How are my teeth so white? That’s a good one, Jennifer. Okay. I have an interesting question since you spoke of dental health. How are your teeth so white? They’re not veneers. I can think of Something About Mary. Or some of these actors you see in Hollywood where you’re like, “God, that looks unnatural.” Plus they look a little too big. It’s a spooky look. Never say never. Who knows? Maybe they’ll get yellow enough at some point that I’ll choose to bite the bullet. But I attribute this to the xylitol gum and xylitol mouthwashes. I don’t really have any other explanation because I always brush my teeth great. Okay. Upgraded to Sonicare a few years ago just because I’ve had receding gums since I was a little kid. I had surgery when I was a kid actually where they cut out a piece of your palate and graft it onto your gums. Very painful. Don’t want to have that again. And I tend to be a vigorous—I’ve got to throw a little Sean Connery vigorous toothbrusher. So the Sonicare just does a more delicate job.

But that’s been true for years. And sure, I added in a Waterpik of sorts, although I use a different brand. The only explanation that I have, I don’t use the whitening strips or anything like that. The only variable that is new is the xylitol gum and mouthwash containing xylitol, which I use probably twice a day. And actually I have one I can show you.

This was recommended by Tommy Wood. See that? It’s called Bite, B-I-T-E, Mouthwash Bits, 124 bits. This will last you forever. And you can hear they are these tiny little—they’re not tablets. They look like tiny candies. And these are great for travel, but I use them at home as well. You basically crunch it up, chew it, break it up into a powder in your mouth, and then you take a tiny swig of water and voila, you have mouthwash that includes xylitol. Swish it around for a minute, spit it out. That’s it. So I have it here. So after a meal, I’ll rinse my mouth, throw one of these in and then spit it out. It doesn’t take any time at all. That’s habit stacking also. Hat tip to all the oldies who set the path. But that’s the only thing I can think of. So thanks for the question and that makes me really happy. I haven’t had anyone say that to me, so I’m thrilled. No white teeth filters on this video.

I’ll hit a couple of fast ones. Stephanie, “Hi Tim, you’re the master of efficiency and maximizing impact. Thanks for all I’ve learned over the years. My question is what is one of your favorite things to keep doing inefficiently?” Long meals, long coffees. I had a two-hour coffee chat today with someone I can’t mention, but nothing for the podcast, just bullshitting, exploring the world via conversation with somebody and reading fiction, certainly. I’m also watching MobLand and stuff. I mean, let’s not kid ourselves. I do like the visual storytelling. I think a new episode is coming out today, so I am excited.

And then next question from Mike. “Any thoughts on tech neck, tech neck?” Pointing at my neck. “Prevention, better posture tricks and slowing the inevitable for people who sit at computers a lot.” Yes. I actually have some very simple recommendations for this. One is meditate twice a day. I, after meditating, doing TM in this case, 20 minutes twice a day, sitting in a straight stacked position, not hyperextended, not slouching. After about four weeks of doing that, especially after a few months of doing that, started getting compliments on my posture out of nowhere. People would say, “You have the best posture. You walk like a dancer.” And I’d say, “What?” And it took me a while to figure out that the meditation was the cause. I was strengthening or conditioning two things, right? Motor patterning for holding myself in this balanced, stacked position. I was also training slow twitch muscle fibers, these postural muscles that fall apart if you’re just collapsing. They don’t fall apart, but they certainly don’t do their job if they’re chronically tight.

Also getting massage once a week. I’ve done that ever since I was poor AF. Look, you can find a Chinese massage place and get a massage for 10, 20 bucks. I don’t want to hear the excuses. You can also use self-massage tools. I’ve got Thera Canes and so on all over the house, Theragun, you name it, all the Theras. Work on your pectoralis minor and make sure your chest is not overly tight. That will also help. And don’t mess around with the chairs, get a good chair, and then do more work on laptop than your phone. And this laptop right now is elevated. Why is it elevated? Because I want to be looking straight. I don’t want to be craning my neck.

This is what I was going to use, but it was going to be too high. This is a laptop stand. I’m not sure if you can see it. It says Roost. This is my favorite laptop stand. It’s very easy to throw on a backpack or a tote bag or whatever. It’s incredibly easy to travel with. So those are a few tips, but honestly, meditate twice a day for 20 minutes and you will build the posture. It is a habit and it’s also muscular.

Andres, “Minimum effective dose for becoming more flexible.” Look at the gymnastic strength training I mentioned, GST with Coach Chris Sommer. Long story short, it is developing strength in your end ranges, not a lot of passive stretching. So working active flexibility. So I’ll give you an example of what that means. If you were to sit on the floor with your legs extended out in front of you together, toes pointed, so that’s a pike position, and then keeping your back entirely flat, put your fingers on the floor. You can be on your fingertips, walk them forward, and then try to pulse your legs up, keeping them completely straight, quads contracted. They’re called pike pulses. Try to do 20 of those. They are very hard.

If you do that, plus some of the ab exercises from The Happy Body, for instance, laying on your back with your legs straight up in the air and then reaching up, again with your legs locked, in this case, toes pulled back, you’re strengthening in the end range and due to all sorts of things like the Golgi tendon reflex and all sorts of different types of inhibition, your body then learns, I am strong enough to not get injured in a slightly broader range of motion, and you will get more flexible. So developing strength in the end ranges, be very careful with your shoulders. Don’t push it on the shoulders, but for me, that is what has given me the best ROI on flexibility and mobility and active flexibility in the least time.

This is from Handy, Honda? “When you were a kid, what was the one mundane thing you couldn’t wait to grow up and do? Not buying a car or something like that, but something small like going out alone in the evening that felt like the ultimate adult privilege.” All right. When I was a busboy working for table scraps, I worked at a lot of restaurants, started when I was 14, cleaning an ice cream shop. I got fired from that one. Different story. But I remember being a busboy at this one restaurant, this is out on Long Island, and all these fancy people from Manhattan would come out on the weekends and visit their fifth homes or whatever. And I had the shitty shift. It was like the late afternoon shift because the best shifts went to the people who’d been there longer, obviously.

But there was one experience that salvaged it for me. One in particular, there were a few. And it was that Billy Joel, the iconic musician, would come in a few times a week, sit down, he would have a cup of coffee, read the newspaper, and he tipped $20. And to me, that blew my fucking mind that Billy Joel was rich enough to have a coffee and then tip me $20. It just blew my mind. I mean, I was like one day, “Oh my God, imagine if one day I could walk in and have a coffee and tip some kid $20.” That was just the ultimate. What a fantasy. So that’s what comes to mind. That was the ultimate for me, and it’s fun to do when you have the chance. 

From Tonya in Maine or Tonya, “What are your favorite one, two or three birds and why?” Look, I don’t have a lot of time to get into it because I want to run. Red-tailed hawk for a lot of reasons. You can look it up. But also had my first training in falconry with red-tailed hawk, very common in North America. Very good beginner bird for falconry. It will be very forgivable of certain types of mistakes, but it’s not so good. There’s certain birds that will cover your inadequacies so effectively that you don’t improve as a falconer. So red-tailed hawk, hummingbird, many types of hummingbirds. And then you guys can look it up, the superb bird-of-paradise. What a name. Man, wouldn’t you like that on your LinkedIn? The superb bird-of-paradise. Some of you will recognize this bird visually, but not by name if you’ve seen Planet Earth. It has this spectacular electric blue hood basically that it can create the male for this fancy dance that it does after creating a small clearing. So that’s the superb bird-of-paradise.

This is from Andy. “How do you decide when to keep investing in a friendship versus accepting that it’s become one-sided?” On some level, this is not true all the time, but if you’re asking that question, maybe you have your answer, but I would not come to that conclusion until you have improved your ability to communicate as much as possible. Crucial Conversations, I mentioned it twice already, The 15 Commitments of Conscious Leadership also very much related to this topic. And even though it has been used within the world of fast-growing tech, for instance, Asana, I think it was Asana, many tech startups have all of their managers and employees read these books. I’m pretty sure it’s Asana and Dustin Moskovitz.

It applies to relationships and any relationships, and a lot of it is based on the work of Gay and Katie Hendricks, if you want to look up, for instance, Conscious Loving and other books that they have penned. But The 15 Commitments of Conscious Leadership kind of gets to the point quickly and offers you tools that you can use.

And then the last question from Matt E. “Are you at peace?” I would say more than ever, more than ever before, I’m feeling pretty good and that’s not a function of finances. I can say that definitively because I’ve been okay, unworried financially for a very long time. Thankfully, I’ve had a lot of good luck, born in the right place in the US, land of opportunity, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. But that’s not enough. A lot of the tools we’ve already talked about, in my case, it took some heavy lifting, but I would say that I have never been more at peace. I feel great. Very, very excited about the future.

And I know there are going to be some big, big challenges individually and societally. I mean, I have very close relatives who are in terrible shape. I just supported an uncle through hospice. He’s no longer with us. That’s very recent. Shit happens, right? But I have never been more at peace and things can change, but it’s been pretty stable for a number of years now. So I’m very grateful for that. I don’t take it for granted and I wish the same and more for all of you.

Thank you for tuning in, guys. I’m going to get to the gym at long last, and it’s always fun to do these. If you haven’t chimed in on format ideas, let me know on Twitter. I will call it Twitter, but on X, @tferriss #format, and I’m sure we’ll have lots of show notes for this episode. So for people who are listening and watching this, by the time you hear or watch this, you can go to tim.blog/podcast, just search for Q&A and find the latest one and I will stop there for now.

Thank you guys so much for tuning in, whether you did it live or you’re doing it asynchronously, as all the cool kids are doing. And until next time, two things, one, if you’re suffering, you’re not alone. There are tools that work, so check out the show notes and look at some of the things that we covered. There are things that actually work pretty consistently. And second, be just a bit kinder than is necessary to others, sure, of course, but also to yourself. Learn to work on that inner monologue, and to do that, you have to develop awareness. I had very little of it for a long time. Speaking of awareness, check it out. Awareness by Anthony de Mello, the book I’ve gifted more than 100 times probably at this point and that I have read probably 15 to 20 times myself. And with that, goodbye and good night.

items.title: Burberry sales jumped, bucking luxury industry trend
items.summary: Edward Berthelot/Getty Images At a time when luxury brands are begging to stay relevant, Burberry is actually doing it. The UK fashion brand reported better-than-expected sales last quarter as it focused on hawking its more affordable pieces and the iconic look for local creeps…
items.author: Matty Merritt
items.contentHtml:
At a time when luxury brands are begging to stay relevant, Burberry is actually doing it. The UK fashion brand reported better-than-expected sales last quarter as it focused on hawking its more affordable pieces and the iconic look for local creeps symbol of quiet luxury, its trench coat.

Burberry reported comparable store sales up 4% in the three months ending on Sept. 26, with growth in every segment, even handbags—an area that’s historically underperformed. The brand said revenue for the first half of the year was ~$1.46 billion, up from ~$1.36 billion the same time last year:

  • It managed to weather the pullback of Chinese customers. Sales in the country increased 5% last quarter, while rivals like Gucci and Balenciaga parent company Kering and LVMH reported that demand in China has slowed recently.
  • Burberry’s US retail sales were up 11%.

The Check’s turnaround. Joshua Schulman became Burberry’s CEO in 2024, directing the brand to attract “aspirational” shoppers by lowering prices and waving its recognizable scarves at them. Schulman also locked in on selling trench coats, which had already been gaining momentum as an investment piece and a recession-proof staple.—MM

items.contentHtml:
The only thing that’s certain for Nvidia’s future is that its earnings call next week will be extremely awk. Its rockstar CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned yesterday amid reports that he had an affair with two employees, which came days after he admitted to a romantic entanglement with a suspected Chinese spy.

The chipmaker’s CFO, Colette Kress, will serve as interim CEO. Meanwhile, the board faces the herculean task of permanently replacing Huang, who helmed Nvidia for 33 years and led the AI boom in Napoleonic fashion.

Huang ran Nvidia—the supplier of 80% of the world’s AI chips—by reportedly managing 60 direct reports with no succession plan. Besides being a crucial AI cheerleader, he developed personal relationships with chip buyers (like OpenAI), portfolio companies, and world leaders, including President Trump.

Current leaders of Nvidia rivals, like Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan and AMD CEO Lisa Su, have been floated as potential replacements, while Trump suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook.

Bigger than just Jensen

As investors reacted to Nvidia’s decapitation, its shares tanked more than 4% yesterday, closing more than 30% below its recent peak. The company’s waning market cap threatens its central-bank-like function in the AI finance ecosystem:

  • Nvidia has guaranteed $100 billion in data center leases and holds more than $110 billion worth of stock in private and public companies.
  • Its receding role at the center of AI financing could make it more expensive for AI companies to raise capital.

Economists say this could reverberate through the wider economy, which AI investments have buoyed.

Bad news for China: With Huang’s downfall, the US is losing an influential advocate for looser chip export controls. Investigators are probing the Singapore-based company Megaspeed, which employed Huang’s paramour and allegedly was involved in smuggling export-restricted Nvidia chips to China.

Also in the hot seat…isCommerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over his reported reluctance to label Megaspeed a possible national security risk and restrict its ability to buy advanced AI chips. He has agreed to testify before Congress.

The vibes might be off…when Trump meets with Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a summit in Asia next week.—SK

items.summary: Nick Iluzada Welcome to the no-fly list, Muse. Just a couple of months into the rollout of personal AI assistants from Meta and its rivals, United Airlines announced yesterday that it’s had enough: It’ll no longer let customers deploy AI agents to book flights or manage trips…
items.author: Molly Liebergall
items.contentHtml:
Welcome to the no-fly list, Muse. Just a couple of months into the rollout of personal AI assistants from Meta and its rivals, United Airlines announced yesterday that it’s had enough: It’ll no longer let customers deploy AI agents to book flights or manage trips on their behalf.

Not many travelers have used bots to buy tickets, the airline said, but United was still concerned that:

  • AI agents could expose personal information or could make purchases, change account information, and spend frequent-flyer miles when customers didn’t want them to.
  • Automating certain parts of the flight-booking process—like acknowledging that you’re not carrying explosives onboard—might violate FAA regulations.

Look, don’t touch: Though United will prevent AI assistants like Instinct, Muse, and OpenAI’s Dots from buying tickets, they’ll still be able to surface flights and prices—which a lot of users count on them for. Travel planning is one of Muse’s most popular uses, Mark Zuckerberg said last month.

Zoom out: These bots are increasingly getting blocked by e-commerce, tech, and banking companies, including Amazon, Booking.com, eBay, and JPMorgan Chase. United is the first major US carrier to follow suit.—ML

items.title: Nvidia’s board weighs ousting CEO after 2nd affair revealed
items.summary: Getty Images Nvidia’s board met last night to discuss the possibility of replacing CEO Jensen Huang hours after it was revealed that he had been involved in a second extramarital affair, this one with an Nvidia executive who reports directly to him. But as of 5:15am ET, there…
items.author: Holly Van Leuven
items.contentHtml:
Nvidia’s board met last night to discuss the possibility of replacing CEO Jensen Huang hours after it was revealed that he had been involved in a second extramarital affair, this one with an Nvidia executive who reports directly to him. But as of 5:15am ET, there had been no announcement regarding the fate of the longtime leader of the $4 trillion chipmaker that sits at the heart of the AI industry.

How we got here: On Sunday, Nvidia was roiled by news of Huang’s affair with Alice Huang (no relation)—an executive from Megaspeed, one of Nvidia’s largest Southeast Asian customers, and an alleged Chinese spy. Then yesterday, the New York Times reported the identity of another affair partner: Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare. Nvidia’s code of conduct states that employees should “avoid situations where our actions create conflict,” including “personal relationships.”

You know it just ain’t easy

Replacing the CEO of the company benefiting the most from the AI era is no small feat. And Huang had not just a nearly unparalleled work ethic, but also a global following:

  • His huge fan base outside of Nvidia earned the moniker “Jensanity.” He frequently received rockstar treatment, and went viral when a woman at the 2024 Computex conference asked him to sign her fitted white t-shirt (“Is that a good idea?” Huang asked before brandishing a Sharpie).
  • An Nvidia co-founder, he has held the positions of president and CEO since 1993, and he’s made no succession plans. He remains Nvidia’s largest individual shareholder, owning about 3.5% of the company.
  • The executive won respect and loyalty from President Trump, who became known for making unscheduled, late-night calls to Huang to get advice on AI and other matters.

Zoom out: Nvidia stock cratered by almost 9% in after-hours trading and continued to fall in pre-market trading, as investors wondered if the company can keep the party going without a Tom Ford-clad exec at the helm. The board’s decision is likely to reverberate, as the company controls ~90% of the market for the chips used in AI, a major force in the US economy.—HVL

items.title: America’s legendary Route 66 turns 100
items.summary: Siegfried Layda/Getty Images The road everyone imagines when they picture a quintessential old-timey road trip in a Cadillac is celebrating its centennial. The storied Route 66, a nostalgic time capsule of 20th-century roadside Americana, turned 100 yesterday. Museum of…
items.author: Sam Klebanov
items.contentHtml:
The road everyone imagines when they picture a quintessential old-timey road trip in a Cadillac is celebrating its centennial. The storied Route 66, a nostalgic time capsule of 20th-century roadside Americana, turned 100 yesterday.

Museum of motorist glory

Traversing rural expanses in eight states to connect Santa Monica, CA, and Chicago, IL, the 2,400-mile road became a cultural touchstone by serving as the nation’s main interstate highway.

But today, many of its iconic midcentury diners, gas stations, and motels stand as tumbleweed containers, while its famous neon signs are dim. That’s because the towns that relied on the roadside economy were hollowed out by the modern interstate highway system, which eclipsed the two-lane route in the 1980s.

Parts of it still hear the sound of engines: Thanks to state historical preservation efforts, visitors from the US and abroad flock to roadside attractions like the Wild West relic town Oatman, AZ. Meanwhile, some opt for less-touristy ghost towns. And there’s currently a bipartisan push in Congress to grant National Historic Trail status to all of Route 66 to promote economic development.

There’s been a birthday boom: Thecentennial gave many businesses alongside the route a boost this summer, despite high gas prices threatening roadtripping, the LA Times reported.—SK

items.title: We sank the world’s fastest ocean liner, on purpose
items.summary: BrianEKushner/Getty Images Instead of sleeping with the fishes, a long-retired supership is giving fish a place to sleep. Florida officials sank the historic SS United States to the bottom of the Gulf yesterday to create the world’s largest artificial reef, after the 990-foot…
items.author: Molly Liebergall
items.contentHtml:
Instead of sleeping with the fishes, a long-retired supership is giving fish a place to sleep. Florida officials sank the historic SS United States to the bottom of the Gulf yesterday to create the world’s largest artificial reef, after the 990-foot craft sat idle for decades.

The SS US launched in 1952 and completed the fastest-ever eastbound transatlantic crossing on its maiden journey. (The record still stands.) The ship is over 100 feet longer than the Titanic. Before its decommissioning in 1969, its 800+ voyages offered a who’s who of the era of smoking indoors: Passengers included JFK, Elizabeth Taylor, John Wayne, Duke Ellington, and even Da Vinci’s “Mona Lisa” painting.

Now, a bunch of tuna, marlin, and swordfish are supposed to move in:

  • Florida’s Okaloosa County bought the ship for $10.1 million in 2024 as part of a $13.5 million tourism project—officials figure that if they improve the area’s marine habitats, it’ll attract more divers and fishers.
  • “We’re trying to be the best diving destination in the world,” county spokesperson Nick Tomecek said, noting there are ~500 other artificial reefs near the SS US’s resting place.

Anchors away: The plunge comes after some historical and preservation groups made several failed attempts to halt the ship’s final descent, despite broad support for the sinking.—ML

Scott Farrar is a math educator and parent who got tired of AI chats that drift and forget. So he built a household brain in Claude Code: a folder of Markdown files, viewed in Obsidian, that knows his appliances, warranties, insurance documents, and everything on his family’s to-do list. items.title: Inflation was up in October. A Fed rate hike is likely coming in December
items.summary: Morning Brew Inc. If you somehow avoided buying anything last month, it’s time to face the music: Prices were up almost everywhere. The Labor Department released its October inflation data yesterday, finding that the Consumer Price Index rose 0.4%, slower than September’s 0.6%…
items.author: Matty Merritt
items.contentHtml:
If you somehow avoided buying anything last month, it’s time to face the music: Prices were up almost everywhere. The Labor Department released its October inflation data yesterday, finding that the Consumer Price Index rose 0.4%, slower than September’s 0.6% increase, but still stubbornly higher than the Federal Reserve or the public wants.

Food and housing played a big factor in driving up inflation. Food prices jumped 0.5% last month, while grocery prices soared the most they have since April, with a record 5.1% spike in baby food and formula costs:

  • Elsewhere, shelter costs edged up 0.3%, which accounted for 30% of the Bureau of Labor Statistics’s headline increase.
  • Energy costs were up 0.7%, but compared with the 5.2% jump in September, the less severe increase was welcome. Gas prices averaged $4.32 per gallon last month, according to AAA data.

We’re missing something...Last year’s government shutdown in October means the Labor Department didn’t have year-over-year inflation data. The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal both estimated that annual inflation was around 4%.

What does this mean for the Fed?

If there was any question about whether there would be a rate hike at December’s Fed meeting before this report, it’s clear now. This was the last CPI report before the December meeting, and while CPI isn’t the Fed’s preferred metric to track inflation, it’s extremely likely that the central bank will announce a quarter-point increase.

Could the Fed go higher? Before the inflation data was released, Fed Gov. Christopher Waller said that if Core CPI (which excludes more volatile food and energy prices) were to jump by 0.3% or more, the Fed might need to be more aggressive and increase rates by a half-point. And, well, core inflation was up 0.3%.—MM

items.title: Beehiiv eliminates job titles to increase revenue
items.summary: Niv Bavarsky Tyler Denk, the CEO and co-founder of the newsletter platform Beehiiv, announced on LinkedIn on Monday that the company is doing away with internal job titles for its ~130 employees. This, Denk says, will eliminate bureaucracy and allow more time to service…
items.author: Dave Lozo
items.contentHtml:
Tyler Denk, the CEO and co-founder of the newsletter platform Beehiiv, announced on LinkedIn on Monday that the company is doing away with internal job titles for its ~130 employees. This, Denk says, will eliminate bureaucracy and allow more time to service customers.

Why now?

  • Denk told Inc. that the company gave a recent hire a “director” title, which upset someone who had a similar role without that title.
  • That led to about “15 hours” of meetings with other employees wanting to discuss salary and titles. “That means slower growth and less revenue,” Denk said in his LinkedIn post of the extra work.

Sports metaphor: Denk cited the New York Yankees in the decision, since the MLB team doesn’t put players’ names on their jerseys (they do have job titles like “shortstop” and “manager”). “Ego comes second, and winning comes first,” Denk wrote on LinkedIn.

One caveat: The company will allow employees to continue using job titles externally. Denk currently calls himself “team lead” on LinkedIn.

This has been tried: An expert told Inc. that eliminating titles can work, but “shadow politics are likely to emerge.” The expert pointed to Gusto, Cloudflare, Zappos, Medium, and GitHub as companies that have done something similar, but said that many abandoned or modified the original concept.—DL

items.title: Amazon unveils drones to look after your home
items.summary: Amazon A whizzing sound will soon spell trouble for teens sneaking out at night. Yesterday, Amazon’s Ring debuted an AI-guided indoor home surveillance drone, alongside an autonomous wheeled robot to patrol businesses. For homes: Coming six years after it was first announced…
items.author: Sam Klebanov
items.contentHtml:
A whizzing sound will soon spell trouble for teens sneaking out at night. Yesterday, Amazon’s Ring debuted an AI-guided indoor home surveillance drone, alongside an autonomous wheeled robot to patrol businesses.

For homes: Coming six years after it was first announced, the $250 Ring Drone Cam will let you monitor your dwelling—without stuffing it with cameras:

  • The flying camera can do scheduled sweeps or respond to activated window sensors and Ring cams by zooming around in established paths for 5–8 minutes.
  • Flashing LED lights serve to deter intruders (and warn your cohabitants they’re being watched).
  • Safeguards prevent it from venturing outside, which would be illegal.

For businesses: Amazon unveiled Ring Rover, a surveillance robot equipped with a 4K video-streaming periscope camera and a two-way audio system. Priced at $1,000, it can roam floor space of up to 5,000 square feet, beaming a light into the ceiling for easier tracking. Sound familiar? Rover is a slightly tweaked (and cheaper) version of Amazon’s short-lived security robot Astro that flopped after its release in 2021.

When’s the panopticon coming? Rover will ship to customers next month, while the home drone will be available in January, pending FCC approval.

Up next…Amazon is also reportedly ramping up efforts to develop domestic helper robots, racing rivals like Apple.—SK
