items.title: State of the tech job market: late 2026
items.summary: 👋 Hey there, I’m Lenny. Each week, I share deeply researched product, growth, and career advice. For more: Lenny’s Jobs | Lenny’s Podcast | Lennybot | How I AI | Become an AI-Native Builder and my other favorite AI/PM courses . Subscribe now P.S. Get a full free year of Cursor…
items.author: Lenny Rachitsky
items.contentHtml:
👋 Hey there, I’m Lenny. Each week, I share deeply researched product, growth, and career advice. For more: Lenny’s Jobs | Lenny’s Podcast | Lennybot | How I AI | Become an AI-Native Builder and my other favorite AI/PM courses.

Subscribe now

P.S. Get a full free year of Cursor, Notion, Replit, Lovable, Wispr Flow, Linear, ElevenLabs, PostHog, Granola, Brain.fm, Waking Up, and more, by becoming an Insider subscriber (while supplies last). Learn more.

Welcome to my latest job market report, my second of 2026. Of the five reports I’ve done over the past few years, this one is the most surprising and interesting.

Here’s what we’re seeing right now:

  1. PMs seem to be winning in the AI era

  2. Engineering demand has stalled

  3. Design is at a record low

  4. Everybody now needs to AI

  5. Tech jobs are concentrating in the Bay Area

  6. Remote is at a record low

  7. The tech job market is growing fast, but mostly outside of software (gasp!)

This analysis is based on two proprietary datasets that I love working with: TrueUp, which powers Lenny’s Jobs and tracks global jobopenings at tech companies (over 9,000 companies). The second dataset comes from Live Data Technologies, which tracks job changes (hires, departures, and promotions) for 124 million professionals, and their hiring numbers below are specifically for the U.S. Looking at these together, we can triangulate common trends, and the differences between the datasets are themselves revealing. Thank you, Amit Taylor and Alex Hamilton, for sharing this amazing data with us. 🙏

Let’s get into it.

P.S. If you’re looking for a job, check out Lenny’s Jobs!

Takeaway 1: Product managers seem to be benefiting most in the AI era

There’s been a lot of talk about AI replacing product managers (“who needs ’em!”). But so far, the data is showing the exact opposite. There are more open PM roles than at any point in nearly four years, up 75% from the March 2023 low, and PM openings have grown faster than any other core tech role since the start of 2023 (+56%, compared with +43% for engineering).

When we look at hiring numbers vs. just job openings, the story gets more interesting. Even though open roles are growing, actual hiring for every core product role has been flat or in decline over the past few years (see takeaway 7 for which roles are now growing fastest). But PM hiring has held up the best (by far). And PM is the only one of the five core roles whose share of hiring grew (from 16% in 2021 to 21% today).

The fact that we’re seeing growth in PM openings(first set of charts) but a flat line and even a decline in hiring (second set of charts) tells me that there’s growing demand for PMs, but that landing great PMs is getting harder.

Takeaway 2: Demand for engineers is plateauing

For the first time in the history of this report, engineering job openings have stalled. Open engineering roles grew 29% through 2024, 15% through 2025, and just 2.5% this past year. There are fewer open eng roles at tech companies today than there were even this past March.

The hiring data shows the same slowdown. Companies in the U.S. hired about 113,000 software engineers over the past 12 months (May 2025 to April 2026)—less than half the 2022 peak (239,000). And the number has dropped every year since 2022.

Just like with PMs, engineeringjob openings are up while actual hiring is down (+44% vs. −17% since January 2024), so even as demand slows, landing great engineers is getting harder too.

Two bright spots for engineers: One, demand for tech recruiters is on an absolute tear. We’re hitting record highs: open recruiter roles are up nearly 300% since mid-2023. This may be a leading indicator of a reacceleration of eng hiring, which we’ll be watching closely.

Another bright spot is that in terms of absolute numbers, engineering is still the largest category of tech hiring, by far. Over 120,000 engineers were hired just in the U.S. in 2025. And there are still plenty of great engineering jobs out there. Over 65,000 to be exact.

One additional new trend to watch within the engineering function is the rise of the forward deployed engineer (FDE). FDE openings are exploding. Historically, there have been only a few dozen open FDE roles globally (mostly at Palantir), but openings started climbing in 2025 and are up 4.6x in the past year alone! There are currently around 1,500 open FDE roles. Note that this growth is likely a combination of increased demand for this job along with other job categories, like “sales engineer,” being rebranded as “FDE.” Either way, FDE is so hot right now.

Also, a telling trend: security engineering is one of the fastest-growing specialties, right behind FDEs. On the flip side, demand for mobile and front-end engineers has been nearly halved in the past year. That’s wild. I think the story here is the collapse of specialized/siloed engineering disciplines, with smaller eng teams having broader ownership (thanks to AI).

Takeaway 3: Demand for designers continues to hit record lows

Unfortunately for my designer friends, design roles continue to decline. There are only about 1,900 open product design roles1 at tech companies globally right now. Not that much higher than just open FDE roles. It’s the lowest we’ve seen since we started tracking, and down 28% from a year ago. 😥

Actual hiring data from Live Data Technologies tells the same story. U.S. companies hired about 12,600 product designers over the past 12 months, less than half as many as in 2022 (27,600), and the number has fallen every year since.

Even more telling, the ratio of open PM roles to open design roles is trending further and further toward PM. There are now 3.8 open PM roles for every open design role. This is up from 2.6 earlier this year and 1.9 in early 2023.

I’m hopeful this turns around, as companies recognize that great design can be a huge differentiator and help their product stand out in an increasingly noisy (and AI-slop-y) market. Katie Dill’s talk about AI and design recently became my most-watched video of all time, so there’s hope.

Sadly, user research has been hit even harder than design. Only about 1,800 user researchers were hired in the U.S. over the past year, down 66% from 5,300 in 2022, the steepest drop of any role we looked at, and hiring fell another 22% from the year before. What hiring remains is concentrated at a few big companies. In 2025, Meta and Google alone made about one in eight of all U.S. user research hires, and so far in 2026, Google is the only company to have hired 50 or more. And there are currently only 108 open UXR jobs at tech companies globally.

My theory is that the increasing pace of product development is responsible. Just as there’s less time for the traditional design process, there’s also less time for (and interest in) the traditional user research process. For better or worse, teams are becoming more comfortable releasing products earlier to avoid falling behind, and learning and iterating post-launch vs. through user research. Also, better UXR tooling (e.g. Listen Labs, Simile) is allowing non-UXR people to do user research themselves. I wonder if UXR as a dedicated function is going extinct . . . 🫣

Takeaway 4: Everybody now needs to AI

When we did this report two years ago, the most mentioned skills in PM job descriptions were SQL, Jira, AWS, and Python. Today, “LLM” is the most mentioned skill in product manager job descriptions.

What’s more, many other AI terms are now some of the most frequently mentioned skills in PM job descriptions. “Claude” is the third most mentioned term, and Cursor, OpenAI, and MCP are in the top eight. SQL, meanwhile, is still holding strong, but as recent podcast guest Emmanuel Ameisen pointed out, we’ll never be better at SQL than AI ever again. So we’ll see how long that lasts. Also, “evals” is gaining momentum (in the top 10)—and I expect this number to grow.

For engineers, “Python” has been the most mentioned skill for years, and it’s still growing! Look at that inflection in early 2025. Three other trends stand out for engineers: (1) “LLM” just passed Java in eng job postings, (2) the general decline of Java over the past year, and (3) the durability of Kubernetes.

Essentially, Python and AI 📈, Java 📉.

For designers, Figma has been mogging every other skill for years. And narrative violation: demand for experience with Figma has actually grown over the past three years.

But as with every other role, AI is ascendant. “Claude” became the second most mentioned skill in designer JDs this spring (crossing CSS!). It’s notable that it’s Claude specifically, vs. “LLM” or ChatGPT. Anthropic seems to be winning the hearts and minds of designers. And Cursor has also edged past CSS. The times, they are a-changin’.

This suggests an answer to the question: If demand for Figma is growing, why has Figma’s stock fallen? Designers may not be dropping Figma, but for the first time in a long time, designers are increasingly reaching for other tools too. And design as a function isn’t growing.

Takeaway 5: Top tech jobs continue to concentrate in the Bay Area

Today, we’re at a record percentage of open tech roles being based in the Bay Area. That’s huge. 15% of all open roles at tech companies are now based in the Bay Area (about one in seven), and the number of open jobs in the Bay Area is up 43% from just a year ago!

The trend is even more pronounced for core product roles. One in four open PM and design roles is now in the Bay Area, and one in five engineering roles. All three are at record highs, and each has nearly doubled its share since 2022.

Takeaway 6: Remote roles continue to decline

The flip side of tech jobs concentrating in the Bay Area is that the number of remote roles continues to decline. Just 14% of open tech roles now offer a remote option, the lowest on record, down from 21% in late 2022.

Remote engineering roles are also at record lows, currently at 14%, and down from the 25% we saw in late 2022. Design is on the same path: 19% of open design roles are remote, down from 34%. PM, however, is the exception, holding steady at about one in five (21%) for the past two years, but still near record lows.

Put all this together, and sometime last year, we crossed a milestone where there are now more open PM/eng/design roles based in the Bay Area than remote roles globally. Remote led almost 2 to 1 in the other direction four years ago.

Takeaway 7: Overall, the tech job market is growing—but outside of software roles (gasp!)

I saved what might be the most interesting takeaway for last.

items.title: MAHA seed oil rejection creates $1 billion industry
items.summary: Morning Brew Inc. Unlike the birds swarming your grandpa’s feeder, many Americans want nothing to do with seeds. Sales of seed-oil-free products soared 72% to $1 billion in the past year, Bloomberg reported yesterday. What’s with the anti-seed sentiment? A legion of MAHA health…
items.author: Sam Klebanov
items.contentHtml:
Unlike the birds swarming your grandpa’s feeder, many Americans want nothing to do with seeds. Sales of seed-oil-free products soared 72% to $1 billion in the past year, Bloomberg reported yesterday.

What’s with the anti-seed sentiment? A legion of MAHA health influencers are promoting theories disputed by scientists that cooking with canola, corn, sunflower, and other seed oils comes with health risks. Instead, they recommend using butter, beef tallow, and olive oil. They say seed oils lack valuable nutrients, contain toxins, and cause inflammation. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. says the oils are behind the surge in obesity.

Catering to these concerned shoppers, health brands and snack giants, including PepsiCo and Utz Brands, are filling shelves with a cornucopia of munchables cooked in costlier alternatives, including beef tallow.

What do health experts think?

Dietitians say seed oils are caloric and may lack the benefits of olive oil but are otherwise healthy if consumed in moderation:

  • Moderate intake of seed oils is associated with improved heart health, as seed oils contain unsaturated fats, while animal oils have cholesterol-boosting saturated fats.
  • Human studies have shown no causal link between seed oil consumption and increased inflammation.
  • One expert told NPR that fears about toxins in seed oil-cooked foods are unfounded.

But…Experts still recommend avoiding ultra-processed foods due to their high sugar and salt content—not because they often contain seed oils.—SK

items.title: Nvidia’s problems could be problems for everyone
items.summary: Illustration: Morning Brew Inc., Photo: Soeren Stache/Getty Images Shares of Nvidia fell 4.3% yesterday, after its CEO Jensen Huang admitted on Sunday to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The plunge wiped out nearly $230 billion of value in the world’s second-largest…
items.author: Dave Lozo
items.contentHtml:
Shares of Nvidia fell 4.3% yesterday, after its CEO Jensen Huang admitted on Sunday to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The plunge wiped out nearly $230 billion of value in the world’s second-largest publicly traded company. And Nvidia’s place at the center of the AI industry means Huang’s infidelity could have ramifications beyond your Fidelity 401(k).

The chipmaker has effectively served as the central bank for the AI race with $500 billion in investments to help companies build out their AI infrastructure. Although the Nasdaq surged 2% yesterday, the reverberations from any negative impact the scandal has on Nvidia—especially if the board ultimately decides to take the complicated step of replacing Huang despite there being no clear succession plan—may be felt in all corners of the incestuous AI industry:

  • Nvidia has billions tied up with OpenAI and Anthropic. Both companies rely heavily on Nvidia GPUs, although Anthropic also uses chips from Amazon and Google, while OpenAI is developing its own in-house chips.
  • The chipmaker has lent ~$165 billion to neoclouds in need of a backstop during tumultuous times or early development stages.
  • Nvidia is also the dominant investor in neolabs, the AI startups focused more on research and less on products.

Waves of change

Investors were alreadywary about the future of data centers after Democrats won control of Congress and several governorships in last week’s elections thanks in part to promises to halt construction of new facilities.

In the past, Huang worked wonders to ease US investors’ panicin the face of cheaper open-source AI models emerging from China…but it might be harder to reassure the market from inside a honeypot.

No cheat code for what happens next: While tech leaders are split on whether Huang will remain as CEO at the conclusion of the company’s investigation, many investors favor him staying put.Dan Ives, the senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CNBC that the idea of replacing Huang is “comedy” and that Nvidia is still two to three years ahead of China on AI chips.—DL

items.title: Italians outraged over KFC’s Alps expansion
items.summary: Niv Bavarsky Colonel Sanders is about to have that classic American tourist experience where you go to Italy and get an unshakable feeling that nobody wants you there. Except in this case, the Colonel’s fried chicken business really isn’t welcome. KFC recently announced it’s…
items.author: Molly Liebergall
items.contentHtml:
Colonel Sanders is about to have that classic American tourist experience where you go to Italy and get an unshakable feeling that nobody wants you there. Except in this case, the Colonel’s fried chicken business really isn’t welcome. KFC recently announced it’s set to open two locations in the Italian Alps next month, igniting backlash from locals who think it will stain the area’s luxurious reputation and authentic Alpine cuisine.

The first fast-food joint on any Italian ski slope: KFC Italy said the new restaurants—set to open on Dec. 5 on the mountains of Cortina d’Ampezzo and Madonna di Campiglio in the Dolomites—are aimed at surprising people and “reaching places” where you wouldn’t expect to find them.

KFC got the surprise part right:

  • Local officials have reportedly asked mountain operators to reconsider the KFC plans after being caught off guard by the finger-lickin’ news.
  • Alberico Zardini, the largest shareholder in a company that manages ski lifts in Cortina, told a local publication that he will pursue legal action against mountain executives if they go ahead with this “disgraceful,” “absurd,” “shameful,” and “mad decision.”

The wing that broke the camel’s back? Between throngs of visitors waiting to take selfies at historic sites, and noise pollution from helicopters and loud DJ sets, Dolomites locals were already concerned that a tourism boom was eroding their Alpine traditions.—ML

items.author: Claire Vo
items.contentHtml:
Anthropic just released Fable 5.2, their new frontier model, and I spent two days actually building things with it before recording this. I made an animated marketing video from a single tweet, assembled a pile of unboxed furniture using only blurry floor photos, and extended our CXO brand sprites into a full bug-defense game complete with a trailer. In this episode I walk through what impressed me, what fell short, and how I’m thinking about routing tasks between Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5 going forward.

Listen or watch on YouTube, , or Apple Podcasts

What you’ll learn:

  1. What Anthropic launched with Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, and when to reach for Fable instead of Opus 5.5

  2. My pros and cons after a couple of days of hands-on testing

  3. How Fable 5.2 turned a tweet and a brand book into an animated video that doesn’t look like slides

  4. The geometry test every other model failed: assembly instructions for flat-pack furniture with no manual

  5. How it handled a real re-architecture of ChatPRD’s product intelligence pipeline

  6. Why I still wouldn’t let it design a website on its own

  7. The 3D typewriter it built me, and how you can get access to the model

In this episode, we cover:

(00:00) Confessions of a Claude hater

(02:54) What Anthropic launched: Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2

(03:16) When to use Fable 5.2 vs. Opus 5.5

(03:30) Black holes, coding claims, and benchmarks

(04:40) Guardrails and anti-distillation safeguards

(05:12) My high-level pros and cons

(07:23) Video generation: turning a tweet into an animated film

(09:47) Animating the invader bots

(11:29) Flat-pack furniture with no instructions

(13:09) The bug factory game and its trailer

(15:16) Real engineering: re-architecting ChatPRD’s product intelligence pipeline

items.contentHtml:
How this founder built a better Duolingo with Codex | William Imoh

Listen now on YouTube • • Apple Podcasts

Brought to you by:

  • WorkOS—Make your app enterprise-ready, with SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and more

  • Vanta—Automate compliance and simplify security

William Imoh is the founder of Hackmamba and the creator of Mural, an AI language tutor he built after a 1,000-day Duolingo streak still left him unable to hold a conversation in Norwegian. In this episode, he shows how he used Codex and GPT-Live to build native iOS and Android apps despite having no Swift or Kotlin experience, and explains how he designed Mural to teach through complete immersion. He also walks through the Lord of the Rings–themed team of Grok Bots that helps him run a 25-person company, from Gandalf as chief of staff to Legolas in marketing and Aragorn in sales.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. When agents write the code, the programming languages you know matter far less. William had never written Swift, but he wanted Mural to feel truly native, so Codex built it in Swift for iOS and Kotlin for Android. The technical stack followed the product vision, not the skills of the founder.

  2. Taste is often just design judgment expressed clearly. William told Codex to create a minimal, Apple-quality app that felt like autumn. When the first version came back in dark mode, he redirected it toward warm colors, gradients, and a lighter visual style.

  3. Product management experience translates directly into better prompting. William structures his requests as epics and user stories tied to specific user problems. That discipline gives the agent clearer goals and consistently produces stronger results.

  4. Real-time voice is finally good enough to build around, but it remains expensive. William says Mural would not have been possible without GPT-Live-1. A 30-minute session costs roughly $3 to $5, which is expensive for software but still cheaper than an on-demand human tutor.

  5. Agents feel more like colleagues when they have clear identities and jobs. William’s Grok Bot team includes Gandalf as chief of staff, Legolas in marketing, Elrond in engineering, and other Lord of the Rings characters across the business. The personas make each agent’s responsibilities easier to understand and delegate to.

  6. Useful context comes from access, not longer prompts. William connected his agents to Google Workspace, Linear, Notion, Pipedrive, QuickBooks, his calendar, and browser tools. He grants broad access by default, while keeping banking and customer data protected.

  7. The future may be custom systems of record with AI on top. William built Three Pipes, an internal HR tool that combines email, calendar, and meeting notes to track and rank candidates. Instead of adapting his workflow to generic software, he created the database his company actually needed.

  8. Better models reduce the need for elaborate skill libraries. Most of William’s skills became unnecessary as the underlying models improved. The few that survived encode durable expertise, including growth strategy, content strategy, and removing AI-style writing.

  9. When an agent stalls, restart with clearer instructions and add a reviewer. William begins a fresh session, breaks the task into steps, and asks the agent to inspect its own work. He also uses Grok Bot to review Cursor’s output.

items.title: Chefs are having reservations about ‘best-of’ lists
items.summary: A scene from inside Disfrutar, a previous The 50 winner. Europa Press News/Getty Images Of all the ways for a chef to taste success, being named the world’s best restaurant has to be one of the sweetest. This year, Asador Etxebarri in Atxondo, Spain, gets to Basque in the glory…
items.author: Brendan Cosgrove
items.contentHtml:
Of all the ways for a chef to taste success, being named the world’s best restaurant has to be one of the sweetest. This year, Asador Etxebarri in Atxondo, Spain, gets to Basque in the glory of that honor, according to The 50, a group that highlights top-notch hospitality establishments. But—like the food at grill-happy Asador Etxebarri—the whole process is getting flamed.

Meal ticket: Being included on The 50’s list boosts visibility and revenue, but that’s also part of the problem, since an owner’s focus can get caught up in making the list rather than improving their restaurant. Or, as Ivan Brehm, the chef-owner of Michelin-starred Nouri in Singapore, told CNBC, “Guides and lists now shape the industry they claim to assess.”

Making the list takes effort, too: Ana Roš, whose Hiša Franko restaurant in Slovenia was ranked 60th, opted to skip this year’s best-of event in Lima, Peru, saying the award ecosystem demands significant time, money, and work commitments, like press events and international travel.

It’s not just restaurants: According to finance platform Tide, the average UK worker spends about 2.8 hours per week on self-promotion, which can include vocalizing wins in meetings and writing performative LinkedIn posts that do things like describe brewing a pot of coffee as “optimizing liquidity ratios.”—BC

items.title: Nvidia CEO admits to extramarital affair with suspected Chinese agent
items.summary: Nadja Wohlleben/Getty Images Yesterday, Nvidia revealed that it was investigating co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang after he told the board that Alice Huang (no relation), his close business contact whom US intelligence determined to be a spy for the Chinese government, was also…
items.author: Holly Van Leuven
items.contentHtml:
Yesterday, Nvidia revealed that it was investigating co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang after he told the board that Alice Huang (no relation), his close business contact whom US intelligence determined to be a spy for the Chinese government, was also his extramarital affair partner.

In a statement to employees, Jensen Huang said, “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

A company spokesman revealed that Huang would remain in charge during the probe, and its board said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.”

Potential ramifications

Lascivious details aside, the situation offers a unique test for the massively valuable semiconductor company. According to Bloomberg:

  • Nvidia’s unconventional organizational structure, designed by Huang—who famously dreamed up his company at a Denny’s—has the CEO overseeing about 60 direct reports tasked with “rapidly implementing his decisions.”
  • Huang has said that keeps the company agile, but it also makes him hard to replace. He has stated publicly that he wants to maintain his role for decades to come.
  • Nvidia doesn’t have a public succession plan, and Huang’s “relentless” schedule means no one is prepared to replace him promptly if the board ever seeks his removal.

This complicates the US–China race for AI supremacy. President Trump has blocked Nvidia’s most advanced chips, Blackwell and Rubin, from entering China. And even before this revelation, Alice Huang’s company, Megaspeed, was investigated by the Commerce Department on suspicion of smuggling the advanced chips into China.

Asked about Huang’s affair last night, President Trump, who has consulted with the Nvidia CEO on AI policy, told reporters, “He has done an amazing job for our country” and that Huang should stay on as CEO.

Big picture: Nvidia is largely seen as the most powerful driver and beneficiary of the AI stock market boom. Last October, it became the first publicly traded company to reach a valuation of $5 trillion.—HVL

items.title: Robbing museums isn’t as lucrative as it seems
items.summary: Kiran Ridley/Getty Images There have been so many high-profile art heists in the last year that you’d think someone put together a super team of thieves to hit museums. And while the art is worth millions, you can’t exactly use a Renoir to buy a meal, so what becomes of these…
items.author: Dave Lozo
items.contentHtml:
There have been so many high-profile art heists in the last year that you’d think someone put together a super team of thieves to hit museums. And while the art is worth millions, you can’t exactly use a Renoir to buy a meal, so what becomes of these works once they’re stolen?

Items with gold can be melted down, and jewel-encrusted objects can be deconstructed and resold, but hocking paintings can be extremely difficult. Interpol and the FBI maintain stolen art databases, which help buyers avoid unwittingly purchasing pilfered merchandise. But the absconders still have options:

  • There’s the black market, where the art can be sold, but often at a fraction of its value.
  • Some thieves will hold art as ransom or use it to negotiate reduced charges on other crimes.
  • Stolen art can be traded for weapons, as was allegedly the case with the Italian mafia.

Once the art is gone, it’s likely gone forever. While two of the four paintings taken from the Renoir Museum this year were dropped right outside its doors, experts say that less than 10% of swiped artwork is ever recovered, with some saying the true number is just 2%–3%, per Euronews.—DL
